articles.title: Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?
articles.excerpt:
Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities

Simon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bail

About 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, ...
articles.body_text:
Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities

Simon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bail

About 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, up a slip road for deliveries to a B&M homewares store, is a stretch of concrete paving behind a 2-metre wall topped with spikes.

This is the patch of ground that Simon Levy tried to turn into his personal killing field.

Twice he went with women, both of whom were sex workers, to the spot just eight minutes’ walk from the north London home he shared with his mother and sister. The spot is out of sight of CCTV cameras dotted around the area, and in the shadow of the Tottenham Hotspur football stadium.

One victim only just survived the sustained attack, including rape and strangulation, he inflicted on her in January 2025. Another, Sheryl Wilkins, paid with her life in August 2025.

Between those attacks Levy had travelled to south London and, in March 2025, he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.

His double murder trial, which ended in convictions on Friday heard from the survivor. Her testimony, the prosecutor Tom Little KC said during the trial, probably revealed what the other victims suffered.

Little said the victims were vulnerable, and Levy believed that by targeting sex workers he was more likely to get away with his crimes.

The survivor, who is 35 and has her anonymity protected by law, had been trafficked to Britain from eastern Europe.

After they went behind the wall for sex, she asked Levy to pay. He jumped on her with such force he broke her clavicle. While raping her, he also started to strangle her.

She told the Old Bailey jury he said: “Shut up. Be quiet. I have got you.”

She added: “He was sticking his fingers in my throat so I could not make noise. I believe I’m going to die. I could not breathe … I was unconscious completely.”

She awoke feeling “burning and pain”, and was bleeding from her genitals.

Days after the attack, the woman was arrested on another matter. She told officers of her ordeal and said she knew Levy by sight; she knew where he lived but did not know his name. She would later correctly pick Levy out of a police lineup.

The Metropolitan police say she was unable to make a full statement for a further six months, despite their efforts to obtain one. The court heard that she was withdrawing from drug use.

Levy, 40, was linked to the murders by DNA samples from the victims, travel card and phone data, and CCTV footage.

After his arrest, he told police his eye injury, sustained during an assault in 2024, meant he rarely went out. He needed an appropriate adult present when detectives interviewed him and had dyslexia, autism and learning difficulties. He is believed to have been long-term unemployed.

Neighbours knew little about him, and searches of his electronic devices showed some viewing of material about crime, violence and sex.

The attacks on the women in 2025 were not Levy’s first.

Levy is suspected of a sexual assault as far back as 2017, which is still under investigation.

His first convictions came in 2021: one for assaulting a woman at a party in Camden in 2018, putting his hands into her underwear and touching her vagina; another for sexual assault by penetration of a woman on her way to the Notting Hill carnival, having penetrated her with his fingers.

He was in prison first from 2021-23 during which time he sexually assaulted a female prison officer at HMP Brixton.. Searches of his electronic devices showed him writing about his attraction to her.

After his release, he carried out his first attack on a train in October 2023, for which he was only identified later.

In 2024 he allegedly raped a woman in Tottenham. He was recalled to prison to complete the sentence he received in 2021, but not charged over the rape allegation, which is under renewed investigation.

Released from prison later in 2024, he then intensified his attacks on London’s transport network, groping and sexually assaulting women on trains, often by trying to force his fingers into their vagina.

In other offences, the court heard, Levy used “the hustle and bustle of busy, rush-hour trains as his cover”. He would get close to women and conceal his hand with a jumper or coat before attacking them.

Peter Fulton, the head of crime for British Transport Police (BTP), said Levy’s victims, who were mostly in their 20s, were attacked at random and on impulse.

Levy crisscrossed London, armed with a stolen travel card, in one case boarding a train just minutes from his home, at White Hart Lane train station, to attack a woman.

After women reported the offences to BTP, Levy was arrested, charged and bailed.

There were so many signs Levy was a danger, but how clear was it that his offending could turn murderous?

After the first killing, in March 2025, Levy was arrested within days. The cause of death was inconclusive and he was bailed.

Police feel aggrieved that attempts to have Levy remanded in jail in May and June 2025, after he had been charged with several train attacks and was a murder suspect, failed.

The deputy assistant commissioner Kevin Southworth, head of public protection for the Metropolitan police, which investigated the killings, said: “I think on the basis that we put, and BTP put, this man before a court on two occasions and requested remand, I think the obvious conclusion is, had he been remanded at that time … he would have been in prison for sufficient period that he couldn’t have then gone on to commit a murder ….”

Experts in tackling male sexual violence see similarities between Levy’s case and that of Wayne Couzens, the Met officer who kidnapped, raped and murdered Sarah Everard in 2021. Previous, lower-level offending by Couzens, such as exposing himself to women, had been inadequately investigated by police.

Harriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the Levy case “shows a very clear pattern of escalating offending, from sexual assaults of women on public transport to rape and murder … perpetrators can become emboldened and move on to even more dangerous offending.”

Wistrich added: “The failure of the criminal justice system to tackle his offending must have given him the message that it was easy to get away with it.”

Southworth said he accepted crucial questions needed answering. “What did our officers know? And what should they have done, if they didn’t do it? I think one of the points of reflection … for the senior leadership of the Met is how do we, as a collective system, reflect on what went wrong here?”

The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the handling of the case.

The revelations follow scandal after scandal over decades about how the criminal justice system fails women.

Wistrich said: “The scale and variety of failings is shocking – in particular because had they been dealt with appropriately, two women need not have lost their lives.

“It is particularly concerning that this has happened within five years of the horrendous revelations around Met police officers Wayne Couzens and David Carrick, the Baroness Casey report into the Met [which found police to be institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic] …

“This type of scandal tells us little, if anything, has improved in practice.”

Lopez-Reyes entered the country on a visa in November 2016 during the Obama administration. DHS said he was arrested in 2021 on charges of criminal mischief and criminal obstruction of breathing and was ultimately convicted of disorderly conduct.

articles.title: US airfares expected to stay high even if Iran ceasefire drops oil prices, experts say
articles.excerpt:
Domestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacity

Even if a lasting ceasefire between the US and Iran lowers oil prices, travelers ...
articles.body_text:
Domestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacity

Even if a lasting ceasefire between the US and Iran lowers oil prices, travelers hoping to snag cheaper airfare should buckle their seatbelts and expect continued turbulence.

US domestic airfares are 26.5% higher than a year ago, according to June’s consumer price index data, and analysts say prices globally are up 25-30% compared with 2025.

Strong demand for travel and reduced global oil refining capacity caused jet fuel prices to spike during the early weeks of the Iranian war. While prices are off their highs, they remain elevated. Jet fuel was trading about $149 a barrel as of 4 August, up from $90 at the start of 2026 – a 65% increase. Crude-oil prices are up about 30% since January, trading around $76 a barrel.

Jet fuel costs rise slightly higher than oil prices because on average, only about 10% of refined oil can be turned into jet fuel. “The more limited the product, the more vulnerable it is to these supply shocks,” said Louise Burke, the global head of aviation at Argus Media, a commodities data provider.

There have been a “substantial” amount of refinery closures, Burke said, a key to why jet fuel prices have soared so much higher than standard crude oil. A new refinery in west Africa has helped bring on supply, and refiners are making tweaks to boost output to about 12-14% to take advantage of the higher jet fuel prices, which has helped to alleviate some of the shortages.

Jet fuel prices are the biggest operating cost for airlines and the hardest to control, said John Grant, the chief analyst at OAG, an aviation data firm. Cost can range between 30% and 35%.

Airlines have little wiggle room to control the impact of higher jet fuel prices. Some airlines may hedge their fuel costs to limit losses, but others buy on the volatile spot market. Each carrier has a strategy to control costs, such as how they use aircraft or cut routes.

But rising jet fuel prices are just part of the reason for expensive plane tickets. Capacity constraints at Boeing and Airbus have delayed some aircraft deliveries, while the US Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) continued staffing issues has led to fewer flights from some of the biggest airports.

The ongoing US-Iran conflict gives carriers cover to pass along more of the costs. “For the airlines, there’s no better time to do it. When there’s a war on, they’ve got a great excuse,” Grant said.

Demand for flying has also persisted despite higher airfares, giving airlines more leeway to continue charging higher prices.

Burke said demand for jet fuel may be peaking with the summer travel season wrapping up, and if there’s a lasting ceasefire, prices could start to normalize. But the impact on energy prices seen after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has shown that it could take a year or so for prices to normalize.

The current US-Iran conflict may play out differently since there is much more volatility, she added, noting that US jet fuel inventories are at the lower end of a five-year average.

Legacy carriers such as American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines said in recent earnings calls that higher airfares helped to offset some of the higher fuel costs, but the volatility of prices makes it hard to forecast the effects, according to a Reuters report.

While some airlines are profitable, many aren’t. In the best cases, airlines have margins of about 15%, Grant said. Globally, there are about 50 airlines who are very profitable, but many are “surviving on cashflow and revenue generated”.

It’s why he doesn’t expect any significant reduction in airfares in the next year. “There isn’t sufficient capacity to come back into the system to create any sort of price war or discounting,” he said.

Katy Nastro, a spokesperson for the travel service website Going.com, concurred. With Spirit Airlines closing earlier this year, she is watching other low-cost airlines, which have largely not been profitable after the pandemic. The loss of Spirit means less competition for other airlines and potentially higher fares for flyers.

The shoulder season of September into October will be a test to see if travel demand continues. Nastro said travel deals come and go more quickly, a signal that airlines are testing consumer appetite in real time as they try to recoup some of their fuel costs. Airlines could trim some routes this fall in anticipation of people traveling less.

For those wanting to travel during the popular fall and winter holidays, Going is seeing Thanksgiving fares up 19% compared with 2025, which she said, “is pretty stark”.

She also recommends not waiting to buy tickets. “Hoping at this point that the flight price that you’re looking at for Thanksgiving is going to drop by $100 is, I think, wishful thinking,” she said.

articles.title: At least one person dead in California wildfire allegedly sparked by chainsaw
articles.excerpt:
Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county

At least one person has died in a wildfire burning in the foothil...
articles.body_text:
Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county

At least one person has died in a wildfire burning in the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range that officials believed was sparked by a man using a chainsaw.

Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has destroyed seven buildings, scorched more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county and killed a well-known dog breeder in the town of Angels Camp.

In an interview with KCRA, Smith told reporters he did not mean to spark the fire. Monday was his birthday, he said, and he had been using machinery to cut scraps in order collect money for a celebratory meal with his wife.

“I’m so sorry for everything that’s happened,” Smith told the news station. “This is going to destroy my life, one way or another.”

Officials allege that Smith is responsible for “recklessly causing” the blaze on Monday while “operating equipment capable of producing sparks” without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California department of forestry and fire protection. Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges.

In 2018, Smith was charged with igniting another fire, KCRA reported, and was accused of “willfully and unlawfully [setting] fire to any forest, brush, or other flammable material which is on any land that is not his own, or under his legal control, without the permission of the owner, lessee, or agent of the owner or lessee of the land”. He pleaded no contest and received a sentence of 36 months’ probation.

As of Friday morning, the Gann fire had burned more than 10,000 acres and was about 40% contained.

Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home near the town of Angels Camp, the Calaveras county sheriff’s office said. Friends have identified the victim as Susan Solari and a neighbor told CBS Sacramento that she refused to leave her dogs.

“I told them she was there, that her dogs were there and she couldn’t get her dogs out,” Joan Wilson told the outlet. “She wasn’t going to leave them.”

The Gann fire comes amid a grueling fire season in the American west. Three major fires have continued to burn around the city of Spokane in north-eastern Washington and have destroyed at least 800 buildings. A 37-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly sparking one of the fires, and court documents accuse him of studying how to maximize the blaze’s destruction.

No deaths have been reported in Washington. Officials reported on Thursday that cooler temperatures and calmer winds have allowed firefighters to make progress.

articles.title: Beachgoers warned after deadly 'flesh-eating' bacteria kills 5 in southern state
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Marc Siegel shares how to stay protected from the 'flesh-eating' bacteria vibrio vulnificus on 'Fox News Live.'

A potentially deadly "flesh-eating" bacteria has killed five people in Louisiana th...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Marc Siegel shares how to stay protected from the 'flesh-eating' bacteria vibrio vulnificus on 'Fox News Live.'

A potentially deadly "flesh-eating" bacteria has killed five people in Louisiana this year, a sharp rise from the state’s typical death toll.

Health officials are warning beachgoers to take extra precautions before heading into the water.

Vibrio vulnificus is part of a wider group of Vibrio bacteria. Found primarily in warm, coastal waters, it can cause serious, potentially life-threatening infections when contaminated seawater enters an open wound, according to the CDC.

DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER

Infections can also occur when someone eats raw or undercooked shellfish, especially oysters.

The Louisiana Department of Health has reported nine cases and five deaths so far this year. All nine cases were linked to people entering seawater with open wounds, and all of the infected patients had existing medical conditions, officials said.

A potentially deadly "flesh-eating" bacteria has killed five people in Louisiana this year, a sharp rise from the state’s typical death toll. (iStock)

In previous years, the state has averaged seven cases and one death.

Vibrio bacteria are found in higher numbers from May to October, when water temperatures are warmer, the health department noted.

Although infections are rare, Vibrio vulnificus can cause an illness called vibriosis, often marked by vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, as well as potentially severe skin infections.

"People with severe infections may require intensive care or limb amputation," Louisiana health officials warned. "About one in five people with Vibrio vulnificus infection dies, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill."

Vibrio bacteria are found in higher numbers from May to October, when water temperatures are warmer, the health department noted. (Allison Joyce / AFP via Getty Images)

Initial signs and symptoms of a Vibrio skin infection include fever, redness, pain, swelling, warmth, discoloration and discharge, per the CDC.

While healthy people generally experience only mild symptoms, those who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease can face serious health risks.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

If Vibrio vulnificus enters the bloodstream, it can cause advanced illness marked by fever, chills, septic shock and blistering skin lesions.

Some severe cases can cause an infection called necrotizing fasciitis, which is when the flesh around an open wound dies, the CDC cautions. This rare side effect has led to Vibrio vulnificus being described as "flesh-eating bacteria."

The bacterial infection is diagnosed by testing cultures obtained from stool, wounds or blood, according to health officials.

For mild infections, the CDC recommends increasing fluid intake to prevent dehydration.

Those with severe or prolonged infections should receive antibiotics to improve survival rates.

Those with severe or prolonged infections should receive antibiotics to improve survival rates. (iStock)

For patients with infected wounds, surgery may be necessary to remove dead tissue.

About one in five people will die from the infection, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill, the CDC states.

Health officials caution against entering warm saltwater or brackish water if any fresh cuts, scrapes or wounds are present.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

It’s also recommended to avoid consuming raw oysters and other raw shellfish, and to avoid cross-contamination of other foods with raw seafood or its juices.

Protective gloves should be worn when handling raw shellfish.

Those with liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV or thalassemia (a group of hereditary blood disorders) — as well as those who are taking immune-suppressing medications — are at a higher risk of complications and should take extra precautions, the CDC warns.

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

articles.body_text:
Three men who escaped the confines of socialism and communism dive into their upbringing under different dictatorships, and why socialist policies forced them to leave.

In the midst of sunshine and summer breeze, in the land of the free and home of the brave, sit three men, all immigrants who fled their "third-world" countries run on the "nightmare" of socialist policies.

"The record in my city was once that we ha[d] three days long without electricity. There were shortage[s] of water like every day… It's a disaster," Emmanuel Rincón, who fled Venezuela in 2017, told Fox News Digital. "If you live in the USA… you are never going to experience that and you're never going to be able to understand that."

"I have spent almost all my life under the Chavismo [Hugo Chavez] rule and my family were always in opposition of the regime. So I always understand the nightmare that socialism is."

TRUMP EXPANDS CUBA SANCTIONS BEYOND US COMPANIES IN MAJOR CRACKDOWN ON FOREIGN ENABLERS

Emmanuel Rincón, a Venezuelan immigrant who left the country under Maduro's rule in 2017, dives into what it's like living under the socialist policies. (Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi)

"In Cuba, there is no water, no electricity, no freedom, no food, no salary, no clothes, no shoes, nothing," Eliécer Ávila, a Cuban immigrant living in Florida who fled the island in 2017 said.

"And the little that there is, is what [families living in the U.S.] send from here," he added.

Ávila was heavily censored alongside his family as they were fired from their jobs and banned from Havana, the capital of his home island, after a video was leaked to the BBC of him asking a series of "uncomfortable questions" to Ricardo Alarcón, former minister of foreign affairs in Cuba who was at the time the president of the national assembly of the country.

DEMOCRATIC GROUP LAUNCHES $15M WAR ON DSA AFTER SOCIALIST PRIMARY WINS: 'MORTAL DANGER'

Eliécer Ávila, a Cuban immigrant who fled from the island to the United States in 2017 and now works as an influencer and computer engineer in Florida. (Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi)

"I was persona non grata inside the capital in my own country. From there, I started a movement of young people and students that were pro-democracy… which put me in jail more than 40 times," Ávila shared.

During that time, he was invited to a Latin American Studies Association (LASA) event with activists and human rights defenders from around the world.

"After I came back [from that trip], the dictatorship didn’t let me enter back in, and they put me in one of the 50 most wanted terrorists. Me, who doesn’t even have a traffic violation, just because I wanted freedom for Cuba," he said.

EXPERT WHO FLED CUBA WARNS OF ‘VICIOUS CYCLE’ THAT WILL LEAD TO ‘COMMUNISTS IN DOUBLE DIGITS’ IN CONGRESS

Gene Maine, who fled the Soviet Union with his mother in 1981, recalls the "third world" of communism he grew up under. (Nikolas Lanum)

A similar sentiment was echoed by Gene Maine, an immigrant who escaped the Soviet Union with his mother in 1981.

"[Growing up] I started noticing that all the propaganda on TV — the two channels that we had — didn't look right. It seemed like it was a lie. We grew up in what turned out to be the third world," Maine said.

"All the trumpeting on the street of how great this is, how this is the best, how evil America is, how evil Western Europe is, and how evil capitalism is — people realized that they couldn't speak freely," he continued.

Three men who escaped the confines of socialism and communism dive into their upbringing under different dictatorships, and why socialist policies forced them to leave. (Fox news)

"There was no religion. The only religion allowed was communism, which is a religion. Let's not have any doubts about it. It is a religion, it replaces Christianity, Judaism. That's the environment I grew up in," Maine said.

"These are not only dictators, they are also narco-terrorists, these are really dangerous people," Rincón added about Venezuela.

"I ha[d] to take out all my family from Venezuela. This is my history, but there are millions of histories like this in Venezuela. These are the things that the people in the USA do[n’t] really understand about socialism," he warned.

Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi is an Associate Producer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans
articles.excerpt:
People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area

A smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-...
articles.body_text:
People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area

A smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford.

On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in the Norfolk market town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers.

“The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town.

“Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers.

For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said.

However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions.

“I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.”

Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday.

Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited.

“I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices.

The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere.

If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger.

Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by the Home Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.

“The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy.

“I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.”

Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office.

Social media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others.

In answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand.

The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023.

Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs.

Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”.

He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford,and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers.

Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said on GB News on Friday that people had a right to protest but that the disorder in Thetford had been “horrendous”.

“What we’ve seen is spilling over into violence, which is just not acceptable,” she said. “Nobody should feel harassed, intimidated or threatened in their home, and certainly we shouldn’t see our emergency workers and our police attacked in the way that we have seen.”

articles.title: Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg claims Democratic moderates 'don't have the right values'
articles.excerpt:
Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg said Democratic moderates ‘don’t have the right values’ when pressed on CNN about what he would say to the party’s centrist wing.

Former Democratic National Committee...
articles.body_text:
Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg said Democratic moderates ‘don’t have the right values’ when pressed on CNN about what he would say to the party’s centrist wing.

Former Democratic National Committee Vice Chair David Hogg told moderate Democrats they "don't have the right values" Thursday during an appearance on "The Source," arguing the party establishment is repeatedly losing because its priorities are out of step with Americans as progressive candidates score primary victories ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Hogg made his sharpest criticism after host Kaitlan Collins asked what he would tell moderates concerned that progressive nominees could struggle against Republicans in general elections.

"The reason why the establishment of our party is being defeated over and over and over again is because they don't have the right values that are aligned with not the Democratic base, but the American people," Hogg said. "Where people are sick and tired of listening to Democrats and tell them all the reasons why they can't solve their problems."

Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg said moderate Democrats "don't have the right values" as he argued the party establishment has repeatedly failed voters. (Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images for Fast Company)

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Hogg told moderates they needed to change their approach rather than ask successful progressive candidates to move toward the center.

"I would say to the moderates in our party, 'You need to figure out how to actually offer something new to voters that isn't just the same message that you gave them in 2024,'" Hogg said.

Steven Bonnell II, the liberal streamer known as "Destiny," pushed back on Hogg's assessment in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying he does not believe the former DNC official represents rank-and-file Democrats.

"I would say that this is outside of the Democratic Party's mainstream views," Destiny said. "Polls seem to evidence this, with a plurality (or majority, in some cases) of Democratic voters feeling as though the party has moved too far to the left."

Liberal streamer Destiny told Fox News Digital Hogg's comments fall outside the Democratic mainstream and could alienate moderate voters. (Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN'

Destiny, who has repeatedly criticized the party's far-left socialist wing, said Hogg's comments were an example of a dynamic that allows progressives to attack moderates without facing similar scrutiny from within the party.

"People in the Democratic Party's extreme fringe have created a ‘ratchet effect,’ where you cannot criticize anyone to the left-of-moderate view point," Destiny said. "Those same people can infinitely attack the moderate wing, leading outsiders (and even people from within) to view the Democratic Party as far more extreme than it actually is."

He warned that a Democratic Party that decides its moderates do not share its values could face consequences at the ballot box.

"I think it would mean the Democratic Party would probably have a hugely difficult time succeeding in the upcoming general in 2028 and possibly even stumble in 2026," Destiny said. "Which is especially ridiculous given how low Trump's popularity is at the moment."

Hogg's remarks came as progressive candidates notch primary victories and Democrats debate the party's ideological direction ahead of the 2026 midterms. (Reuters)

SEN MARK KELLY WARNS FAR-LEFT POLICIES THAT ‘DON’T MAKE SENSE’ COULD COST DEMOCRATS SEATS

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville has taken the opposite side of the party's ideological battle, telling Fox News Digital Thursday that Democratic primary voters would ultimately reject the socialist wing.

"I think it's more likely than not that the Democrats embrace sanity," Carville said.

Carville said a takeover by the socialist wing could ultimately fracture the party, reiterating comments he has made amid the growing influence of figures including self-described socialist streamer Hasan Piker.

"That probably would result in some kind of schism in the party," Carville said. "I'm going to let Democratic voters determine the direction that party goes in, and if it goes in the direction — which I'm pretty confident it won't — but if it goes in that direction, then I'm going to be 82. OK, fine, go ahead, but not with me."

Carville has also said he would leave the party if Piker became a significant force within it, while Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., responded that Carville could "start his own party."

Fox News Digital reached out to the DNC for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital's Alexander Hall contributed to this article.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

articles.title: Duke Law's alleged race-based admissions accused of defying Supreme Court ruling: DOJ
articles.excerpt: The House committee debates the influence of DEI policies on medical school admissions and patient care standards. Lawmakers question deans from major medical schools about allegations from the Justic...
articles.body_text:
The House committee debates the influence of DEI policies on medical school admissions and patient care standards. Lawmakers question deans from major medical schools about allegations from the Justice Department that UCLA granted an illegal edge to Black and Hispanic applicants.

The Justice Department is accusing Duke University School of Law of favoring Black and Hispanic applicants over White and Asian applicants with the same academic records in its admissions process, which the Trump administration argues the law school used to meet its "diversity goals."

"Duke Law School doesn’t get a free pass to discriminate against white and Asian students simply because it thinks it has good intentions," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said.

In 2023, the Supreme Court ruled in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (SFFA) that it was unconstitutional for colleges and higher education institutions to consider a student's race in their admissions processes. The decision prompted the Trump administration to open investigations into alleged race-based discrimination at dozens of colleges and universities.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT ZEROES IN ON UCLA FOR ALLEGED ILLEGAL DEI ADMISSIONS AS ELITE SCHOOL CRACKDOWN EXPANDS

A photo of Duke University's west campus in Fall 202 (Duke University - Jared Lazarus)

The Civil Rights Division, which began investigating Duke Law in April 2025, found that Black applicants who applied in 2025 had roughly 3.5 times the chance of admission as Asian applicants with the same academic credentials, according to a Justice Department letter sent to Duke Law. Investigators found that the median LSAT score for accepted Black applicants was lower than the median score for rejected Asian and White applicants.

"This consistent difference in the test scores between students of different racial groups is substantial and cannot be explained by a coincidence," the letter stated. "The magnitude and durability of these preferences across multiple cycles (including post-SFFA) confirm intentional discrimination."

The Trump administration’s review of internal communications found that the law school began preparing for the Supreme Court’s SFFA ruling so its admissions process could continue "to meet the Law School's goals for a broadly diverse student body."

For instance, Duke Law's post-SFFA guidance for admissions allowed officials to "consider applicants' discussion of how race affected their life, be it through discrimination, inspiration, or otherwise." Applicants provided these discussions in short-answer essays, where admissions officials could then "tag" the responses to provide context for weaker academic records when evaluating applicants.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon arrives for a news conference at the Justice Department on September 29, 2025, in Washington, DC. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Duke Law states that it values "students with a wide range of experiences, backgrounds, and interests that may not be directly related to their legal ambitions," encouraging applicants to "highlight different elements" of who they are.

"Using ‘diversity’ essay questions to identify preferred races for admission is still illegal discrimination based on race, and this Department is committed to eliminating it everywhere we find it, including in our nation’s law schools," Dhillon said in a statement.

After SFFA, Duke Law admissions continued to release reports highlighting the school's diversity and its efforts to achieve "race-neutral" admissions standards. In a May 2024 annual review, the associate dean of admissions highlighted the diversity of the incoming fall 2023 class, including the number of Latino, Black and Asian or Asian American students.

In the school's 2025 Annual Review Memorandum, the admissions dean suggested that the law school can gauge the diversity of its student body by observing students on campus rather than compiling formal statistics.

FILE - This Jan. 28, 2019 file photo shows the entrance to the main Duke University campus in Durham, N.C.  (AP Photo/Gerry Broome, File)

A Duke University spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the university is aware of the Justice Department's allegations.

"The Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division issued a letter of findings related to Duke Law’s admissions practices. We are reviewing the letter and its conclusions carefully. Duke is committed to complying with the law and will continue to do so in a manner that is consistent with our academic mission," a Duke University spokesperson said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for additional comment.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: Several killed in attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv hits Russian e-commerce giant
articles.excerpt:
Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine have killed at least six people, local authorities say, as Moscow and Kyiv trade intensifying strikes targeting each other’s economic and energy infrastructure.

A w...
articles.body_text:
Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine have killed at least six people, local authorities say, as Moscow and Kyiv trade intensifying strikes targeting each other’s economic and energy infrastructure.

A wave of Russian attacks killed two people and wounded six in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region on Friday, with strikes reported in five districts, governor Oleksandr Hanzha wrote on Telegram. He said five people were killed on Thursday in the same region by a barrage of Russian attacks.

Russia’s military struck Dnipropetrovsk at least 50 times with drones, artillery and aerial bombs on Friday, Hanzha added.

In southern Ukraine’s Kherson, a Molniya drone struck a car driving along a road killing a 77-year-old woman, the local military administration said on Telegram. Eight bus passengers were among dozens wounded in other attacks.

Two people were killed in Kharkiv by cluster munitions, according to the city’s military administration. Governor Oleh Syniehubov said 21 settlements reported strikes from “various” weapons that included missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), wounding at least 18 people.

The governor of Donetsk, Vadym Filashkin, reported one death on Friday morning, noting that Russia shelled the region at least 44 times since Thursday.

In Russian-controlled Crimea, a Ukrainian drone killed two people when it hit an apartment building, said the Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov.

Ukraine’s president arrived for his first official visit to Serbia on Friday. Volodymyr Zelenskyy posted on X that he planned to discuss “expanding economic ties between our countries, relations with the European Union, and other things that can work for our peoples”.

The meeting was expected to anger Russia, Serbia’s long-time ally and natural gas supplier.

Ukraine’s military has continued to take aim at Wildberries, the so-called “Amazon of Russia”.

Multiple drones were seen flying over a Wildberries logistics facility in Yekaterinburg early on Friday, before large fires broke out. The company confirmed the attack on Telegram, saying the facility was evacuated beforehand and the flames had been contained.

The strike, roughly 2,000 km from the frontline, showed “strategic and economic importance”, as well as being a “blow to the consumer economy”, reported Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova from Moscow.

The attack was the latest to target Wildberries since mid-July, when Kyiv began attacking at least 20 of the company’s sites, killing at least 13 people, triggering fires and destroying stock.

Ukraine says Wildberries supports the war effort, a charge Moscow and the company deny.

As it seeks to curtail Russia’s energy infrastructure, Ukraine says its 40-day strike spree has hit 14 refineries, several oil depots and loading terminals, 14 aircraft and four airfields.

For its part, Russia attacked seven oil and gas production facilities in eastern Ukraine overnight into Friday, according to the state oil and gas company Naftogaz, which claimed on Telegram to have destroyed “critical” equipment.

“Russia is systematically attacking Ukraine’s oil and gas production sector in an attempt to inflict maximum damage on our infrastructure ahead of winter,” acting CEO Sergiy Fedorenko said.

The Russian Defence Ministry said forces hit two more cargo vessels in the Black Sea that it said were being utilised for “the interests of the Ukrainian military”.

Russian forces also hit fuel storage facilities at the port of Pivdennyi, the ministry added.

articles.title: Trump renews bid to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook despite supreme court ruling
articles.excerpt:
White House continues to target Cook despite decision from justices that upheld Federal Reserve’s independence

Donald Trump is attempting once again to oust US Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook over...
articles.body_text:
White House continues to target Cook despite decision from justices that upheld Federal Reserve’s independence

Donald Trump is attempting once again to oust US Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook over allegations of mortgage fraud, despite a recent US supreme court decision that upheld the central bank’s independence.

Cook reportedly received a letter from the White House this week that provided notice, in accordance to the supreme court’s June ruling, that Trump is “considering removing” her from her Fed position over the same claims of mortgage fraud that he levied against her last summer.

The letter, first reported by ABC News, accused Cook of falling “well short of the standard” required of a sitting Fed governor and requested she provide a written response to the allegations within three weeks.

The supreme court in June ruled 5-4 that Cook was entitled to stay on as Fed governor while she fights the president’s allegations, writing in its majority opinion that Trump “failed to afford Cook the procedural protections to which she was entitled by statute”.

“Without such protections, she could not properly dispute the charges the president laid against her,” the justices said.

In response to the White House’s letter, one of Cook’s lawyers, Abbe D Lowell, called the allegations “as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve”.

“No matter what President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent – there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook,” Lowell said in a statement. “As we did before, we will challenge this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term that will end in 2038. She is the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor. Before she joined the Fed, she served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers and has taught at Harvard University and Stanford University.

Trump first abruptly fired Cook last August in an unprecedented attack on the central bank’s independence. The White House accused her of wrongly designating two separate properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property for two years. Cook denied the allegations and sued the Trump administration for firing her without cause or proper procedure.

Cook and her legal team have maintained that the claims of mortgage fraud are based on “inadvertent” paperwork errors and that the administration is “cherrypicking” facts.

Cook’s firing and ongoing legal battles also coincided with Trump’s attacks on the Fed for not lowering rates. Cook, along with then Fed chair, Jerome Powell, had backed the central bank’s decision not to lower rates, which drew the ire of the White House. Trump called Powell “too stupid and too political” and launched a justice department investigation into his renovations of the Fed’s headquarters in Washington, which has since been dropped.

The Fed is now under the leadership of Kevin Warsh, a Trump pick who had previously shown favor towards cutting rates. Warsh has maintained that he will make decisions based on economic data, not the will of the president, and has made it his mission to fight the country’s heightened inflation, which typically is addressed by rate hikes.

“We’re an independent central bank,” he said in response to questioning from Democratic House members at a hearing in July. “We’re honored to be independent.”

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Title IX defender Payton McNabb praises Sophie Cunningham, reacts to Caitlin Clark
articles.excerpt: McNabb reflects on the rapid growth of her advocacy movement over the past three years. She discusses evolving from cautious messaging to testifying before Congress about the biological differences be...
articles.body_text:
McNabb reflects on the rapid growth of her advocacy movement over the past three years. She discusses evolving from cautious messaging to testifying before Congress about the biological differences between men and women.

Long before Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham challenged the conversation surrounding women's sports, Payton McNabb was living its consequences.

A high school volleyball match changed McNabb's life. Years later, she sees Cunningham taking on a fight that has followed her all the way to Capitol Hill.

WATCH PAYTON MCNABB'S FULL INTERVIEW WITH OUTKICK:

After suffering a traumatic brain injury and partial paralysis on her right side from a ball spiked by a biological male opponent, McNabb took her fight from a North Carolina volleyball court to Washington, where she has testified before lawmakers in defense of women's sports and Title IX.

Payton McNabb, a former high school athlete, is recognized by President Donald Trump during an address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)

JD VANCE PRAISES SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FOR 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISM

Now 21, McNabb sees that same battle reaching the WNBA and believes the league's response is exposing a glaring double standard.

Speaking exclusively with OutKick, McNabb applauded Cunningham for taking a stand, ripped Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve over her support for transgender inclusion and explained why Caitlin Clark's voice could carry enormous weight with the next generation of female athletes.

"I started speaking out when I was 18," McNabb told OutKick. "I'm 21 now, but within the last few years, why have I had to go in front of Congress and explain that there's a biological difference between a man and a woman? It makes no sense, and it sounds like such a dumb argument."

Payton McNabb, a former North Carolina high school volleyball player injured by a transgender opponent, speaks during a hearing on "Unfair Play: Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" held by the Department of Government Efficiency Subcommittee at the U.S. Capitol on May 7, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

Cunningham's willingness to speak out has particularly impressed McNabb, especially as the Fever guard's profile has soared.

"What we've seen through Sophie Cunningham has been so courageous," McNabb said. "I just applaud her so much because it takes a lot to say this, unfortunately, and it shouldn't, but it does."

"For her to say it now and not wait until it's safe ... and her career is really taking off, I think it just adds a whole other layer on top of how special it really is," McNabb continued. "We don't really have a lot of big-name athletes willing to say it, and that's really unfortunate, but that's just the way it is. But it's because of how they get treated."

McNabb pointed to the backlash Cunningham has received as evidence of that risk.

"She's getting vilified or villainized for literally just saying what everyone already knows and thinks, but are just too afraid to admit," McNabb said. "It's just crazy because there wouldn't be a WNBA. We wouldn't know who [Lynx coach] Cheryl Reeve is or even Sophie Cunningham or any of these girls if it wasn't for Title IX."

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

McNabb had far less praise for Reeve, who has publicly defended trans participation in sports and wore a Trans Kids Belong shirt during a matchup against Cunningham and the Fever to prove it.

Payton McNabb, a former North Carolina high school volleyball player injured by a transgender opponent, speaks during a hearing on "Unfair Play: Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" held by the Department of Government Efficiency Subcommittee at the U.S. Capitol on May 7, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

"It just seems like women like Cheryl Reeve who were fighting against other women and girls, I just will never understand that," McNabb said. "You have little girls who are showing up to the game and excited about their favorite player standing up for them and wanting the same opportunities that she has to be in place for them. And the coach seems to be pulling up the ladder."

McNabb called out the glaring hypocrisy of demanding empowerment for female athletes while simultaneously opening the door for biological men to take their spots.

"You can't complain on one hand about not getting as much as the men or not getting as many opportunities or viewers ... and then on the next, you're encouraging men to take over the very category you're wanting separate from them," McNabb said.

McNabb predicted the league's virtue signaling will evaporate the second a biological male steps onto a WNBA court and forces players to face reality.

McNabb pointed to Julie Tétart, a 6-foot-3 biological male dominating a French women's league who (with the help of OutKick's Joe Kinsey and founder Clay Travis) recently signaled interest in making the jump to the WNBA.

"I think it's gonna have to take this dude from France to come in here and like dunk on Angel Reese and then maybe they'll be like, 'Oh, maybe this isn't allowed,'" McNabb said. "I don't know. It's going to have to affect them personally."

Make no mistake: McNabb isn't rooting for biological men to wreck the WNBA. She wants these athletes protected, even if they won't fight for themselves.

CLAY TRAVIS SETS SIGHTS ON FRENCH TRANS PHENOM JULIE TETART FOR PROPOSED 'INCLUSIVE' WNBA EXPANSION TEAM

"Of course, I don't want that to happen," she said. "I'm fighting for the girls that are even going against us because I want them to have the protections and the opportunities whether they like it or not."

McNabb challenged the league's progressive establishment to put its money where its mouth is: if biological males belong in girls' high school athletics, they belong in WNBA coaching spots, too.

"I want transgender coaches," McNabb said. "I think that there should be a transgender coach taking Cheryl Reeve's place because that will be just as much of a woman as she is. ... If they're saying this is okay for the high school girls, then it should be okay for them."

THE LEFT WANTS CAITLIN CLARK, SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM TO SHUT UP AND DRIBBLE WHEN IT COMES TO TRANS SPORTS

McNabb understands why the Fever superstar has largely kept the focus on basketball rather than wading into another contentious issue.

"She gets a lot of backlash for literally no reason, from jealousy," McNabb said. "I could imagine not wanting more of that would probably be ideal."

Payton McNabb and Second Lady Usha Vance attend President Donald Trump's address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2025. (Getty Images)

Still, McNabb believes Clark's enormous influence makes her part of the Title IX debate whether she addresses it publicly or not.

"Whether Caitlin Clark likes it, she's a part of the conversation, and it would just mean so much to the next generation," McNabb said. "To all the little girls in the stands that are wearing number 22, it would mean a lot to them."

THESE FEMALE ATHLETES NEED TO SPEAK UP ABOUT KEEPING WOMEN'S SPORTS FOR WOMEN, LIKE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DID

Few voices in women's basketball, McNabb argues, could carry more weight.

"She's the best player in the WNBA, and for her to be able to take a stance and say something, that would be huge," McNabb said. "She's where she is today because of Title IX, and she needs to be able to acknowledge that and accept that and want that for the next generation of girls."

For McNabb, the issue remains deeply personal.

More than three years after the volleyball injury that changed her life, McNabb said her health has finally reached a significant turning point.

"The doctors didn't know if I would ever get back to how I was, and they said it could take three years before I could see real progress," McNabb said. "It's so weird, because it actually took exactly three years for me to see a difference in coming back and bouncing back with my health."

The teenager who once failed public speaking has since testified before Congress and become an Independent Women ambassador, using the injury that changed her life to try to prevent other girls from enduring the same thing.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"I wasn't planning on going into politics, really had no idea what was going on at all," McNabb said. "I just had a genuine story that happened to a real person and affected a real family and community."

"I've really just tried to use the story to spread awareness in hopes no other girl has to go through what I went through."

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: California woman who admitted to stabbing wife had also killed husband
articles.excerpt:
Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, who served a decade for killing her husband,  pleaded guilty to murder of Rebecca Marodi, a fire captain who fought the Eaton blaze

A California woman this week admitted to...
articles.body_text:
Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, who served a decade for killing her husband,  pleaded guilty to murder of Rebecca Marodi, a fire captain who fought the Eaton blaze

A California woman this week admitted to killing her wife, a decorated fire captain who fought the deadly 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, by stabbing her – the same fate she previously delivered to her husband and had served a decade in prison for.

Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to second-degree murder after killing her wife, Rebecca “Becky” Marodi, 49, a California fire captain, at their home in February 2025, just a month after Becky, as she was known, battled the Eaton blaze that killed 19.

Rebecca Marodi, who was assigned to the French Valley Cal Fire station in Riverside county was found with multiple stab wounds to her neck, chest and back at the couple’s home in Ramona, near San Diego. She had said she wanted to end the marriage.

A warrant for Olejniczak Marodi’s arrest was issued days later. Detectives said home security footage had shown Rebecca Marodi running from her wife of two years, screaming: “Yolanda! Please! I don’t want to die!”

According to investigators, Olejniczak Marodi, who was seen holding a knife and with blood on her arms in the surveillance film, replied: “You should have thought of that before.”

Olejniczak Marodi was captured on video loading “pets, random items and some luggage” and loading them into an SUV, according to the warrant seen at the time by ABC News. About 75 minutes after the attack, records from homeland security showed Olejniczak Marodi crossing the nearby border into Mexico.

Investigators later found that the then suspect messaged a friend: “Rebecca came home and told me she was leaving me. We had a big fight, and I hurt her. I’m sorry.”

Soon after the murder it emerged that Olejniczak Marodi had been in prison from 2004 to 2013 after being convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the 2000 stabbing death of her then-husband, Jim Olejniczak. He, too, had recently informed her he was ending the marriage.

After she fled this time, Mexican law enforcement officers arrested her at a hotel in Mexicali in March 2025 and she was later handed over to US marshals in San Diego and booked on suspicion of murder. She initially pleaded not guilty.

Andrea Winter, a friend of Rebecca, told the Los Angeles Times that Olejniczak Marodi was jealous of her wife’s popularity and exhibited “controlling, isolating behavior” before the killing. Winter said Rebecca had not disclosed that her wife had been convicted of stabbing her previous husband to death.

“Yolanda was very insecure,” Winter told the outlet. “Becky has this magnetic personality and everybody liked her. I think Yolanda was very jealous of that and that Becky was this bright light.

“Becky was a kind person and paid the absolute price for that by trusting the wrong person,” Winter added.

Olejniczak Marodi is scheduled to be sentenced on 2 September and faces 36 years to life in a state prison.

articles.body_text:
On this episode of Don't @ Me, Dan Dakich breaks down the WNBA's latest controversy after Indiana Fever head coach Stephanie White claimed she lacked sufficient biological information to comment on males playing women's sports.

Former NBA Draft first round pick (3rd overall in 2011) Enes Kanter Freedom, who has been an adamant opponent of LeBron James, the Chinese Communist Party, Nike, along with more political activism, which he believes blackballed him from the NBA, has officially declared himself a prospect for the 2027 WNBA Draft. Yes, I’m serious.

In the aftermath of Sophie Cuningham making a definitive stance that women’s sports should remain female, many coaches and players have opened up the floodgates for men in their league. Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Willliams even said, "I would welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team any time." Throughout this whole saga, the WNBA has remained silent about protecting fairness in their league, so Freedom is putting their feet to the fire in a hilarious way.

FILE - In this March 19, 2018, file photo, New York Knicks center Enes Kanter (00) drives to the basket against the Chicago Bulls during the first quarter of an NBA basketball game in New York. Kanter informed the Knicks on Friday, June 29, 2018, that he was opting into his contract for next season, rather than becoming a free agent. (AP Photo/Julie Jacobson, File) ( )

JD VANCE PRAISES SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FOR 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISM

"If simply declaring who you are is all that’s required, then I meet every requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," Freedom stated in a social media post seated behind a studio desk wearing an orange WNBA sweatshirt with the Nike logo crossed out.

Outkick contributor Riley Gaines called the declaration "genius" and "perfect", while sarcastically saying, "Waiting to see which WNBA team recruits Enes Freedom."

Freedom, who hasn’t played in the NBA since being waived by the Houston Rockets in 2022 following a trade from the Boston Celtics went on to say, "My team and I have carefully reviewed the WNBA’s eligibility criteria and government framework surrounding self identification and inclusion."

According to Freedom, "Based on the current guidelines, I can and am officially declaring my eligibility for the upcoming WNBA Draft in May 2027."

Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve reacts in the second half against the Indiana Fever at Target Center on Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Star Tribune via Getty Images)

TRUMP'S REMARKS ON RECRUITING LEBRON JAMES TO WOMEN'S BASKETBALL RESURFACE AMID WNBA TRANS ATHLETE DEBATE

The way I see it, what makes this any different than Lia Thomas at UPenn? When going by the name Will Thomas, he spent three seasons on the men’s team before transitioning to the female team and division.

The WNBA has also undoubtedly asked for this. Now is the time for them to put their money where their mouth is. If you’re really so "inclusive," you should have no problem with this.

If he identifies as a woman, who are they to tell him who he is? Who are they to tell him if this is genuine or not? This is a great way to put their feet to the fire. It has the opportunity to show that all of this "trans acceptance" talk is just virtue signaling.

"I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices," Freedom added. "I’m simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."

A view of the Wilson ball before the 2023 WNBA Draft on April 10, 2023 at Spring Studios in New York, New York. (Michelle Farsi/NBAE via Getty Images)

WNBA STAR SAYS SHE WOULD WELCOME A TRANS PLAYER TO HER TEAM, AND THEN SAYS SOMETHING EVEN DUMBER

Players like Gabby Williams, Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase, Seattle Storm center Stefanie Dolson, and the majority of WNBA fans have made it clear they are supportive of men in women’s sports.

Freedom wrapped up his WNBA Draft announcement stating, "My team and I are prepared to ensure these guidelines are applied equally, consistently, and without exception, and I look forward to the WNBA honoring its stated principles. See you at training camp." The WNBA will now have to put their foot down to protect the fairness, integrity and safety of their league, or allow their progressive politics to ruin it.

Not one WNBA "reporter" asked Commissioner Cathy Engelbert about Sophie Cunningham's stance on trans-identifying athletes. (TNS)

This whole situation will be hilarious to witness. If the league allows Freedom to be eligible, irrationally sticking to their anti-women progressive politics, but no team drafts Freedom in April 2027, it could be seen as discrimination. If they say their sport is for females only, they run into the fury of their liberal foundation, which many of their fans, players, and coaches hold to.

This’ll be a great way to expose the hypocrisy or idiocy of the progressive movement ingrained in the league.

Jon is a writer and content creator for OutKick

articles.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
articles.excerpt:
Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians

Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United ...
articles.body_text:
Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians

Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. Those ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

articles.title: Heidi Klum goes topless in racy anniversary beach snaps with husband on St Barts vacation

Heidi Klum turned up the heat this week with several topless beach snaps.
...
articles.body_text:
‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital it’s ‘no big deal’ that she went topless during her vacation.

Heidi Klum turned up the heat this week with several topless beach snaps.

The former Victoria’s Secret Angel shared several photos on her Instagram page, including a couple where she appeared to be napping on a Gucci towel next to her husband, Tom Kaulitz, with only a hat and a black thong bikini bottom to cover herself.

"No caption needed," the "Project Runway" judge cheekily captioned the photo dump that also showed her locking lips with the Tokio Hotel guitarist and walking into the water topless while holding her rescue dog Fritz.

GISELE BÜNDCHEN CELEBRATES BIRTHDAY IN LEOPARD-PRINT BIKINI AS SHE REFLECTS ON GRATITUDE

Heidi Klum shared a photo of her lying on a beach with her husband in St. Barts on their anniversary. (Heidi Klum/Instagram)

The couple is celebrating their seventh wedding anniversary in St. Barts.

The photos got love in the comments, with fellow former Victoria's Secret Angel Alessandra Ambrosio leaving seven heart emoji.

Heidi Klum lies on a beach with Tom Kaulitz and her rescue dog, Fritz. (Heidi Klum/Instagram)

Klum and Kaulitz got married in a lavish yacht ceremony Aug. 3, 2019, in Capri, Italy, after secretly marrying in February of that year.

Klum also shared photos of her surrounded by red heart balloons, looking over a bouquet of red roses and one of the couple enjoying a glass of wine with some heart-shaped Brie cheese.

CARMEN ELECTRA SAYS 'DON'T LET ANYONE TELL YOU YOU'RE TOO OLD' AFTER PLAYBOY RETURN AT 54

"For the first time, I have a partner who I can discuss everything with," Klum, who turned 53 in June, told People in 2020. "Someone who shares duties that we all have in our life. I used to be on my own with everything. For the first time, I get to experience what it is actually like to have a partner."

Heidi Klum and husband Tom Kaulitz shared a kiss on their seventh anniversary in St. Barts. (Heidi Klum/Instagram)

The supermodel told Harper's Bazaar last year that as she gets older, loving her body is more about "appreciating change."

Heidi Klum attends the red carpet at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025. (WireImage)

"I am heavier than I was before — not intentionally. But when you're younger, your metabolism is different," she said. "When I was younger, I never tried to look the way I looked. Now, I’ve evolved a little bit, and I feel great in my skin — way more now than back then. Accepting these changes is just the course of life; I have love handles, but I'm not even worried about it."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: US Army offering defense firms 'concierge access' to test weapons at military ranges
articles.excerpt: A top NATO commander raises alarms on weapons production, citing concerns about the U.S. military's method of designing and producing missile systems. The report details a critical munition shortage, ...
articles.body_text:
A top NATO commander raises alarms on weapons production, citing concerns about the U.S. military's method of designing and producing missile systems. The report details a critical munition shortage, particularly with Patriot missiles, exacerbated by current conflicts.

The U.S. Army is opening up military test ranges to private defense companies and promising "concierge" access aimed at dramatically cutting the time it takes companies to test new weapons and technologies.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll told reporters in a call on Friday that companies will be able to secure testing opportunities within 30 days of submitting a request, compared with a typical wait of roughly 18 months.

"We just had to get out of our own way," Driscoll said. "And so the 30-day clock starts today. So if somebody goes to testrange.army.mil, submits it in the next hour, we will have you on a range within 30 days."

'A NEW KIND OF WAR': INSIDE UKRAINE'S HIDDEN FACTORIES MASS-PRODUCING COMBAT DRONES

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll briefed reporters on Army modernization. (Cheriss May/Getty Images)

The move is part of a broader Army effort to speed up the development and delivery of technologies including drones, counter-drone systems, long-range fires and low-cost interceptors.

"If you look at what is occurring all over the world today, if you look what Ukraine has done so incredibly well, it's this innovation through necessity and it's innovation at the speed that is near or close to matching the commercial sector," Driscoll said. "And so what we, the Army, are trying to do is break down every single barrier that we have put up over the last 20 and 30 years."

The Army is opening four stateside locations to industry: Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, Camp Shelby Joint Forces Training Center in Mississippi and Camp Grayling Joint Maneuver Training Center in Michigan.

PENTAGON PLOTS NEW NUCLEAR OPTIONS FOR TRUMP AS AMERICA’S BIGGEST ADVERSARIES RAISE STAKES: REPORT

Anti-drone laser system trialed on a Stryker combat military vehicle with a machine gun aimed at the sky in Ukraine during a counteroffensive. (Michelle Ursi/Getty Images)

The Army is also working with U.S. Africa Command and partners to provide industry access to the Multidomain Training Area in Morocco, according to an Army press release. Companies will be able to request test range time through a new online portal and will be assigned a dedicated "concierge" to help navigate the scheduling process. Companies do not need an existing federal contract or prior relationship with the U.S. government to apply.

"A company with a good idea shouldn’t need a team of lawyers and a program of record just to prove their equipment works," Driscoll said.

ANTARES REACHES REACTOR CRITICALITY UNDER TRUMP PILOT PROGRAM, MARKING MAJOR NUCLEAR MILESTONE

The ranges are intended to give companies access to realistic environments where they can rapidly test and refine emerging technologies, including under conditions resembling those encountered on modern battlefields.

The Army cautioned that submitting a request does not guarantee a company its preferred location or testing date because of capacity constraints, but said its concierge team will work with applicants to identify available testing windows and locations.

Liz Friden is a Pentagon producer based in Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Socialist House nominee's radical law-and-order vision: 'What are illegals?'
articles.excerpt:
Fox News host Sean Hannity questions Democratic Socialists of America–supported Pennsylvania congressional nominee Chris Rabb on his support for the DSA's platform on 'Hannity.'

The socialist Democra...
articles.body_text:
