articles.title: Iran’s grip on trade is a potent weapon, but it has an expiry date
articles.excerpt:
Professor in Economics of the Middle East, Philipps-Universität Marburg, Germany.

Iran has turned its ability to restrict commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz into a potent economic weapon...
articles.body_text:
Professor in Economics of the Middle East, Philipps-Universität Marburg, Germany.

Iran has turned its ability to restrict commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz into a potent economic weapon in the war imposed by the United States and Israel.

IMF PortWatch shows that in the seven days ending August 2, an average of only about four ships per day passed through the strait, compared with about 90 during the corresponding week of 2025. Estimated transit volume fell from 3.5 million to about 143,000 metric tonnes per day. Both indicators declined by approximately 96 percent.

This was not a temporary collapse in traffic but a sustained disruption. Since February 28, both vessel traffic and estimated tonnage have remained far below their levels in the previous year, with only brief recoveries. Tehran has therefore already demonstrated that it can impose severe disruption on commercial traffic. The question is no longer whether Iran can disrupt trade through Hormuz, but how effectively it can convert that disruption into political leverage, and for how long.

A useful framework for understanding this strategy comes from political scientists Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman, who describe how states can turn control over central nodes in international networks into coercive power, a process they call “weaponised interdependence”. In Hormuz, the critical node is physical rather than financial or digital. Geography gives Iran leverage over a corridor on which energy producers, shipping companies and importing economies remain heavily dependent.

The scale of that dependence shows Tehran’s leverage. In 2025, almost 20 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products crossed Hormuz each day, equivalent to about one-quarter of global seaborne oil trade. Around 80 percent of those flows went to Asia. China and India alone received 44 percent of the crude oil that passed through the strait. Qatar and the United Arab Emirates also shipped liquefied natural gas (LNG) equivalent to almost one-fifth of global LNG trade through Hormuz, with no practical alternative export route.

The economic effects begin before any formal closure. Shipping companies and insurers respond to perceived risk as well as actual attacks. Even the threat of missiles, mines, drones or vessel seizures can increase insurance premiums, freight rates and waiting times. Research published in Nature Communications shows that disruptions at maritime chokepoints transmit economic losses through delays, rerouting, insurance costs and interruptions to production.

Iran can therefore exert pressure on several audiences at the same time. Gulf states face risks to export revenues, ports and logistics. Major Asian importers such as India face higher energy costs and possible supply shortages. The US imports comparatively little oil through the Strait of Hormuz, yet it remains exposed to higher global energy and domestic fuel prices, and the military costs of protecting commercial navigation. Tehran’s strongest leverage may therefore come indirectly by pushing Gulf governments and Asian importers to press Washington for de-escalation.

The consequences also extend to less obvious areas, including the emerging competition over artificial intelligence. Gulf states are investing heavily in data centres and computing infrastructure, seeking to use their access to relatively inexpensive energy to become important hubs in the global AI economy. By raising energy prices and increasing risks to Gulf infrastructure, disruption at Hormuz can raise the cost of expanding AI capacity and weaken one of the region’s central economic diversification strategies.

Hormuz also carries commodities whose importance is often obscured by the focus on oil. In our recent Nature Food study, we showed that several major agricultural economies depend heavily on fertilisers exported through the Strait of Hormuz. For example, India sources around half of its imported ammonia and nitrogen fertilisers, about nine million tonnes, from Gulf producers. Disruption would combine lower fertiliser availability with higher natural gas and shipping costs, increasing risks to crop yields and food prices in the short term, especially in food-importing countries.

Helium provides another example of this less visible dependence. Qatar and the UAE supply helium used in semiconductor production, medical imaging, scientific research and clean technologies. Helium is difficult to store, liquefaction capacity is concentrated, and there are few substitutes for several applications. Our analysis shows that several economies responsible for more than 60 percent of global integrated-circuit exports are highly dependent on helium supplied through the Strait of Hormuz. Hormuz therefore links a regional security crisis to advanced manufacturing and healthcare supply chains in Asia.

These vulnerabilities give Iran bargaining power in the war imposed by the US and Israel. Yet they also define the limits of that power.

First, disruption harms Iran itself. Iran’s petroleum exports, food imports, industrial inputs and maritime trade depend heavily on its southern waterways. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have pipelines that can redirect an estimated 3.5 to 5.5 million barrels per day away from Hormuz. These countries will therefore have stronger incentives and greater resources to expand alternative routes. Iran’s Jask route outside the strait remains effectively non-operational. A prolonged interruption would therefore deprive Tehran of export earnings while worsening inflation and shortages at home. The US blockade of Iran’s southern ports compounds this vulnerability for as long as tensions over Hormuz persist. Of Iran’s roughly 170 million tonnes of annual foreign trade, about 160 million tonnes, or 94 percent, pass through southern ports. By comparison, northern ports on the Caspian Sea handle only about 4 percent of that trade and could probably increase their share to no more than 10 to 15 percent, even in a crisis. Northern routes and sanctions-evasion networks may sustain selected shipments, but they cannot replace the southern ports as gateways for large volumes of oil, grain, steel and containerised goods.

Second, Iran can make navigation dangerous, but sustaining that disruption is costly. A US Congressional Research Service assessment concludes that Iran can disrupt shipping through mines, speedboats, submarines, shore-based missiles and aircraft, but that US forces could eventually restore traffic, although this might take days, weeks or months. Iran’s advantage therefore lies less in controlling Hormuz than in imposing uncertainty and delay. But the same uncertainty also harms its own economy: even a prolonged “no war, no peace” environment can weaken investment, government revenues and the fiscal capacity needed to sustain military pressure. Iran’s military capacity also depends heavily on public revenues, which sanctions have constrained. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Iran’s military spending in 2025 was about 2 percent of GDP, compared with 3 percent in the United States and between 5 and 8 percent in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Iran can therefore disrupt the waterway, but it cannot sustain that disruption indefinitely at an acceptable economic and military cost.

Third, repeated use of the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon invites adaptation. Just as Iran has sought to adapt to sanctions, GCC energy producers will have stronger incentives to bypass Hormuz by expanding pipelines to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Importing countries will diversify suppliers, invest in strategic reserves and develop alternative sources of LNG, fertilisers and critical materials. Companies will re-evaluate supply chains built around a single passage.

After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, governments, especially in the European Union, increasingly treated domestically generated renewable electricity as a security asset. The International Energy Agency subsequently raised its five-year forecast for global renewable capacity expansion by almost 30 percent, partly because energy insecurity accelerated policy support.

Such adjustments will be gradual. Alternatives cannot quickly replace oil in transport and petrochemicals, LNG in some electricity systems, natural gas in fertiliser production or helium in specialised industrial uses. Low-income countries also face financial and institutional constraints that may slow diversification and investment in renewables. Even so, persistent insecurity strengthens the economic case for projects that reduce dependence on Hormuz.

Tehran therefore faces a difficult trade-off. Limited, calibrated disruption can raise the costs of US military pressure, divide opposing coalitions and create bargaining space over sanctions and regional security. Prolonged or indiscriminate disruption would damage Iran’s own economy, alienate Asian partners such as China and accelerate investments that weaken its future leverage. Hormuz is therefore a powerful economic weapon, but one that Iran cannot use without also bearing some of its costs.

Hormuz is a powerful weapon because current dependence is high and short-term alternatives are limited. But its effectiveness has an expiry date. When that date arrives will depend on technological progress, available capital, political will and, crucially, on how aggressively Iran chooses to wield it. Iran can weaponise Hormuz to influence negotiations today. But every time it does, it gives others another reason to reduce their dependence on the strait. The more aggressively Iran wields the weapon, the faster it may blunt it.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Argentina and Mexico join Africa in backing FIFA’s Infantino: What to know
articles.excerpt: World football’s growing divide has deepened with the declarations of support for FIFA’s defiant Gianni Infantino by Argentina and Mexico, coming only a day after Africa unanimously voted to back the ...
articles.body_text:
World football’s growing divide has deepened with the declarations of support for FIFA’s defiant Gianni Infantino by Argentina and Mexico, coming only a day after Africa unanimously voted to back the president of football’s global governing body.

Infantino continues to face fierce backlash over a now-abandoned proposal to sell off a number of commercial rights to the World Cup and other FIFA events.

Following a meeting in Rabat this week, FIFA said it had apologised to its members for mistakes around the proposal. It also pledged to review the processes that led to the controversy, but backed its president.

Infantino’s biggest opponent remains UEFA, the sport’s governing body in Europe, which confirmed on Thursday that it stands by its vote to boycott FIFA. One of its members, Norway, has now called for the Swiss Italian’s resignation.

Al Jazeera takes a look at the growing standoff, which is pushing countries and entire continents in different directions.

Although only football associations, not continental confederations, the move by Mexico and Argentina will come as a significant boost to Infantino, but is also a prime example of the civil war brewing in the so-called “people’s game”.

In supporting Infantino, the Mexican ⁠Football Federation (FMF), cohosts of the recently concluded 2026 World Cup, have crucially broken ranks with their own regional confederation by backing Infantino after CONCACAF called for a “comprehensive reckoning” with his presidency.

“The FMF will neither recognise nor ‌approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made … by President Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations,” it said in a statement.

“The FMF supports President Infantino’s leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening.”

South America’s CONMEBOL issued a statement on Thursday rejecting any attempt to oust Infantino that did not involve a vote of all 211 members – a move that seems to counter the stance taken by UEFA.

In a letter to Infantino, Argentina’s football association (AFA), whose team failed to defend their Qatar 2022 title in the final of the 2026 edition, moved beyond the statement from its confederation by expressing its outright support of Infantino.

The AFA cited FIFA’s work over ⁠the last 10 years, saying it had “centred on the development of football worldwide and institutional strength based on a clear, stable, and transparent governance model”.

While the AFA acknowledged that the proposal generated far ⁠more uncertainties than certainties and that errors had been made, it said the ⁠way forward was to continue working under FIFA’s leadership before next year’s Congress.

That will be staged in Morocco in March, where Infantino is expected to be challenged for the presidency, having been unopposed in his two re-elections.

CONMEBOL’s earlier statement had expressed concerns over the “repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue”, stressing the importance of institutional reforms FIFA introduced more than a decade ago to promote transparency.

On Thursday, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously backed Infantino’s leadership.

Africa’s body is the second-largest on football’s global stage with 54 members, only one less than UEFA.

That is a significant number for Infantino to call upon to counter UEFA’s threat, if he can continue to draw upon the support he has so far been given from parts of Asia.

CAF President Patrice Motsepe is a longtime ally of Infantino, but to have secured the backing of the entire membership on the continent strengthens Infantino’s hand against any short-term challenges – as well as before his bid for a fourth presidential term.

Norwegian Football ⁠Federation (NFF) ⁠President Lise Klaveness called for the resignation of Infantino on Friday, saying he no longer ⁠had the confidence of the football community.

“He does not have the institutional trust required to govern ‌FIFA stably in the times we are in,” Klaveness ⁠told reporters following the ⁠NFF’s monthly board meeting.

“There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in ⁠trouble, and we must ⁠have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the ⁠FIFA president to resign now.”

Asia’s confederation said it “stood in solidarity” with UEFA and CONCACAF, which runs football in North and Central America as well as the Caribbean.

Asian Football Confederation ‌(AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa issued his own statement, before his organisation’s public stance, to brand FIFA’s lack of consultation over its plan ⁠to sell stakes in ⁠the World Cup to private investors “totally unacceptable”, saying the move undermined the sport’s existing continental structure.

The AFC did not threaten a boycott in its backing of UEFA and CONCACAF, but has since welcomed the withdrawal of Infantino’s proposal.

An interesting twist is Sheikh Salman’s failed presidential bid in 2016 when he was defeated by Infantino, and the speculation that he is set to stand again in the upcoming election.

Indonesia, Qatar, Kuwait, Sri Lanka and the Philippines, who are all part of the AFC bloc, have come out in support of Infantino.

The Croatian Football Federation on Thursday were among the individual national associations to withdraw support ‌for Infantino, following similar moves from England and Albania.

“This decision followed a thorough reassessment within the federation in light of recent developments surrounding the FIFA World Cup 2026 and discussions within our governing bodies,” Croatia’s federation said.

Also on Thursday, players’ union FIFPRO said Infantino’s proposal ‌was ‌not just a governance failure but a “profound abuse of presidential power”.

FIFA has said that all actions taken over the commercial rights proposal complied with its regulations and stressed that mistakes related to process and communication rather than breaches of governance rules.

articles.title: First Thing: Soaring oil profits from US-Iran conflict drive calls for windfall tax
articles.excerpt:
Environmentalists and activists furious as Trump’s policies raise costs for Americans. Plus, the masterpiece that was left lying in museum storage

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up...
articles.body_text:
Environmentalists and activists furious as Trump’s policies raise costs for Americans. Plus, the masterpiece that was left lying in museum storage

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. Donald Trump’s statement that oil companies have made “too much money” from the Iran war has angered environmentalists, who say his policies were designed to benefit those very corporations.

Americans have paid more than $78bn more at the pump since the start of the Iran war, according to a Brown University tracker. A recent analysis from the environmental advocacy group Climate Power and the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal thinktank, found that Trump’s policies had cost the average American family $285 more when filling up their cars.

As oil companies have reaped billions from the Iran war’s impact on fossil fuel prices, the Rhode Island senator Sheldon Whitehouse and the California congressman Ro Khanna have proposed taxing big oil’s windfall profits from the crisis, and said proceeds from that tax should go to American families who are paying more for fuel.

What policies has Trump enacted to help the oil industry? Since re-entering the White House last year, he has eased dozens of restrictions and regulations on fossil fuel expansion, exempted fossil fuel producers from environmental rules, and signed an executive order last year directing the attorney general to prioritize blocking climate lawsuits targeting oil majors. Trump has also personally invested in major oil companies.

Donald Trump has made a second attempt to restrict the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, just weeks after the US supreme court rejected his initial, more sweeping attempt to deny automatic citizenship to children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents.

Trump on Thursday signed two executive orders that seek to broaden the categories of children ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”. The directives are expected to face legal challenges. Trump’s obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had an overtly political element from the start – his original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claims about Barack Obama’s eligibility for office, something he repeated when facing Kamala Harris as an electoral opponent.

What did the supreme court previously rule? In the court’s June decision, the chief justice, John Roberts, said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.”

Law enforcement officials provided false information to federal judges as they sought to build a criminal case against the independent journalist Georgia Fort in connection with a January protest, her lawyers said in court filings on Thursday asking that the charges against her be dismissed.

Fort was one of nearly 40 people charged after demonstrators interrupted a service at Cities church in St Paul, Minnesota, after they learned that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official was a pastor there. Trump administration officials vowed to arrest anyone involved in the protest.

How has the Trump administration expanded the tracking of immigrants? The US is tracking nearly 54,000 immigrants through GPS-enabled ankle monitors as part of an ICE electronic surveillance program, according to The Geo Group, a private prison corporation. Early last year, just 17,000 immigrants were wearing the devices. Executives said a large number of participants had been shifted from less intensive forms of surveillance, such as phone check-ins, to ankle monitors.

Why have airports become an increased target for ICE enforcement? With a goal of 2,000 daily immigration arrests, ICE has started detaining people – many of whom have overstayed visas after coming to the US legally and have pending applications for immigration relief – in public places far from security checkpoints, whether at ticket counters or near gates. Authorities have generally avoided immigration enforcement at airports so as not to disrupt domestic travel.

A Thai teenager killed two of his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence.

Donald Trump has doubled down on his criticism of Jeanine Pirro after the US attorney for the District of Columbia publicly challenged his claims that vandals had damaged the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.

The FCC has scrapped the limit on local TV ownership, in a win for major media conglomerates.

Donald Trump has ordered a new 15% tariff on imported products made of polysilicon, a key material for solar panels and microchips that is primarily produced by China.

The Republican US senator Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation center after a fall that left him hospitalized.

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media firm’s platforms. The ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial that the company lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company had knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms

James McClellan argues that modern aesthetics lack the texture that horror movies need to thrive, a texture that can be more easily found in past eras – whether smacking a TV to improve a fuzzy signal in Backrooms, or the kitschy, old-fashioned gag gift that is central to Obsession.

The University of Minnesota withdrew an offer for Raz Segal to lead its Center for Holocaust and Genocide Studies after an organized campaign against his hiring. Alice Speri has the story.

There seems to be a fight over datacenters in nearly every city in the US right now. And despite the extreme polarization of today’s politics, the opposition tends to be bipartisan. George Chidi has been in Little Rock, Arkansas, to observe one such clash.

Much of the continent is battling wildfires and drought during a summer of extreme heat, and our picture editors have selected some of the most striking images of the impact for this gallery.

The curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing a work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artists after the curator chanced upon an unattributed still life in the museum’s storage area.

articles.title: William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69
articles.excerpt:
Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee

William Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive...
articles.body_text:
Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee

William Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive style invigorated work by Madonna, Blur, All Saints, U2 and more, has died aged 69.

A statement on his social media, attributed to family and friends, said he died at home on 23 July. “He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness,” the statement read. No cause of death was given.

Orbit was most famous for his collaboration with Madonna on her 1998 album Ray of Light: his strikingly original backings, rooted in trip-hop, jungle and techno, marked a new chapter for one of pop’s greatest stars, resulting in hits such as Frozen, The Power of Goodbye and the giddy title track. It had multi-platinum sales across the world, won Madonna three of the five Grammy awards she was nominated for in 1999, and has become seen by many as Madonna’s single greatest studio album.

But his work stretched far beyond one client, spanning Blur’s exploratory, emotionally scarred album 13, All Saints’ UK No 1 Pure Shores, Pink’s UK No 3 new wave hit Feel Good Time and more. He was credited as a guest artist on the latter, and released a raft of albums and singles under his own name: his electronic twist on Samuel Barber’s Adagio for Strings, aided by a trance remix by Ferry Corsten, reached the UK Top 5 in 1999.

Success came relatively late for Orbit – at least in pop music terms. He was born William Wainwright in 1956 and raised in north London, the son of two teachers he described as “decidedly working class and poor … they’d struggled to become middle class”. He left school at 16 and became what he described as a “post-hippie”, living in a squat, doing occasional low-paid labour and, by his recollection, consuming “a Mars bar and an acid tab a day”.

In 1980 he formed the electronic/ambient trio Torch Song with Laurie Mayer and Grant Gilbert, and were signed to the label IRS, releasing three albums between 1984 and 1987. Well versed in electronic music production after gradually assembling a studio full of digital and analogue gear, he was hired to create the soundtrack to the Rob Lowe and Patrick Swayze film Youngblood, and remixes for pop artists – including Madonna. Wielding hip-house breakbeats and puckish instrumentation, he gave a chirpier cast to her prowling, sexually infatuated early 90s singles Justify My Love and Erotica.

He was now on Madonna’s radar, but it would be later in the decade they would work together on original tracks. In the interim, Torch Song released another album in 1995 and he had another successful project, Bassomatic, whose psychedelic baggy epic Fascinating Rhythm hit the UK Top 10. He’d released his solo debut album in 1987, and found acclaim in the 90s with a series of albums with the title Strange Cargo. 1993’s Strange Cargo III featured a young Beth Orton on a track; Orbit produced her debut album Superpinkymandy the same year, and went on to remix her single Central Reservation.

Meanwhile, Madonna was struggling to make a new album and redefine herself: she had scrapped sessions with R&B producer Babyface in favour of a search for a new collaborator, and only had a small handful of songs for a new album. Orbit’s pedigree meant he was invited by her manager to submit tracks and was hired: “Just hang in there, work on your stuff, get your chops together and eventually you get a stroke of luck,” he later reflected. He and Madonna worked up much of the album together in studios in New York and Los Angeles.

“William is a complete madman genius,” Madonna said of the Ray of Light sessions. “I’d come to him with an idea of where I wanted to go musically, hum melodies or read lyrics, and then leave him alone in the laboratory. Sometimes he’d go in the direction I wanted and sometimes he’d swerve off somewhere else entirely. We’d end up with trance tracks that were eight minutes long and then keep adding and subtracting until we had real verses and choruses. We really put our noses to the grindstone.”

Orbit’s astonishing range of sound – heavy breakbeats, acoustic guitars, trance synths and more – was put to use on everything from sweeping ballads to the pell-mell acid house of the title track, re-establishing Madonna’s credentials as a vanguard pop star and earning her first non-video Grammy award wins.

Eager not to repeat herself, she switched her core producer up again for her next album Music, to Mirwais, though Orbit was retained for three of its tracks. He also produced two successful standalone Madonna singles which appeared on soundtracks: 1999’s Beautiful Stranger, from Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, and her 2000 cover of Don McLean’s American Pie, from The Next Best Thing (which she also starred in). Orbit returned for her 2012 album MDNA, co-producing six of its songs. Earlier this year, Orbit said: “I will always love that woman. For real. She made my career.”

The late 1990s were a hugely industrious period for Orbit. In 1999, he released Pieces in a Modern Style, an album of classical reworkings including his successful take on Samuel Barber (an earlier 1995 version had been deleted from sale after an objection from composer Arvo Pärt).

1999 also saw the release of Blur’s album 13: similarly to Madonna, Blur wanted to reinvent themselves after five albums with producer Stephen Street, and had been impressed by Orbit’s earlier remixes of their work (collected on the album Bustin’ and Dronin’). 13 charted Damon Albarn’s breakup from musician Justine Frischmann, and the frontman later described Orbit’s role on the album as “a psychiatrist”. Like Ray of Light, 13 is regarded as one of the most singular and brilliantly realised albums in Blur’s catalogue, with Orbit crafting experimental yet commercial material with the group, including hit singles Tender and Coffee and TV.

Ray of Light’s success meant that he was also courted by a range of pop artists in the years that followed, including Britney Spears, Melanie C, Robbie Williams, Chris Brown, Pink, No Doubt and ex-Girls Aloud singer Nadine Coyle. He collaborated with co-writer Beck on Pink’s Feel Good Time – another film soundtrack hit, for 2003’s Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle.

He brought the psychedelic Ray of Light palette of guitars, bleeps and breakbeats to two superb singles by British girl group All Saints: Black Coffee and Pure Shores, both UK chart-toppers. Regarded by pop fans as some of Orbit’s masterpieces, he told the Guardian in 2021 he initially thought the latter song was “pure shite” because it had taken so long to make: “When you really slave over something, it takes years until you can really listen to it with pleasure.” He worked with All Saints again on two tracks from 2018 album Testament.

Orbit produced two new songs for U2 which appeared on their compilation The Best of 1990-2000: Electrical Storm, which reached No 5 in the UK, and The Hands That Built America, which was used as the theme for Martin Scorsese’s 2002 film Gangs of New York.

Orbit’s only other full-album project for a pop artist was Katie Melua’s fourth album The House, released in 2010. His work rate slowed thereafter, though he did bring a long-lost pop curio to fruition: There Must Be More to Life Than This, a Freddie Mercury and Michael Jackson duet, originally recorded in the early 1980s but eventually produced by Orbit and released in 2014.

Orbit also continued to release solo albums, adding six more after Pieces in a Modern Style, including a 2010 sequel to that release. His most recent album is 2022’s The Painter.

In March this year, he scotched rumours of a possible new project with Madonna. “Let’s put this Madonna ROL [Ray of Light] 2.0 thing to rest here and now folks. Can get exhausting. Is not going to happen … I have an album ready that imho is indeed the successor to ROL. Everything about how it was made and how it sounds yells that from the first few bars. And I reached out. And there has been heard. Nil response.”

He told the Guardian in 2021 that he struggled with substance use four years before. As well as heavy marijuana use, he was taking “LSD, mushrooms, MDMA, coke, some hormones that everybody was experimenting with. Codeine. I wasn’t aware of what I was doing and I ended up having a psychotic episode.” He was sectioned. “Fortunately, once the drugs were out of my system, I finally got back to being normal – and out I was,” he said.

articles.title: GOP senator deals crushing blow to Trump's AG nominee after Alaska lobbying blitz
articles.excerpt: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Senate impasse over President Donald Trump's nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general as Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis remain noncommittal....
articles.body_text:
Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Senate impasse over President Donald Trump's nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general as Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis remain noncommittal.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche just lost the last little bit of cushion he had left to survive confirmation.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, announced that she would not support Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s top prosecutor and law enforcement official, dealing another blow to his rocky confirmation process.

Her defection, despite a heavy lobbying effort by Blanche that saw him make the trek to Alaska, means that Senate Republican leadership can’t afford to lose anymore votes to get him across the finish line, given that Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., though now back home, has still not returned to the Senate.

COLLINS DROPS THE HAMMER ON TRUMP'S PICK TO LEAD DOJ, JEOPARDIZING PATH TO CONFIRMATION

Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, speaks to members of the media following a vote outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on Friday, Oct. 3, 2025. (Graeme Sloan/Getty Images)

Murkowski acknowledged Blanche’s visit to Alaska and heavy lobbying effort throughout the last few weeks, but it’s his connection to President Donald Trump’s nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, and broader concerns of a weaponized Justice Department, that proved the nail in the coffin for her.

"The politicization — even weaponization — of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it," Murkowski said in a statement. "I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators."

"I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage," she continued. "Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds."

TRUMP'S AG PICK SURVIVES — FOR NOW — AS REPUBLICANS QUESTION IF WHITE HOUSE DEAL WILL HOLD

To Murkowski’s latter issue, several lawmakers in both sides of the aisle acknowledge that though Blanche and the Department of Justice (DOJ) agreed to permanently rescind the fund in writing to Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, there’s nothing stopping Trump from reviving it.

And he’s on several occasions made clear he wants to see it come back.

Before making her decision, Trump already took a snipe at her during an interview with Punch Bowl News published Friday morning.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) arrives for a meeting with Senate Republicans in the U.S. Capitol on June 28, 2025 in Washington, DC. Senate Republicans overnight released a new version of the "One, Big, Beautiful Bill," as they approach U.S. President Donald Trump's July 4 deadline. (Photo by Al Drago/Getty Images)

"I’m against Murkowski," Trump said. "I do more for Alaska than any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s not good."

Meanwhile, it’s unclear whether the Senate will actually vote on Blanche on Friday, which could be the upper chamber’s grand finale of the summer before it exits Washington, D.C., for the remainder of August.

And there’s still one more Republican that hasn’t weighed in on how they’ll vote: Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La.

If he defects, and McConnell is still gone, it will be a 50-50 vote. That means Vice President JD Vance would need to break the tie. But for now, only Murkowski and Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, are publicly opposing Blanche’s confirmation.

"The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration," Murkowski said. "I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Murkowski won’t vote for Trump’s nomination of Blanche as attorney general
articles.excerpt:
Alaska Republican is concerned that proposed fund to compensate January 6 rioters will proceed even though Blanche confirmed it was dead

Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, announce...
articles.body_text:
Alaska Republican is concerned that proposed fund to compensate January 6 rioters will proceed even though Blanche confirmed it was dead

Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, announced early on Friday that she will not vote for Donald Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche as US attorney general, leaving his elevation from “acting” to official confirmation in the post even narrower.

Murkowski issued a statement expressing her concerns that the Trump administration could proceed with its proposed fund to compensate rioters who invaded the US Capitol on January 6 in a failed attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s defeat of Trump in the 2020 presidential election.

She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber.

Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund.

Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche.

Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with.

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky is not currently attending sessions because of his health, giving the GOP little room to lose senators and still confirm the president’s pick.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: US cities expand cooling centers but struggle to get people inside
articles.excerpt:
More air-conditioned spaces are open during extreme heat, but distance, stigma and risk perception keep many away

Responding to an uptick in extreme heat waves this summer, US cities have increased t...
articles.body_text:
More air-conditioned spaces are open during extreme heat, but distance, stigma and risk perception keep many away

Responding to an uptick in extreme heat waves this summer, US cities have increased their efforts to establish cooling centers to keep people safe but continue to encounter a problem: actually getting people to enter the public air-conditioned spaces.

Lower-income people, who often do not have – or cannot afford to operate – air conditioning, face a greater risk of heat-related illness or deaths, which means public agencies in the US concentrate their efforts on trying to reach them.

But for various reasons, including the length of a commute to a cooling center or a sense that the extreme heat is not especially dangerous, they often still remain outdoors or at home, experts say.

“It’s not easy to survive unsheltered in New York City, even in the best of weather,” David Giffen, executive director of the Coalition for the Homeless, a non-profit in New York. “These are individuals that have skills and strength and resilience that has allowed them to survive like that, so they don’t necessarily think, ‘Oh, now it’s getting hot, and I should finally come indoors.’”

The United States and other parts of the world have this year repeatedly experienced heat domes, a phenomenon in which high pressure traps hot air over a region, preventing cool air from entering. The continental US endured the second-hottest first half of the year on record in 2026, according to the National Centers for Environmental Information.

The affected areas have seen a spike in heat-related illnesses and deaths. On 3 July in New York, when temperatures reached more than 100F, hospitals saw 156 visits to emergency rooms because of heat-related illnesses, the highest number since at least 2017, according to city data. On 4 July and the week prior in Maine, hospitals received 128 heat-related visits to emergency rooms, which was also the highest number since at least 2017, according to state data.

This summer in Maryland, there have been at least 38 heat-related deaths, already surpassing the total number from 2025, the Baltimore Sun reported.

To prevent such outcomes, New York officials added 23 cooling centers to the city’s network. This year, the city has had an average of 585 cooling centers open on weekdays; last year, it averaged 560, according to New York City emergency management.

The centers are air-conditioned facilities such as libraries, community centers and senior centers.

In addition to having air conditioning and drinking water, the spaces must also feature staff who tell visitors, “Hey, we are a cooling center. Is there anything that you might need?” said Jocelyn Rajaballey, a human services specialist at the emergency management agency.

The city’s health system started using vans too this year to reach older adult and homeless populations and offer wellness checks, medical care, water, and transport to cooling centers or healthcare facilities, according to the city.

In Maine, where residents are less likely to have or use air conditioning than much of the country, the state had until recently seen about 60 to 70 cooling centers open over a five-day period during the summer; this year and last year, the state had stretches were the government opened more than 100 centers, according to Bill Guindon, mass care coordinator at the Maine emergency management agency.

“It’s kind of a resort for people that don’t have access to cooling resources,” Guindon said. “In some areas, with the individual on fixed incomes … they have to choose between feeding and heat and air conditioning.”

Still, some cooling centers are often underutilized, even during extreme heatwaves.

Maine used to have more mild summers and people are accustomed to not needing air conditioning, said Vanessa Corson, public information officer for the state’s emergency management agency.

The state is largely rural, which means residents might have to travel a fair distance to get to a center.

They “may not feel like getting up to go to a cooling center and think, ‘I can just tough it out at home,’” Corson said. “Another challenge is, honestly, swallowing your pride, and there are people who think that they don’t need a cooling center.”

New York City has tried to help residents by installing kiosks with walking directions to the nearest cooling center.

But people who are homeless and stay away from shelters because of a bad experience might also avoid the centers, Giffen said.

Emergency management officials encourage people to check on their neighbors during extreme heatwaves.

Particularly since the Covid-19 pandemic, “we tend to be not as socially connected to our own neighbors as we once were”, Guindon, from Maine, said. “The communities that have had success on this know their neighbors and where the needs are.”

articles.title: Ghostly outline of long-lost garden at Winston Churchill's birthplace revealed in aerial photos
articles.excerpt:
Ahead of the nation's 250th birthday, archaeologists are digging at the site of the Battle of Bunker Hill in search of clues to a history older than the United States.

Sweltering heat in the United K...
articles.body_text:
Ahead of the nation's 250th birthday, archaeologists are digging at the site of the Battle of Bunker Hill in search of clues to a history older than the United States.

Sweltering heat in the United Kingdom has revealed the remains of a long-lost 18th-century garden at a major tourist attraction.

Aerial photos show the outline of the 300-year-old formal garden at Blenheim Palace, an estate about eight miles northwest of Oxford, England, news agency SWNS reported.

Blenheim Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built between 1705 and 1722, is famously the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill, as well as the ancestral home of the Dukes of Marlborough.

HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR

The outline was revealed during the latest heat wave this summer after prolonged dry weather created parch marks, or dry patches in the grass, across the grounds.

A spokesperson from Blenheim Palace told Fox News Digital the marks will be visible "until cooler temperatures arrive and sufficient rain falls to green up the shallow-rooted grass."

Sweltering summer heat in the United Kingdom has revealed the outline of a long-lost 18th-century formal garden at Blenheim Palace, Winston Churchill's birthplace, after prolonged dry weather. (Pete Seaward/SWNS)

"There isn't currently any rain in the forecast for the next few weeks, so it will be visible for a while yet," the representative added.

The patches, officials say, reveal the outline of the original garden, giving a glimpse of what it looked like 300 years ago.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND

It was originally created in 1705 by royal gardener Henry Wise and was once protected by a high stone wall with bastions.

The garden was dismantled in 1760s, SWNS said, when Blenheim Palace's gardener Lancelot "Capability" Brown redesigned the palace grounds.

Blenheim Palace visitors can explore the historic estate, including the room where Sir Winston Churchill was born, alongside its expansive gardens and State Rooms. (Bettmann via Getty Images; Pete Seaward/SWNS)

The technical term for the garden is a "parterre," from the French term par terre, meaning "on the ground."

Pictures show that the parterre consisted of symmetrical flower beds and paths.

DNA CRACKS CENTURIES-OLD MURDER MYSTERY INVOLVING ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS FAMILIES

In a statement, Blenheim Palace head gardener Andy Mills said the parch marks "allow us to trace the intricate design and scale of the original parterre."

"The excessively dry weather has given us a fascinating bird's-eye view into Blenheim’s past," said Mills, as SWNS noted.

"It’s a brilliant reminder of the formal gardens that came before."

Mills added, "It’s a brilliant reminder of the formal gardens that came before and the layers of history that continue to shape the palace’s landscape."

The palace is popular among tourists for its opulent State Rooms and extensive gardens, as well as the room where Churchill was born.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Blenheim Palace welcomed 980,678 visitors in 2025, according to visitor data compiled by Historic Houses.

Blenheim Palace is the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill and remains one of Britain's most significant historic estates and tourist attractions. (Pete Seaward / SWNS; Roger Viollet via Getty Images/Roger Viollet via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Blenheim Palace for further comment.

The discovery follows other recent historical finds shedding light on life in 18th-century Britain.

Blenheim Palace, Oxfordshire, England, is the principal residence of the Dukes of Marlborough, and the only non-royal, non-episcopal country house in England to hold the title of palace. The palace, one of England's largest houses, was built between 1705 and 1722. (Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Last summer, archaeologists unveiled the remarkably well-preserved wreck of the British warship The Northumberland, which sank off the coast of Kent, England in 1703.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Earlier this year, construction workers in England unearthed a 300-year-old cannon during routine work in the city of Kingston upon Hull.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Knockout at Maui beach caps turbulent stretch for Democratic candidate facing felony allegations
articles.excerpt: Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a k...
articles.body_text:
Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a knife. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

A Democratic congressional candidate knocked unconscious in a Maui beach fight now faces felony charges in three separate cases, including allegations he threatened a county employee with what appeared to be a gun and assaulted a hospital nurse.

Kirill Basin, 40, was charged with two counts of first-degree terroristic threatening after the Aug. 1 confrontation at Keawakapu Beach in South Kihei.

Video captured an argument over music that escalated when Basin shoved Kama Homan and swung a beach chair at him. Homan pushed the chair away and knocked Basin unconscious.

HAWAII DEMOCRATIC HOUSE CANDIDATE FACES FELONY THREAT CHARGES AFTER BEACH FIGHT CAUGHT ON VIDEO

A criminal complaint alleges Basin later threatened Homan with a knife. At Tuesday’s court hearing, a judge maintained Basin’s $1 million bail, ordered him not to contact Homan or four others and barred him from Keawakapu Beach and its parking lot.

Kirill Basin, right, confronts another man during a beach altercation at Keawakapu Beach on Maui that was captured on video. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

But the beach confrontation was not Basin’s first trip through the criminal justice system this year.

Four days later, prosecutors used the beach arrest to seek revocation of Basin’s bail in a separate case accusing him of assaulting a Maui Memorial Medical Center nurse.

Prosecutors said Basin threatened beachgoers, telling them, "I’ll put you in the ground" and "I’ll kill you."

HAWAII DEMOCRATIC HOUSE CANDIDATE FACES FELONY THREAT CHARGES AFTER BEACH FIGHT CAUGHT ON VIDEO

He then allegedly reached into a small black bag and said, "Do I have a gun? I’ll kill you," before producing and brandishing a knife as a beachgoer tried to de-escalate the confrontation, the Aug. 5 court filing says.

In the new beach case, Judge Christopher Dunn found probable cause to support a first-degree terroristic-threatening charge, the filing says. In the separate hospital-assault case, a judge issued a $400,000 bench warrant.

That filing connected the beach confrontation to a criminal case that had been pending since June, extending a court record that began months before Basin was knocked unconscious on the sand.

Hawaii Democratic congressional candidate Kirill Basin is seen during a confrontation with beachgoers at Keawakapu Beach on Maui before his arrest on felony terroristic threatening charges. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

Basin’s first court case this year began May 2, when police arrested him on a disorderly-conduct charge. Prosecutors say he fought or threatened people, made too much noise or used offensive language, even after he was told to stop.

Later that month, a Maui grand jury indicted Basin on two counts of first-degree terroristic threatening over a May 29 encounter with a County of Maui employee.

Kirill Basin is seen near beach chairs during the confrontation at Keawakapu Beach that ended with his arrest on felony terroristic threatening charges. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

Prosecutors alleged in a July court filing that Basin pulled a tan-and-green handgun from a backpack and made threats involving the weapon while two other county employees watched.

"On May 29, 2026, [Basin] approached a County of Maui employee … pulled out a tan and green colored handgun from his backpack, and made verbal threats about using the handgun," prosecutors wrote.

"Further, two other County of Maui employees were also present and both felt threatened for their lives due to [Basin’s] actions," the filing said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Basin’s lawyers sharply disputed that version. In a later filing, they said police reports and surveillance footage showed Basin briefly displayed a muzzle-down pellet gun, did not point it at anyone and told witnesses to call police.

Within two weeks, Basin was facing a second felony case, this one over an alleged encounter at Maui Memorial Medical Center.

Basin was charged with second-degree assault and two counts of harassment after the hospital incident.

Prosecutors wrote that Basin had been admitted to Maui Memorial’s behavioral-health unit for evaluation, became aggressive and attempted to leave the emergency room before discharge. When nurses tried to restrain him, prosecutors alleged, Basin kicked one of them in the thigh.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Basin pleaded not guilty. On July 20, the court granted his request to leave Hawaii for inpatient treatment in Arizona, subject to conditions that included surrendering his passport, following a court-approved itinerary and appearing remotely for hearings.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

By July 27, the court was told Basin was in the Maui Recovery program in Lahaina. But after the Aug. 1 beach arrest, the court issued a $400,000 bench warrant in the hospital-assault case as prosecutors sought to revoke his bail.

Fox News Digital has requested Maui Police Department reports, body-camera footage, dispatch audio, witness statements and evidence logs tied to the four criminal incidents. Fox News Digital also reached out to Basin’s attorney, Brandon Segal, for comment.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Weather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heat
articles.excerpt:
High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia

Another pulse of heat is expected to affect central and western Europe next week. The lat...
articles.body_text:
High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia

Another pulse of heat is expected to affect central and western Europe next week. The latest forecast models show daily maximum temperatures well into the high 30s celsius widely across France, Spain and Italy during the first half of the week, while Germany, Poland and Czechia will experience the highest temperatures towards the end of the week. The shift in the focus of the heat as the week progresses can be attributed to the movement of high pressure. At the start of the week, low pressure centred in the Atlantic and high pressure centred over the low countries will draw warm air from southern Europe northwards into parts of France. During the working week, the high pressure will slip a little farther south and east, enabling the warm air once situated over western Europe to make inroads into parts of Germany and central Europe.

The heat in central and western Europe this summer has been unrelenting. Last week’s weather tracker highlighted record-breaking temperatures for the month of July in Austria. However, only a few days later, on 4 August, the all-time record was shattered with 41.0C achieved in Stammersdorf, north-east of the capital, Vienna. This comfortably broke the previous all-time record set in August 2003 by 0.7C. Unbelievably, that record was broken again the following day when 41.2C was recorded in Deutsch-Altenburg. Slovakia also set an all-time record on the same day, of 41.4C. The continuing European heatwave, associated with a vertically extensive anticyclone, raised the freezing level above 4,000 metres across much of the Alpine region. This represents a level in the atmosphere well above many Alpine glaciers, accelerating the seasonal melting process. On the opposite side of the Atlantic, 51.8C was recorded in Badwater, California, the highest temperature in the US for 2026 so far.

Although south-eastern parts of Europe have eluded the worst of the summer heat, wildfires have ignited in recent days. Extremely strong northerly wind gusts in excess of 70mph ripped through the Greek Islands on 29 July, causing medium-voltage power lines to sway and produce sparks that set fire to vegetation below. Part of the palm forest at Preveli beach, Crete, was damaged by a wildfire but the centre of the forest was spared from the worst of the destruction.

articles.title: Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war
articles.excerpt:
By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back

Tehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed t...
articles.body_text:
By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back

Tehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed to keep Donald Trump embroiled in the Iran conflict until the midterm elections, in the hope of inflicting the same ruinous blow on his presidency as Jimmy Carter suffered over the 1979-81 US embassy hostage crisis.

For many inside Iran, inflicting meaningful revenge on Trump is a legitimate and self-standing war aim, reflected in the mood of those attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei where demands for retribution were ubiquitous.

While Iranian officials since the 1979 Islamic revolution have never trusted the US, that animus is now also directed personally towards Trump. He not only tore up the painfully negotiated nuclear deal in 2018, but he sanctioned the assassination of the military leader Qassem Suleimani and twice involved Iran in negotiations on its nuclear programme only to launch wars against it. He shows no remorse for the killing of the country’s supreme leader, or for the attempt on the life of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian.

As the countdown to November’s midterms begins, what could be Trump’s political demise has become a subject of obsessive speculation in Tehran. Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to the war’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined.

But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency that after agreeing a route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said.

To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms.

If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to the Trump administration … It will continue to play games.”

Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said.

From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on the battlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come.

Few in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.”

Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”.

Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.”

Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war.

The bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving.

Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy.

But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said.

Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases.

Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”.

If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.”

Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.

articles.title: Which teams are overrated or underrated in new preseason college football Coaches Poll?
articles.excerpt:
On this episode of Don't @ Me, Dan Dakich absolutely exposes the University of Michigan as the most corrupt college football program in history

The release of the preseason Coaches Poll means one thi...
articles.body_text:
On this episode of Don't @ Me, Dan Dakich absolutely exposes the University of Michigan as the most corrupt college football program in history

The release of the preseason Coaches Poll means one thing: college football season is almost here. And it's time to start the arguing.

That arguing this offseason has mostly centered on the fight for supremacy between the SEC and Big Ten Conferences, thanks to the Indiana Hoosiers winning the National Championship and closing out an undefeated 16-0 season. That was just a few months after Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian said undefeated teams were a thing of the past in the NIL era.

But 2026 is a new season, and thanks to the transfer portal and NIL, it's harder than ever to gauge the strength of a team or roster from year to year. This upcoming season might be even harder than most, considering the turnover among coaches at top-tier programs.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS FINALLY BACK AFTER MONTHS OF NCAA LAWSUITS, NIL DRAMA AND CONGRESSIONAL FIGHTS

LSU new head coach Lane Kiffin speaks at South Stadium Club at Tiger Stadium on Dec. 1, 2025. (Matthew Hinton/Imagn Images)

The Florida Gators have a new head coach in Jon Sumrall. Lane Kiffin fled Ole Miss for the LSU Tigers, while Pete Golding took over in Oxford. Auburn hired Alex Golesh from USF. Penn State replaced James Franklin with Matt Campbell. Kyle Whittingham left his longtime home at Utah to run a Michigan Wolverines program beset by turmoil after the departure of Sherrone Moore. Morgan Scalley is the new head coach in Salt Lake, while UCLA brought in Bob Chesney to try and revitalize the program.

So how did the coaches, or more accurately, the staffers who actually do the voting in the poll, do in evaluating all of these changes heading into 2026?

To evaluate it, we can compare it against a potentially less biased source: analytics-driven ranking systems. These polls, which rely on efficiency numbers on offense, defense, and special teams, adjusted for opponent, are often a better indication of a team's underlying quality. Though it's up to human voters to weigh the importance of wins and losses, relative to how a team played.

THREE TEAMS RANKED OUTSIDE THE TOP-12 OF THE COACHES POLL WHO WILL MAKE THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

For example, if say, LSU racks up 700 yards on offense, allows 75 yards on defense, but fumbles at the 1-yard line every drive, the Tigers would get credit for the efficiency they demonstrated on offense and defense, even if they lose 3-0. Evaluating the importance of how a team played to wins and losses is one of the most important things poll voters, and now the selection committee, can do. And they often do it poorly.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Ohio State head coach Ryan Day shouts to his team against Rutgers during the first half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Nov. 22, 2025, in Columbus, Ohio. (AP Photo/Jay LaPrete)

But to test these preseason rankings, we can compare it to SP+, created by Bill Connelly and housed at ESPN. One of the best of this type of metric-driven ranking systems, SP+ released its preseason "poll" ahead of the 2026 season, evaluating last year's performances, returning production, and recruiting rankings.

Impressively, the top three are almost identical. Ohio State and Oregon are the top two teams in SP+, and the top two teams in the Coaches Poll. Georgia sits third in the poll, and fourth in SP+. They're followed by Texas and Notre Dame in the poll, though the Irish are third in SP+ and Texas is just sixth.

So the top five or six teams are fairly close, implying that the poll does a good job of reflecting which teams are expected to be the strongest in 2026. Though some of the divergence towards the middle part of the poll does reflect a common, and often predictable, bias.

Oklahoma and Ole Miss, both playoff teams in 2025, sit ninth and 10th in the poll, but just 12th and 16th in SP+. And that's where the "human element" comes into play. Analytics systems weren't as high on either team as humans were in 2025. But both play in the SEC, which frequently means they're ranked higher than they should be in preseason polls. See Florida and LSU in 2025, which were 15th and ninth in the preseason AP Poll in 2025, only to finish 4-8 and 7-6 respectively. Big program names and passionate fan bases may "mean more," but they don't always translate to on-field success.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

On the other hand, a few SEC teams might feel a bit undervalued by the coaches, including, oddly enough, LSU. The Tigers are 13th in the poll, but 10th in SP+. The numbers expect big things from their big transfer portal class, especially with the quarterback quality and depth they'll have in Kiffin's first season. Tennessee, too, is a bit underrated, coming in 18th in the poll, but 15th in SP+. The Volunteers had some impressive performances last year, though weren't able to get the job done in big games. While that'll have to change to return to the playoff, they're on the bubble, quality-wise.

Another underrated team? The Texas Tech Red Raiders. Perhaps no team has utilized NIL and the portal as well as Texas Tech to rebuild its program overnight, and it worked swimmingly in 2025. Yes, the Red Raiders were shut out by Oregon in the playoff, but they are expected to have a top-10 offense, and top-11 defense. That's a pretty good combination, which is why they're seventh in SP+, but just 12th in the poll.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Texas Tech's Brendan Sorsby looks on during the spring football game at Jones AT&T Stadium on April 17, 2026. (© Nathan Giese/Avalanche-Journal / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

The biggest miss? Houston, of all teams. The Cougars sit at No. 24 in the poll, but just 36th in SP+. That Houston-Texas Tech game in Week 3 will likely be a matchup of two "ranked" teams, but one is very different than the other.

Still, all in all, the Coaches Poll isn't as bad as it could be. Yes, there are some misses, but for the most part, teams are within a few spots of where they'd be with a more advanced form of ranking than just guessing based on 2025. And hey, for fans of those teams in the 10-20 range, remember Indiana started last season at No. 19, before going 16-0 and winning a title. That's the best part of college football, you just never know.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence pact
articles.excerpt:
Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan (left) and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (right) met ahead of the signing

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an att...
articles.body_text:
Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan (left) and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (right) met ahead of the signing

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an attack on one of them would be seen as an attack on all three.

The pact was announced at a meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif in the Saudi city of Mecca.

The three countries have been looking to strengthen security ties as the war between the US and Iran has drawn in Saudi Arabia and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and Pakistan announced a joint defence pact last year.

Iran and its allies have launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and blockaded their shipments after the US and Israel attacked it on 28 February.

In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels – who control the north of the country - have been fighting government forces, which are backed by a Saudi-led coalition.

Last month the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and targeted Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia has responded with strikes targeting Houthi positions and by forming a new naval coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Announcing the pact on Friday, Pakistan's foreign ministry said an attack on any of the three states "shall be regarded as an attack against them all".
