The charge relates to ⁠an assault that allegedly took place on December 6 last ...
articles.body_text:
England striker Ivan Toney ⁠has ⁠been charged with assault at a Soho nightclub, London’s ⁠Metropolitan Police has said.

The charge relates to ⁠an assault that allegedly took place on December 6 last year at a nightclub ‌on Wardour Street.

“Ivan Toney, 30, of Northampton, was charged on Thursday, 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm,” the police said ⁠in a statement.

“He ⁠will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, 24 September.”

Toney plays ⁠for Saudi Pro League club ⁠Al-Ahli and scored 42 ⁠goals last season, having transferred from English Premier League club Brentford for a fee of 53.8 million pounds ($72.3m) in 2024.

The England international was part of his nation’s squad for the ‌2026 World Cup, making two appearances – in the semifinal defeat by Argentina and in the third-place playoff victory over France.

Toney started his career at his local club, Northampton Town, before making the move to the English top flight with Newcastle United in 2015.

He was something of a late bloomer at the highest level, having had to wait until 2023 for his England debut, when he came on as a substitute for Harry Kane in a match against Ukraine.

Al-Ahli begin the new Saudi Pro League campaign on August 13, 2026, away against Diriyah Club, having finished third last season.

articles.title: ‘De-escalation’: Europe hesitates as US pushes for Hormuz naval mission
articles.excerpt:
The United States has spent months trying to forge an international naval coalition to escort vessels through the embattled Strait of Hormuz.

But Washington’s European allies, including the United Ki...
articles.body_text:
The United States has spent months trying to forge an international naval coalition to escort vessels through the embattled Strait of Hormuz.

But Washington’s European allies, including the United Kingdom and France, who previously agreed to head such a mission in the event of a sustainable truce, appear reluctant to move forward, even as ongoing disruption in the vital waterway strains the global economy.

Analysts say the stalled coalition effort reflects deep caution among European governments about becoming entangled in an unpredictable conflict they neither initiated nor supported, particularly without clear backing from Gulf partners.

“Neither UK nor France has much appetite for being drawn into a confrontation with Iran on behalf of others, particularly if there is no clear regional demand for it,” HA Hellyer, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and Center for American Progress, told Al Jazeera.

The US first raised the idea of an international maritime coalition to secure shipping in the waterway in March, as President Donald Trump called on allies, as well as China, to send warships as part of the effort.

Most countries initially declined or were noncommittal, though the UK and France left the door open to participating.

US officials continued to promote the idea of a maritime coalition as its war against Iran dragged on, as Trump lambasted US allies for what he deemed insufficient support for Washington in the conflict.

In mid-April, then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced plans for the UK and France to lead an international mission to secure shipping in the strait, stressing it would be “strictly peaceful and defensive”.

The following month, the UK Ministry of Defence promised to send drones, fighter jets and a warship as part of the mission, which it said had the support of dozens of other countries and would kick off “when conditions allow”.

But months later, the effort appears to be stalled, despite British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying his country is “absolutely aligned” with the US on “securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz”.

A European diplomatic source told Al Jazeera that following a France-UK initiative for a multinational mission for the “freedom of navigation” in the Strait of Hormuz, a new meeting gathering more than 30 states “at a technical level” took place on Thursday.

A UK Defence Ministry spokesperson told Al Jazeera that Streeting expects further talks on “planning and coordination for a future multinational mission”.

“Operational activity remains contingent on conditions on the ground and a durable political agreement,” they said, adding that the UK remains “committed” to securing commercial shipping across the Gulf region.

Hellyer said the Hormuz naval coalition has been delayed “because the politics have never matched the rhetoric”.

“The UK and France may support freedom of navigation in principle, but they are highly unlikely to lead an operation that key Gulf partners do not actively support,” he said.

Neither country wants to be seen as “imposing a security architecture that regional governments regard as unnecessarily escalatory,” he said.

Amjed Rasheed, lecturer in defence studies at King’s College London, said any European involvement would likely be limited, conditional and purely defensive.

Already dealing with a closer security threat on its eastern front with Russia, Europe wants “de-escalation and stability” in the Gulf, Rasheed told Al Jazeera.

“The decision to attack Iran was made in Washington and Tel Aviv,” Rasheed added. “The two did not consult European powers about it. European powers were/are not ready to become part of a war they did not participate in [the architecture of]”.

Hellyer said he believes a “defensive maritime presence” in Hormuz with European involvement is still possible, though he doubts “a more muscular coalition” will take shape.

“I would expect any European mission to remain deliberately narrow, focused on reassurance and commercial shipping, rather than evolving into a broader security operation,” he said.

The status of the Strait of Hormuz – through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas usually flows – has become a major point of contention between the US and Iran in negotiations to end the conflict.

The US insists that Iran does not control the strait, through which there should be free, unfettered passage as per international law, while Iran has sought to shore up control over the waterway and direct vessels to pass through routes it approves.

On Wednesday, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said an understanding with Oman over a new protocol for managing traffic in Hormuz was “on the verge of being finalised”.

Under the arrangement, which would last two to four months, Gharibabadi said large parts of a new designated shipping route would go through Iran’s territorial waters and others would pass through Oman’s waters, while current temporary routes would be closed.

Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East politics at George Washington University, told Al Jazeera he doubts the status of the Strait of Hormuz will ever return to how it was before the US-Israeli war on Iran began.

“The Iranians have learned that by blockading the Strait of Hormuz, they can make the global economy scream,” he told Al Jazeera. “This is a strategic asset, and I don’t think they will let go of it easily.”

articles.title: Prince Harry's most controversial royal plan could still become reality, author says
articles.excerpt:
Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," explains why Prince Harry expected a half-in, half-out role and what led to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit from royal duties.

One royal auth...
articles.body_text:
Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," explains why Prince Harry expected a half-in, half-out role and what led to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit from royal duties.

One royal author believes Prince Harry's controversial "half-in, half-out" proposal may still have a future within the monarchy.

Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," told Fox News Digital that while Buckingham Palace quickly rejected the proposal in 2020, he believes a similar model is ultimately inevitable.

"Harry did think that there was a hybrid version that they could do," said Vigar. "And I think in years to come, there will be a hybrid version. I think he's right. There has to be a hybrid version of this where people don't get accused of cashing in but can support their cousins or their brother or whatever."

PRINCE HARRY LONGS FOR HIS OLD ROYAL LIFE AS AMERICA ISN'T WHAT HE EXPECTED, EXPERTS SAY

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were on a four-day visit to Australia, with engagements across Melbourne, Canberra and Sydney. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

"[The Sussexes] thought they could have a hybrid role of having a business life and a private life, while also spending a few months in the U.K. supporting the queen," he shared. "Harry believed that was an option, which was whipped away from him."

In 2020, Harry attended the Sandringham Summit at Queen Elizabeth II's Norfolk estate, where senior royals decided the terms of his and Meghan's departure from royal life.

A view of Sandringham House, Queen Elizabeth II's Sandringham estate, in Norfolk, England. (Radcliffe/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

According to People magazine, it was there that the late queen drew a firm line. After intense discussions, the answer was made clear to Harry: There would be no "half-in, half-out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't be working royals while also pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR

That year, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals, citing intrusive coverage by the British press and a lack of support from the palace.

In the couple's Netflix series, "Harry & Meghan," the prince said the decision to step down was his.

Simon Vigar's "The Four Wives of Windsor" is available now. Vigar is one of British television's longest-serving royal correspondents. (Penguin)

"In fact, it was my decision," he said. "She never asked to leave. I was the one that had to see it for myself. But it's misogyny at its best."

Office workers in London watch the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's "Harry & Meghan" docuseries on Netflix on Dec. 8, 2022. (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)

In a statement, the queen publicly confirmed the decision, making it clear that it was "not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service." The Sussexes responded with a statement of their own: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."

In the Netflix docuseries, Harry claimed that William "screamed and shouted" at him during the "Sandringham Summit."

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father King Charles III at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"It was terrifying to have my brother scream and shout at me, and my father say things that just simply weren't true, and my grandmother quietly sit there and sort of take it all in," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

In "Spare," Harry wrote that he arrived at Sandringham with the impression that the family would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" was a full departure. After an hour, the queen's private secretary, nicknamed by Harry "The Bee," distributed drafts of a statement announcing "Option Five." Harry said he was stunned.

"Wait. I'm confused," he wrote. "You've already drafted a statement? Before any discussion? Announcing Option Five? In other words, the fix was in this whole time? This summit was just for show?"

Britain's Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, looks on as Britain's King Charles III leaves Westminster Abbey after the coronation ceremonies in central London on May 6, 2023. He was sitting a few rows away from his family. (Ben Stansall/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by not considering the option.

Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London, England, on July 10, 2018. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The half-in, half-out approach advocated by Harry and Meghan is the modern-day method of how royal families should operate," he said. "The late queen was extremely badly advised not to accept the formula laid out by Harry as he attempted to protect Meghan from the ravages of sustained attacks."

But not everyone agrees. Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that while Harry may eventually have a better personal relationship with his family, a return as a working royal — especially under a "half-in, half-out" model — is highly unlikely.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex depart Canada House in London, on Jan. 7, 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"There's always room for Harry to support his family privately as a son and brother," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "That's very different from supporting the monarchy publicly as a working royal. The monarchy has successfully adapted to a smaller working team."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"We continue to see King Charles, Queen Camilla, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Princess Royal, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh and the Duke of Gloucester carrying out official duties," she pointed out. "While it's a leaner operation, it has demonstrated that it can function without reopening the constitutional questions raised in 2020."

After moving to California, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex publicly aired their grievances in interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further strained his relationship with his family.

Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

On July 10, Charles hosted Harry and met with his family for the first time in years as they attempted to repair their rift. At Highgrove House, Charles' country estate, Harry and Meghan, along with their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, reunited with the king and Queen Camilla.

A photo of Highgrove House, King Charles III's country estate. (Neil Bennett/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

Harry had arrived in the U.K. for several charity events that were overshadowed by speculation about whether he would meet with his father. The 41-year-old prince has said he wants to reconcile with the monarch, 77, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.

Father and son met briefly for tea in September 2025, marking the first time they had seen each other in well over a year.

King Charles III is seen arriving at Clarence House on Sept. 10, 2025, in London, England. The monarch had a private tea with his son, Prince Harry. (Belinda Jiao/Getty Images)

The Duke of Sussex is expected to visit the U.K. in September of this year. The Sun reported that the king will offer his younger son a room at Buckingham Palace during his stay. Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Archewell, which oversees the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, for comment.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, poses for a selfie with well-wishers as he attends Scotty's Summer Festival at Maxstoke Castle in Birmingham, England. (Heathcliff O'Malley-Pool/Getty Images)

"Harry's issue isn't that he left," said Schofield. "It's what he did after he left. Between the Oprah interview, the Netflix series, ‘Spare,’ and years of public criticism, he established a pattern of taking private family matters and turning them into commercial products. That's exactly the type of risk the late queen was trying to avoid."

"If anything, Harry's conduct since 2020 has validated her decision rather than undermined it," she argued. "In any professional organization, that wouldn't strengthen your case for rejoining the leadership team. It would be cited as evidence that you cannot be trusted with confidential information or institutional responsibilities."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle meet well-wishers during a visit to Reprezent 107.3FM in London on Jan. 9, 2018. The "Suits" alum became the Duchess of Sussex when she married the British prince later that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

"The monarchy runs on trust," Schofield continued. "Harry has spent the last several years demonstrating a pattern of monetizing privileged access to the royal family. The palace would have to ask itself whether Harry could be trusted to represent the institution. I think the answer to that question is no."

Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, departs after attending a bingo night at The Royal Hospital Chelsea in London on April 29, 2025. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Schofield pointed to Sophie, now the Duchess of Edinburgh, as a cautionary tale. In 2001, she gave up her public relations career after an undercover reporter posing as a prospective client secretly recorded her discussing her royal connections. The controversy reinforced the palace's view that commercial work and official royal duties could create conflicts, and Sophie went on to become a full-time working royal.

Today, she is widely regarded as one of the monarchy's most valuable assets.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting Queen Elizabeth II's coffin to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven't spoken since 2022, when their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, died.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that, at most, she expects Harry to be offered "informal, limited and tightly controlled opportunities" while in the U.K. as he continues reconciliation efforts with his family. She said he will continue to participate in events supporting his charitable causes in his home country. However, a functional hybrid role isn't in the cards, she insisted.

KING CHARLES MAKES RISKY MOVE TOWARD PRINCE HARRY AS PRINCE WILLIAM 'REMAINS WARY': EXPERTS

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, take part in a Scar Tree Walk in Melbourne, Australia, on April 16, 2026. (Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images)

"Prince William has been consistent in his opposition," said Fordwich, referring to the king's heir. "Princess Catherine is by his side on this, as are the courtiers and those whose role it is to protect the monarchy."

The Sussexes continue to raise their children in the wealthy, coastal city of Montecito. As Harry continues to rebuild his relationship with his father, Schofield doesn't believe a "half-in, half-out" role would ever be reconsidered.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, are seen here waving from the balcony of the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Fiji, on Oct. 23, 2018. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were on their official 16-day autumn tour visiting cities in Australia, Fiji, Tonga and New Zealand. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"The late queen's decision wasn't a personal preference," she said. "It was an institutional decision designed to protect the Crown's impartiality and integrity. I don't see King Charles reversing it.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. Multiple royal experts told Fox News Digital that there's no doubt King Charles' younger son misses his life in the U.K. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)

"The strongest opposition would likely come from those responsible for protecting the monarchy's long-term stability, including Prince William and senior officials who understand the reputational risks. Once you allow one royal to commercially monetize royal status while carrying out official duties, it becomes incredibly difficult to explain why others cannot do the same."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump-backed incumbent ousted in House primary as GOP redistricting push set to reshape Tennessee
articles.excerpt: Fox News contributor Joe Concha joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze new polling in the Michigan, Wisconsin and Texas races. Concha also discusses the rally supporting WNBA player Sophie Cunningham ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News contributor Joe Concha joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze new polling in the Michigan, Wisconsin and Texas races. Concha also discusses the rally supporting WNBA player Sophie Cunningham for defending women's sports.

President Donald Trump’s clout with Republican voters was put to the test in Tennessee Thursday, as voters headed to the polls for the state’s first primaries under a newly redrawn congressional map designed to bolster Republicans’ chances of expanding their thin majority in the U.S. House this fall.

The night delivered a split verdict for Trump in two of the state’s closely watched Republican House primaries. Trump-backed state Sen. Brent Taylor captured the GOP nomination in the newly redrawn 9th Congressional District, while former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher toppled Trump-endorsed incumbent Rep. Andy Ogles in the 5th District.

Taylor’s victory sets up a November showdown against AOC-backed progressive state Rep. Justin Pearson, one of the so-called "Tennessee Three" lawmakers who gained national attention after he was expelled following a gun control protest in 2023.

Elsewhere, Sen. Marsha Blackburn captured the Republican gubernatorial nomination, putting her on course to potentially become Tennessee’s first female governor and eventually create an opening for another U.S. Senate appointment.

SQUAD-BACKED ‘TENNESSEE THREE’ LAWMAKER WINS HOUSE PRIMARY IN NEWLY REDRAWN DISTRICT

Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., on Capitol Hill. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"From the bottom of my heart, thank you, Tennessee! One year ago, we set out on this journey with one goal: to make Tennessee America's conservative leader and show the nation what strong, bold, conservative leadership looks like," Blackburn said following her win Thursday night. "I am humbled and honored that you've chosen me as your Republican nominee for Governor. Together, we've taken a major step toward that goal. I won't let you down. On to November."

Ogles’ defeat was a glaring setback for Trump on the night. The president threw his support behind the conservative House Freedom Caucus member and stepped in as the race tightened, praising Ogles as a strong businessman and America First lawmaker during a virtual tele-rally last month. Hatcher, endorsed by term-limited Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, handed the two-term incumbent an upset defeat despite Trump’s intervention.

Ogles, backed by Speaker Mike Johnson in addition to Trump, faced a high-dollar outside effort to knock him out of the race. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a clean-energy super PAC largely bankrolled by California crypto billionaire and major Democratic donor Chris Larsen, spent roughly $1 million opposing Ogles and supporting Hatcher before purchasing another $700,000 in advertising ahead of the primary, according to a Fox News Digital review of federal filings.

Ogles accused the group of trying to punish him for opposing Biden-era clean-energy subsidies and suggested his close ties to Trump had also put a target on his back.

The Trump-backed incumbent was also running on unfamiliar terrain after Tennessee Republicans dramatically redrew his 5th District. While the change made the district significantly more Republican for November, it left Ogles to face a significantly new GOP electorate than what had elected him in the past.

TENNESSEE PASSES NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP LIKELY TO FLIP FINAL DEM SEAT AS PROTESTS ERUPT INSIDE CAPITOL

Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., walks through the U.S. Capitol on February 03, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Ogles’ district was not the only one transformed. Tennessee Republicans redrew the state’s congressional lines this spring, breaking apart the Democratic-controlled 9th District and giving Republicans a chance to turn Tennessee’s current 8-1 GOP delegation into a 9-0 sweep.

The effort prompted longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen to abandon his reelection bid in that Memphis-area district, which was transformed from a district that previously favored Democrats into one that now tilts Republican.

Thursday's primaries now set up a particularly nationalized fight for that seat.

DARLINE GRAHAM CONSIDERING RUNNING FOR FULL A SENATE TERM AS MEMORIAL SERVICES SET FOR LINDSEY GRAHAM: REPORT

Taylor, who won the GOP 9th district primary Thursday, carries Trump’s endorsement, while Pearson, the winner of the 9th district's Democratic primary, has been embraced by members of the far-left "Squad" on Capitol Hill, including, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, raises his fist after visiting with supporters in the gallery of the House chamber Thursday, April 6, 2023, in Nashville, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Taylor will try to deliver Republicans the final seat needed for a clean sweep of Tennessee’s congressional delegation, while Pearson will attempt to preserve a Democratic foothold in the Memphis-area district despite a less favorable map.

Blackburn, meanwhile, defeated Rep. John Rose in the Republican gubernatorial primary to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Lee, clearing a major hurdle between her and the governor’s mansion in the heavily Republican state. If elected in November, Blackburn would become Tennessee’s first female governor.

Her victory could also produce consequences in Washington. Blackburn was reelected to a six-year Senate term in 2024, meaning she did not have to surrender her seat to run for governor, as Rose had to. But, she would have to give up her seat if elected governor, which would create a Senate vacancy and another round of political jockeying over who could succeed her.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: Trump’s Smithsonian clash exposes striking pattern among museum curators
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Jody Edward Ginn, historian and museum professional, told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from education to activism after his recent visit.

The scholars behind a Smithsonian exhibit...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Jody Edward Ginn, historian and museum professional, told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from education to activism after his recent visit.

The scholars behind a Smithsonian exhibition targeted by the Trump administration have built their careers around the same race, gender, sexuality and social-justice themes now fueling accusations of ideological bias at the museum, a Fox News Digital review found.

Entertainment Nation, which opened in December 2022, is an ongoing exhibition at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that uses artifacts from music, film, television, theater and sports to examine how popular culture has shaped American life.

Every member of the exhibit’s seven-person curatorial team has incorporated themes involving racial injustice, gender inequality, sexuality or other progressive social causes into their academic work, public commentary or prior museum projects. Fox News Digital’s review found praise for communist-linked figures, alignment with progressive activist movements and explicit statements connecting museum work to social justice.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

A video playing at the entrance of the National Museum of American History’s Entertainment Nation exhibit features scantily clad women and a clip from the feminist thriller The Handmaid’s Tale. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

Speaking to Fox News Digital previously, a senior White House official accused Entertainment Nation of promoting "fringe or activist ideologies masquerading as history."

John Troutman, the exhibit’s lead curator, told The Washington Post in 2023 that the project was meant to do more than present a conventional history of entertainment, saying it was not intended to serve as "a gallery that provides a history of entertainment," but instead to examine broader social movements reflected in popular culture.

Troutman’s colleagues have similarly examined entertainment through themes of racial exclusion, gender stereotypes, homophobia and other social conflicts commonly emphasized by the political left.

Curator Kenneth Cohen, for example, published "They Will Have Their Game" in 2017, a book examining how the development of sports in the United States "produced a sense of democracy while also reinforcing racial, gender, and class divisions," according to a description from his publisher. The book, per the description, examines how sports contributed to the "creation of the white male republic" in the United States.

"Although competition and risk were central to understandings of ‘sport’ in early Anglo-America, the formation of a sporting culture based on those elements was not inevitable," Cohen's book reads. "It was a purposeful choice, made largely by empowered white men, to construct sporting culture around traits that encouraged engagement within their ranks and helped to define them as a group despite internal class and ethnic divides."

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

A placard in the "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. honors Dr. Anthony Fauci. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Cohen’s colleague on the exhibit, curator Krystal Klingenberg, has similarly focused much of her scholarship on music, race, social justice and the Black Lives Matter movement.

For another Smithsonian project she worked on in 2022, Klingenberg stated that her goal was to "connect history with the ongoing fight for civil rights and social justice in American society." Klingenberg lists "social justice" as one of her scholarly interests on her CV, alongside a number of scholarly projects related to it.

The entrance to the Entertainment Nation exhibit in the Smithsonian's National Museum for American History.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

An exhibit in Entertainment Nation examining the history of American colonialism.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

In this Entertainment Nation exhibit, curators rib Indiana Jones as a "stoic white male."  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

Objects representing various progressive athletes, including a tie bearing the names of slain African Americans, are displayed at the National Museum of American History.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

A National Museum of American History placard calling Alexander Hamilton a "flawed founding father" and praising Lin-Manuel Miranda for casting people of color to play the founding fathers.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

A sign reading "I feel very proud to be Mexican" in the Entertainment Nation section of the National Museum of American History.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

A placard in the "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. honors Dr. Anthony Fauci. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Among them are an academic discussion she facilitated dubbed "​​Black Lives Matter: Music, Race, and Justice," a presentation on ethnomusicology she gave titled "American Hate: How Do We Respond?" and another talk she gave called "Teaching Race and Ethnicity Through Music: Intersectionality."

Klingenberg also co-hosted the Collected podcast where she examined "why Black feminist critique remains crucial to understanding the times we are living in."

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

The "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

All seven curators have, to varying degrees, examined race, gender, sexuality, inequality or identity in their academic or museum work.

Fox News Digital reached all seven curators and the Smithsonian for comment.

The current conservative crusade against the Smithsonian launched in March 2025 when President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing his administration to review the Smithsonian's exhibits and programs.

Allegations of bias in Entertainment Nation drew renewed national attention in July amid a congressional hearing scrutinizing the National Museum of American History and the release of a 162-page White House report documenting what the administration described as evidence of ideological bias across the Smithsonian.

"American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives," a White House official previously told Fox News Digital. "The Smithsonian Institution should present history in a way that is accurate, balanced and consistent with the values that make the United States of America exceptional."

The White House official’s criticism followed reports in 2025 of displays within Entertainment Nation that allegedly used left-of-center language to portray America negatively.

SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES

(From left to right) Krystal Klingenberg, John Troutman, Ashley Mayor and Theodore Gonzalves speak during an Entertainment Nation event in 2024. (YouTube/National Museum of American History) (YouTube/National Museum of American History)

These displays included a section that claimed circuses "expressed the colonial impulse to claim dominion over the world," a placard arguing that Mickey Mouse’s "outsized facial features, white gloves and trickster temperament were vestiges of longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy," and a placard describing Alexander Hamilton as an "influential and flawed founding father," language the White House report criticized as unfairly diminishing him.

Some of the curators have publicly commented on their rationale behind procuring specific items for the exhibit.

Ryan Lintelman, another of Entertainment Nation’s curators, was instrumental in acquiring one of the iconic red costumes from the Hulu adaptation of "The Handmaid’s Tale," according to an interview he gave to Variety. The dystopian novel written by feminist author Margaret Atwood depicts a world where America has become a totalitarian theocracy that strips females of their rights and forces fertile women, known as "Handmaids," into reproductive servitude.

Lintelman stated that the costume’s importance to liberal protest movements motivated his work to acquire one for the Smithsonian.

FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Demonstrators dressed as handmaidens from "The Handmaid's Tale" take part in an anti-Trump protest marking one year since the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump, in Washington, D.C., U.S., November 5, 2025. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

"I believe that popular culture is a unique and accessible lens to introduce the museum’s audiences to complex narratives involving race, sexuality, gender, identity, representation, economics, migration, social change, and power," he wrote for his Smithsonian biography.

The 2017 Women’s March, where the Handmaid’s costume featured prominently, was seen as one of the most important early expressions of resistance to the first Trump administration. Theodore Gonzalves, another Entertainment Nation curator, also cited the march approvingly in a 2018 essay praising Barbara Dane, a lifelong socialist and former Communist Party USA member.

Dane was an acclaimed folk musician who spent much of her career involved in left-wing politics, most notably defying the United States government by visiting Cuba while it was under the rule of dictator Fidel Castro. She went on to found a record label that produced songs praising communist figures such as Mao Zedong, calling him China’s "savior," and Ho Chi Minh, actively supporting America’s enemy in the Vietnam War.

Gonzalves described Dane as "singing truth to power" and creating music that "reflected the stakes and the hopeful dreams of millions trying to make sense of a world dominated by superpowers with world-ending weaponry."

Gonzalves, whose scholarship has examined historical abuses against Asian Americans, also uses the term "Filipinx" in his work – which is a gender-neutral term for Filipinos similar to the term "Latinx."

Ashley Mayor, another Entertainment Nation curator who specializes in "Latinx and Afro-Latinx music and culture," regularly shares posts from left-wing organizations on social media. Eric Jentsch, the seventh curator, has also written about race and racism in American sports history, Fox News Digital found.

In its July report, the White House charged that the Smithsonian "no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens."

articles.title: Controversial grocery store move evokes expert's blunt advice: 'If you shuck it, buy it'
articles.excerpt:
Rico, a 9-year-old prehensile-tailed Brazilian porcupine who has been delighting visitors at the Cincinnati Zoo for years, loves to eat, especially corn on the cob.

The arrival of fresh summer corn a...
articles.body_text:
Rico, a 9-year-old prehensile-tailed Brazilian porcupine who has been delighting visitors at the Cincinnati Zoo for years, loves to eat, especially corn on the cob.

The arrival of fresh summer corn at grocery stores and farmers markets across the country is reviving a long-running debate: Should shoppers shuck corn before buying it?

Shucking corn involves peeling off the outer green husks and removing the corn silk to get to the edible kernels underneath. Some shoppers shuck ears of corn before they buy it to inspect the kernels for quality and check for insects.

"Some stores encourage customers to shuck corn in the store by providing trash bins beside the corn display," Florida-based etiquette expert Jacqueline Whitmore told Fox News Digital. "Here's the caveat: If you shuck it, buy it. If the ear of corn is bad, let a manager know or discard it in the trash bin provided."

BABY BOOMERS HATE 10 THINGS ABOUT TODAY'S GROCERY STORES

Partially shucking corn at the market and putting it back can also make it unappealing to the next shopper and increase the chance of food waste.

"If no bin is provided, don't shuck the corn," Whitmore said. "It can be messy and wasteful. Plus, no one wants to buy corn that has already been shucked."

An etiquette expert says it's OK to shuck corn at a grocery store, provided there's a trash bin. But if you shuck it, buy it, she adds. (iStock)

Beyond etiquette concerns about the mess shucking corn can create, sanitation is also a factor. Husks act as a barrier to protect the corn from dirt, bacteria and moisture loss.

By partially shucking corn before buying it, shoppers may expose the kernels to bacteria from hands, shopping carts and store conveyor belts.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Experts advise waiting until just before preparing and eating corn to shuck it, because the husk also preserves the kernels' freshness. Shucking too early exposes the kernels to oxygen, leading to moisture loss. Sugars will also turn into starch more quickly, which will reduce the corn's sweetness.

Shucking corn and discarding the debris is also wasteful, Ohio-based farmer Lee Jones of The Chef's Garden farm told Delish.

"No one wants to go home and open it to find moldy, gross corn."

"What some people don't realize is that you can use every part of an ear of corn," he said. "Corn is such an iconic American food, and chefs are finding creative ways to use every part of the plant — from the stalk and silk to the husk and cob. Each part of the plant's life adds something unique to the plate."

Corn husks are used for teas, soup stocks and as wraps for grilling or steaming, Delish reported.

Many Reddit users admitted to pulling back corn husks to examine ears before purchasing them.

Corn husks are used for teas, soup stocks and as wraps for grilling or steaming. (iStock)

"Sometimes the husk hides worms or bad spots that would make you not want to buy or eat it," one user wrote in a forum asking why people are shucking corn in the grocery store.

"Do you know how expensive things are? No one wants to go home and open it to find moldy, gross corn," someone else wrote.

"Shucking? Or just peeking? Because sometimes you have to throw away a whole ear," commented another user.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Shucking," another Redditor replied. "Grocery stores around here put a bin at the corn table just for this. That way I don't have to do it at home into my little kitchen trash can and get the threads absolutely everywhere."

Experts say there are better ways to judge an ear's quality without peeling back the husk.

Start by comparing weights and giving the corn a squeeze. Heavier ears generally contain more moisture, making for juicer, sweeter kernels, according to America's Test Kitchen. The ear itself should feel firm, full and plump.

Corn husks protect kernels from contamination and also help preserve their freshness and sweetness. (iStock)

Inspect the corn tassels, or silk, and the husk itself. If the silk is light brown, golden or slightly sticky, the corn is likely fresher, Lisa Lin, a California-based food writer who runs the Healthy Nibbles website, noted in a 2023 post. Black or dried-out silk indicates corn is older.

The husk should be bright green and wrap tightly around the ear if the corn was harvested recently. Faded or brittle husks could mean the corn has been sitting around. Also look for holes in the husk, which can be a sign of insect damage, Australia-based horticulturist Toni Salter wrote on her website.

If you don't plan to eat corn right away, keep it cool and covered. Always wash produce before consuming it to remove dirt, bacteria and potential pesticide residue, according to Everyday Health.

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Bryan Kohberger's post-conviction relief bid enabled by flawed plea deal, psychologist argues
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Kris Mohandie, a renowned forensic psychologist who predicted Bryan Kohberger would attempt to appeal his guilty plea last year, weighs in on Kohberger's "narcissism" and latest legal move.

The f...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Kris Mohandie, a renowned forensic psychologist who predicted Bryan Kohberger would attempt to appeal his guilty plea last year, weighs in on Kohberger's "narcissism" and latest legal move.

The forensic psychologist who publicly warned last year that Bryan Kohberger's plea agreement was part of the killer's calculated "long game" plans is arguing that prosecutors missed a critical opportunity by not requiring Kohberger to fully explain the Idaho student murders as part of the deal, leaving him room to reshape his story as he returns to court despite waiving his right to appeal.

"It was a real mistake and series of heavy mistakes by the DA's office to enter into this deal, because now here we are, putting the victims through all this again with having gotten nothing," said Dr. Kris Mohandie, a police and forensic psychologist and expert on violent behavior.

Kohberger, who took a deal to escape the potential death penalty, is serving four consecutive sentences of life without the chance of parole, plus another 10 years.

BRYAN KOHBERGER GETS NEW ATTORNEY APPOINTED AFTER HE ASKS COURT FOR POST-CONVICTION RELIEF IN IDAHO MURDERS

The University of Idaho stabbing victims, from left: Madison Mogen, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and Kaylee Goncalves. (Instagram: @maddiemogen, @kayleegoncalves, @ethanchapin4)

Last month, however, he filed a petition for post-conviction relief, claiming that he had ineffective counsel and that he'd been misled — while insisting that he's innocent of the murders.

Police found his DNA on a knife sheath recovered from the crime scene, in a bed with two of the four University of Idaho students Kohberger admitted to killing in a July 2025 change of plea hearing.

Mohandie said prosecutors should have required Kohberger to provide a full account of the killings before accepting the plea, even if, as Latah County Prosecutor Bill Thompson said after sentencing, they believed he would lie.

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students. Netflix's documentary about the case, "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," is now streaming. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

"Well, that's a lame excuse, in my opinion, because at least you've got him admitting something," Mohandie said. "This way, he can pull back and say, 'I didn't admit to doing anything...I said nothing. There are no stories or statements related to me. And I was coerced into this. I had terrible counsel.' It enables him to have a complete playing field for him to dance around. With now an infinite array of lies. So pin him to a story is part of why you do this."

KOHBERGER DEFENSE EXPERT WANTS HIS LAWYERS UNDER OATH AFTER KILLER CITES FINDINGS IN BID TO UNDO GUILTY PLEA

Mohandie said the absence of any detailed confession now gives Kohberger room to challenge the case while forcing victims' families to relive the proceedings.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

A watchman parked outside 1122 King Road on Dec. 11, 2022, four weeks after four students were stabbed to death inside. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

"It was ill-conceived, it was poorly designed, and at the end of the day, you know the victims are being re-traumatized by all of this," he said.

The psychologist also argued that Kohberger's handwritten post-conviction petition and attempts to regain the spotlight for himself are consistent with the personality traits he has long associated with the convicted killer.

"First and foremost is his desire to get away with things and to outsmart the system, and I do believe that notoriety and fueling his notoriety, continuing to fuel that, is the secondary gain as well," Mohandie said.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S CHOICE OF 'A HOUSE FULL OF WOMEN' MAY HOLD THE KEY TO THE IDAHO MURDERS' BIGGEST MYSTERY

Illustrating that was Kohberger's decision to call a reporter from prison before filing the petition, he said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"He is a common archetype, if you will," Mohandie said. "He's not special, but he believes he's special, which is the commonality among these people — the belief that you're special when you're not; the belief that you're smarter than other people and can outwit them."

Mohandie said that's why he believes the public should resist looking at killers as fascinating figures.

"They are terrible people and monsters," he said.

articles.title: Moment earthquake shakes hospital operating room in Japan
articles.excerpt:
Newly-released security camera footage shows the moment last month's magnitude 6.8 quake shook Kumamoto General Hospital in Japan.

Four surgeries were under way at the time. Footage from a camera in ...
articles.body_text:
Newly-released security camera footage shows the moment last month's magnitude 6.8 quake shook Kumamoto General Hospital in Japan.

Four surgeries were under way at the time. Footage from a camera in an operating room where an abdominal surgery was being performed shows medical staff shielding the patient with their bodies as equipment swayed violently, and a nurse opening a door to secure an evacuation route.

According to the hospital, all four operations were successfully completed.

Kumamoto General Hospital resumed normal outpatient services on 5 August , after suspending them following the earthquake on 28 July.

articles.title: ‘Still searching for truth’: Daughter of Sikh activist killed 30 years ago
articles.excerpt:
On the morning of September 6, 1995, human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra was washing his car outside his home in Amritsar city, India’s Punjab state.

His wife, Paramjit Kaur Khalra, a libraria...
articles.body_text:
On the morning of September 6, 1995, human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra was washing his car outside his home in Amritsar city, India’s Punjab state.

His wife, Paramjit Kaur Khalra, a librarian, was getting ready to leave for work; their son, Janmeet, and daughter, Navkiran, were getting ready for school.

Nothing about the morning suggested that, within hours, their lives would be changed forever.

Minutes after Paramjit and the children left home, Khalra was picked up by the police, secretly tortured for days in custody, and later murdered. His body was never found.

Khalra was killed because of his investigation into thousands of disappearances and extrajudicial killings by the Indian security forces during a separatist movement launched by Punjab’s Sikh community in the 1980s to establish a homeland, called Khalistan.

In June 1984, the government sent troops inside Amritsar’s Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site, where hundreds of rebels were believed to be hiding. Hundreds of people, including Sikh religious leader Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, were killed in Operation Blue Star.

The military operation led to the assassination of the then-Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by two of her Sikh bodyguards in October that year. Gandhi’s assassination triggered anti-Sikh riots across the country, killing thousands.

In Punjab, a brutal crackdown on the Khalistan movement started, with security forces given special powers to torture, forcibly disappear and even kill thousands of rebels and suspects.

Among those forcibly disappeared were one of Khalra’s friends and the friend’s mother, pushing the 42-year-old bank manager on a pursuit that saw him investigate thousands of similar cases.

In 1995, Khalra filed a petition with the Supreme Court of India, claiming the police had cremated 25,000 such bodies, labelling them “unidentified” and “unclaimed”. Police said his claim was exaggerated.

As he mobilised families who had lost loved ones and continued to seek answers from the police, he was repeatedly threatened with consequences and eventually abducted from his home and killed.

Khalra’s abduction and murder became one of India’s most consequential human rights cases. His wife’s campaign for justice forced the government to order an investigation. Five police officials are currently serving life sentences for Khalra’s killing.

But for three decades now, thousands of other people across Punjab and beyond are still seeking justice and closure over the disappearance and presumed killing of their loved ones.

Last month, a feature film, titled Satluj – after a river in Punjab in which many bodies, including Khalra’s, are believed to have been thrown – attempted to answer some of their questions by revisiting his life and work.

The government blocked the film within 48 hours of its release on a streaming platform over “security concerns”. But Sikh groups and rights activists organised community screenings of the film across Punjab and other parts of India and abroad, reigniting a decades-old debate over Khalra’s legacy, state accountability, and freedom of expression.

Thirty years after her father’s disappearance and murder, Navkiran Kaur Khalra reflects on his life, legacy and the long fight for justice, in an exclusive conversation with Al Jazeera.

Al Jazeera: Take us back to September 6, 1995. What do you remember about the day your father disappeared?

Navkiran Kaur Khalra: It was an ordinary morning. My mother was getting ready for work, and my brother and I left for school. As she stepped outside around 9am, she noticed several police officers standing outside our house. She didn’t think much of it and went to work. When I returned from school later that day, my brother came running towards me in panic and said, ‘The police have taken Papa’. That was the beginning of a nightmare that changed our lives forever.

AJ: When did your family realise his was not a routine detention, and that your father had been forcibly disappeared?

Khalra: We immediately went to the police station in Tarn Taran [a place in Punjab], but the officers denied everything. They said it was impossible that anyone had picked him up from their jurisdiction and discouraged us from filing a complaint. Later, my mother started receiving phone calls from the then-deputy inspector general of police. He told her, ‘Withdraw the case against us and we’ll tell you where he is.’ He even said they could bring my father back alive and create a story that he had gone to Pakistan and had now returned. For years, we searched everywhere. We explored every possibility because we genuinely believed he might still be alive.

AJ: People around the world know Jaswant Singh Khalra as a human rights activist. Who was he to you as a father?

Khalra: Before he became known internationally, he was simply our father. He was a Sikh, a human rights activist and a concerned citizen, but at home, he loved spending time with us. He brought us gifts, took us on family vacations, and made time for us whenever he could. We were an ordinary middle-class family. No matter how busy he was, he always came home. He travelled to Chandigarh [Punjab’s capital] almost every day, spending five or six hours on the road, but however late it became, he returned home to us.

AJ: What kind of home did you grow up in during Punjab’s insurgency?

Khalra: As children, we didn’t fully understand what was happening around us. Our home was always full of lawyers, activists, journalists and visitors from India and abroad. The walls were covered with photographs of people who had been killed in alleged extrajudicial killings across Punjab. Those images became part of our childhood. Looking back, I realise how unusual that was.

AJ: At what point did your family realise your father’s work had put him in serious danger?

Khalra: By early 1995, the threats had become very serious. When the police claimed that missing people had simply gone abroad, my father would hold press conferences and ask, ‘If they have gone abroad, why are their names in the cremation records?’

Around February 1995, my grandfather received a message from a ruling party legislator, telling my father to stop his work before it was too late. We were also told that permission had been obtained from the government to eliminate him.

Friends and lawyers urged him to seek police protection, but he refused. He used to say, ‘I visit families whose loved ones have disappeared because of the police. How can I go to them with the same police standing beside me?’

AJ: Shortly before he disappeared, your father asked your mother if she could take care of the children. Looking back, what does that moment mean to you?

Khalra: A day before he was abducted, he turned to my mother and asked, ‘Will you be able to take care of the children?’ At the time, she didn’t think much about it. It sounded like an ordinary question. Only afterwards did we realise he may have known something was going to happen.

AJ: Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh was assassinated in a suicide bombing on August 31, 1995, only days before your father was abducted. Singh’s government had led the state’s crackdown on the Sikh rebellion, and the killing triggered fears of a renewed security response. Your father had been documenting alleged police abuses during that period. How did Singh’s assassination impact your family?

Khalra: I remember we were at a grocery store when we heard on television that Beant Singh had been assassinated. Everything changed after that. Friends, colleagues and even my grandfather urged my father to leave home for a few days because they feared the police would come after him. Many other activists had already left their homes. But my father refused. Instead, he began sleeping near the entrance of our house because he said that if the police came during the night, they would reach him first and would not harm the rest of the family. Less than a week later, they came.

AJ: What was life like for your family in the years after your father’s disappearance, when you still believed he might return?

Khalra: We lived in two different worlds. In one world, we went to school and tried to live ordinary lives. Many people around us didn’t even know who my father was or what had happened to him. In the other world, we spent our time with families whose loved ones had also disappeared. They understood our pain because they were living through the same uncertainty. For more than three years, we held on to the hope that my father was still alive. We searched everywhere, believing he would one day come home.

AJ: For more than three years, there was no official account of what had happened to your father. Then, in 1998, Kuldip Singh, a former special police officer with the Punjab police, became the prosecution’s key witness and testified about your father’s illegal detention, torture and killing. How did hearing that testimony change things for your family?

Khalra: That was the moment everything changed. Until then, we still believed my father might be alive. When Kuldip Singh described my father’s illegal detention, torture and killing, we finally had to accept the truth. My grandfather gathered the family together, and we performed my father’s last prayers. We never recovered his body, and neither our family nor anyone in the human rights community ever saw him again after September 6, 1995.

AJ: Several police officers were eventually convicted. Did those verdicts bring justice?

Khalra: The trial ended, but justice never happened. As Sikhs, we have grown up believing there is no equal rule of law for our community. My father may have had political differences with the state, but he was a law-abiding citizen. The legal battle lasted 16 years, and our childhood was shaped by it. We experienced how justice could be denied at every level – not only by the police and the courts but also through society and the education system. Families like ours were labelled as separatists.

The trial ended, but justice never happened. As Sikhs, we have grown up believing there is no equal rule of law for our community.

AJ: What was your father ultimately fighting for?

Khalra: People often think my father’s work was only about documenting killings. It wasn’t. He used to say, ‘You have mocked a community that is simply asking for death certificates.’ Even today, many families still don’t have official confirmation of what happened to their loved ones. Without death certificates, they cannot access bank accounts, transfer property or settle inheritance claims. The system didn’t just take one person away; it condemned entire families to decades of uncertainty. That is why my father’s work still matters.

AJ: You said many filmmakers approached your family. But you declined. What made you decide to support Satluj?

Khalra: Many filmmakers approached us over the years, but we always refused. We weren’t interested in making a film for the sake of it. What we wanted was to take our case to the people’s court, to the people of India. We wanted them to hear our story, not only the version presented through state institutions. When [Satluj writer-director] Honey Trehan approached us during the COVID-19 pandemic, we asked him to come back with a script. He spent years researching the case and returned with a draft that reflected the facts and the spirit of my father’s work. Only then did we agree to be part of the project.

AJ: After Satluj was removed from streaming platforms in India, public screenings sprang up across Punjab. What did that response mean to your family?

Khalra: We had expected resistance. We even warned the filmmakers that telling my father’s story would be controversial because he wasn’t just one voice in Punjab. He represented thousands of untold stories.

When the film disappeared, we weren’t surprised. What surprised us was what happened afterwards. Farmers’ organisations and local communities organised public screenings across Punjab. People set up projectors in villages, on buses and in community spaces so others could watch it.

The state miscalculated. They underestimated how many people still wanted to hear my father’s story. Thirty years later, people are still searching for truth, justice and accountability. That is why his story continues to matter.

articles.title: Primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemployment
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16

What can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on quest to learn

Primary schools in En...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16

What can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on quest to learn

Primary schools in England should be required to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job, a government review is to recommend.

Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, said he would call for sweeping changes in education policy alongside a shake-up of the benefits system to address the problem.

Speaking to the Guardian, he said ministers needed to “make somebody responsible” for identifying and supporting the children who risked becoming Neet (not in employment, education or training) after their GCSE year up to the age of 24.

“The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,” he said.

“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”

In an interview during a visit to Dublin this week, the former Labour health secretary said the recommendation would form part of his final report into Britain’s youth worklessness crisis, which is expected this autumn.

Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are Neet surpassing a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.

Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill-health and a tough jobs market.

Milburn’s review comes as Andy Burnham puts tackling the crisis in youth employment at the top of his agenda for government, including changes in his first weeks as prime minister to retool technical education and apprenticeships.

Labour is also gearing up for a fresh tilt at welfare reform amid concerns over a spiralling benefits bill and the hit to the economy and people’s lives from a prolonged period out of work.

Milburn said welfare reform would form a critical plank of his final report, but cautioned that any steps to restrict benefit payments for young people would need to be accompanied by higher levels of education, health and job support.

He said that by the time a young person reached the benefit system it represented an “upstream failure” in education, skills and health policy because a functioning system could have helped them to find a job.

“I think we’ve got to turbocharge that education; that support. We’ve got to turbocharge opportunities for young people; we’ve got to make it easier for young people to get a job,” he said.

“And alongside opportunities, of course, there has got to be some obligations. Of course.”

Burnham has said he is determined to reform the welfare system as part of his efforts to fix Britain’s dismal track record on youth employment, but would also provide more support for young people.

Speaking on a fact-finding mission to the Republic of Ireland, which has recorded the fastest fall in Neet rates in the EU over the past decade, Milburn said that far too often youth disengagement began long before the age of 16.

Suggesting that it can start before a child even reaches the school gates, he highlighted a study in Bradford that found children who were not school-ready at the age of 4 to 5 were almost three times as likely to become Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 17.

“We know what the correlated factors are [for a child at risk of becoming Neet] – whether that is poverty; mental health, or being in care. What we don’t do is take that knowledge and turn it into action.”

Under the proposal to be outlined in his final report, schools in England would be expected to flag a child’s risk of becoming Neet from the end of primary school, including by drawing on attendance records.

The Department for Education would also be asked to refresh its pupil premium guidance to emphasise that the extra money schools in England receive for supporting the most disadvantaged children could be used for tutoring and mentoring schemes for those at risk of becoming Neet.

Official figures show rates of school absence have ballooned since the Covid pandemic, with the number of pupils persistently absent – missing at least a 10th of school time – almost doubling to 1.3 million pupils in 2024 and 2025. Rates of severe absence – missing half of class time – and persistent absenteeism have also dramatically increased.

Milburn’s interim report in May warned that persistent absenteeism was associated with a 3.9 times greater risk of a young person being Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 18, and a 6.3 times greater risk of a young person being locked out of earning or learning for a sustained period.

While some schools have strategies using so-called “Roni” (risk of Neet indicator) tools, the practice is not widespread or mandated.

“We’ve got to get upstream because what we’re doing is we’re paying – this country, and young people – are paying the price of failure,” said Milburn.

articles.title: Meet the offenders cleaning canals in the West Midlands as an alternative to prison
articles.excerpt:
With the debate over prison overcrowding and what to do about it raging, one initiative offers an alternative solution

As the prison overcrowding crisis shows no sign of abating and the debate rages ...
articles.body_text:
With the debate over prison overcrowding and what to do about it raging, one initiative offers an alternative solution

As the prison overcrowding crisis shows no sign of abating and the debate rages over early releases, an initiative in the West Midlands offers an alternative to custodial sentences.

The Guardian was offered rare access to the project, under which, instead of being sent to prison, convicted offenders work on the improvement of waterways and green spaces around Smethwick. It is a small part of the community payback scheme, which in total clocked up an estimated 5m hours across England and Wales in the last year.

Community payback is not suitable for everyone but covers a wide range of adult offending and can be included as part of suspended sentences. The Sentencing Act, which received royal assent in January, introduces a presumption for courts to suspend short custodial sentences of 12 months, which will mean more offenders carrying out community-based punishments.

On the day the Guardian visited the Smethwick project last month, the temperature was already in the high 20s by 9.30am when the participants arrived at the canal for a day of strimming and cutting back overgrown vegetation, and clearing beer cans, plastic bags, bottles and condoms from the towpath and the canal itself.

Among them was Steve Warmer, a 54-year-old with a painful hip, dressed in a grey tracksuit, who was recently convicted of an offence that can attract a fine, a driving ban and up to six months in prison. As two of his fellow participants were given nets to trawl the canal for rubbish and thick, green duckweed, Warmer was handed a picker and the first of many black rubbish bags.

Warmer, a factory worker from Dudley, said he was “the last one standing [alive]” out of his group of friends. “I actually enjoy this work,” he said. “It gives me knowledge of life and other people.”

The aim of community payback is to combine punishment with rehabilitation, and Warmer added: “Me and my wife now litter pick in our own street.”

Not everyone working at the canal was as positive as Warmer, who had completed 126 of 250 hours of a community payback sentence. In the hot weather, the work was particularly demanding, with plenty of water breaks needed as the temperature rose further in the afternoon.

Courts can order between 40 and 300 hours of community payback, to be completed within a specific timeframe. Offenders must work up to 28 hours each week over three or four days if they are unemployed. If they are employed, it will be organised around their working hours. Failure to comply without reasonable excuse can result in enforcement action and a return to court.

The supervisor at the Smethwick project on the day Warmer was there was Mo Ghatnoor, who spent 10 years as a corporate banker and whose responsibilities now included driving the van that transported the offenders and equipment to the site.

“This is 100% more fulfilling’ he said. “I used to help businesses with profit but I was just a voice on the phone. Here I make a difference in the heart of my own community. I help my own mental health and that of others, the community and individuals.”

Other forms of community payback, formerly known as community sentences, include removing graffiti, decorating public places and buildings such as community centres, and planting trees. Anyone can nominate a project for the scheme, provided it benefits the local community, does not take paid work away from others, and doesn’t make a profit for anyone.

Among the offenders who will spend less time in prison and more time in the community as a result of the Sentencing Act are burglars, shoplifters and criminals convicted of assault.

The latest statistics, from July to September 2024, show that adults released from custody with sentences of less than 12 months had a reoffending rate of 68.2%, compared with 22.9% for sentences of 12 months or more.

While critics might see community payback as a soft sentencing option, it is not a view shared by Ghatnoor. “We look at the individual to whom it gives a structure to their life,” he said. “It often breaks a negative cycle and changes their mindset, and therefore brings reoffending down.”

articles.title: Alan Jones trial: complainant wants to ‘humiliate’ broadcaster by revealing intimate details of alleged assaults, defence tells court
articles.excerpt:
Barrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Follow our Australia news live bl...
articles.body_text:
Barrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Alan Jones’s defence barrister has told a Sydney court one of the broadcaster’s alleged victims invented details of alleged indecent assaults at a Fitzroy Falls farm to “humiliate” and “smear” the former media titan.

Complainant J told the court during evidence-in-chief earlier this week that during one alleged incident in the property’s bedroom, Jones’s penis was not fully erect and “not very big”.

On Friday, J, during cross-examination, denied fabricating his account of alleged indecent assaults at Jones’s farm in the southern highlands more than 20 years ago.

Complainant J, aged in his 40s, is the first alleged victim to give evidence in the trial at Downing Centre local court. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges involving six men.

J this week alleged in court he did not consent to a kiss near the farm’s pigsty, the touching of his penis on a lounge room couch or sexual touching in the guest bedroom.

Under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, complainant J on Friday denied inventing details about Jones’s genitals to humiliate the older man.

Bashir asked: “This account you’ve given of ‘penis wiggling’ is an attempt to humiliate Mr Jones, isn’t it?”

Bashir suggested in court that it was “an attempt to smear him, isn’t it?” J again said: “No.”

J has previously alleged that when visiting the farm as a teenager, he heard a “tap, tap, tap” before Jones came into the bedroom. He told the court that, while they were both wearing robes, Jones wiggled his hips so their penises crossed.

Bashir said: “You cast yourself as ‘impressive’ and Alan as not achieving an erection as part of the humiliation you are trying to describe, didn’t you? So too your comment on Tuesday that ‘it wasn’t very big’.”

Bashir alleged: “You wouldn’t know because you have never seen Mr Jones’s penis.”

Complainant J then said: “Yes, I have.” J said that Jones had remarked that the then teenager’s penis was “impressive”.

He had earlier told the court that Jones’s penis was circumcised and his genitals were hairy. Bashir suggested that he guessed the details because circumcision was likely for an “Anglo-Saxon man of his age – and so too the hair on the genitals”.

Throughout the cross-examination, Bashir alleged that J was forgetting key details because he had made the whole thing up.

Bashir told the court: “Are you making your evidence up as you go along?”

Bashir challenged J’s memory of his visits to the southern highlands property in the mid-2000s, suggesting in court that he had mixed up occasions, dates and fellow guests.

J agreed that his family was invited to visit the property, and he accompanied them. Bashir said there were inconsistencies in his police statement and his evidence in court regarding how many nights he stayed and which vehicle he drove.

Bashir questioned J in detail about an alleged kiss by Jones while the two men were looking at a pigsty on the farm.

Bashir told the court: “There was no kiss at the pigsty. It was a fabrication.”

The defence barrister said if J was afraid of being assaulted, as he claimed, he didn’t have to walk into the lounge room wearing a robe after Jones instructed him to shower and come back wearing the robe and nothing else.

She pointed to inconsistencies between his police statement and evidence-in-chief.

Bashir said: “There is nothing in your statement about a robe.” J replied: “I remember he was in a robe.”

Bashir suggested he read about Jones wearing a robe in the media. J denied this but agreed there was no mention of Jones wearing a robe in his statement.

The defence barrister said J’s account of the alleged assaults did not make sense because he was young and fit – and he could have pushed the older Jones away.

Bashir asked if Jones had ever threatened to withdraw his stipend and J said no.

Bashir said: “He never said to you he would pull the money if you didn’t do what he wanted, did he?” J replied: “No.”

J agreed that there were “no repercussions” when he couldn’t make invitations from Jones and that Jones didn’t ask him for favours in return for financial support

Bashir said: “All Mr Jones asked of you was that you dedicate yourself to your career.” J told the court: “That’s not all he asked me.”
