articles.title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health
articles.excerpt:
Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m int...
articles.body_text:
Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.

The Thursday ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and imposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.

The ruling on Thursday an additional to that fine, bringing the total amount Meta is responsible for to $942m.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money – $420m – would be used for treatment services for young people in New Mexico. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.

The March trial was the first to find Meta liable for acts committed on its platform, and followed a 2023 Guardian investigation that revealed how Facebook and Instagram had become marketplaces for child sex trafficking.

Several former Meta moderators told the Guardian there were instances where they flagged harmful content related to child grooming, but the cases were not escalated.

In the second phase of the trial, which began in May, prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification, and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.

The judge has also ordered other changes, including that Facebook and Instagram build banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices, and tools to address inappropriate comment.

Those changes, and an educational campaign in New Mexico, would be subject to review by the state.

The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The court also noted that ordering verification of children’s ages only for Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company.

Instead, the court ordered Meta to continue to improve its age-assurance tools in New Mexico, which include using artificial intelligence to determine people’s age based on signals such as who their friends are and what types of content they post and consume. Meta must also attempt to develop a dedicated “under-13-years-of-age prediction model” in the next two years.

Additionally, Meta should also request proof of age for Instagram and Facebook users in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13. If it determines a user to be under 13, or under 18 but without being able to estimate a specific age, Meta must treat the user as under 13 or under 18 until the user verifies their age.

The company must also partner with schools or a child safety organization to create a reporting portal where school staff can flag users who may be under 13. And it must delete personal information it has collected on users under 13. The court also ordered Meta to report on its progress twice a year on how it is complying with the abatement measures.

New Mexico attorney general Raúl Torrez hailed the judgment.

“This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” Torrez said in a statement.

“Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.”

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian on Thursday that the company “disagrees with the ruling” and plans to appeal.

“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” the statement continued.

The total amount Meta is responsible for is a small fraction of of its annual profit, which was about $60bn in 2025. Still, it represents another setback for Meta as it faces a wave of accusations from families of children harmed by social media.

The company is embroiled in a slew of lawsuits in other US states over its alleged harms to young people. In a trial in Tennessee that began last month, the state has accused the company of disregarding internal warnings about teenagers’ compulsive use of Instagram, which has been linked to eating disorders and depression, among other adverse effects. Meta is also gearing up for a trial later this month in federal court in Oakland, California.

What comes out of New Mexico is the first of many dominoes that could fall for Meta, said Laura Edelson, an assistant professor at Northeastern University focusing on social media and cybersecurity.

“America is not going to pass a law that bans social media,” Edelson said. “But if companies like Meta know they’re causing harm to users by product design, the states are finally finding a way to rein this in.”

articles.title: Trump-backed incumbent loses primary after super PAC bankrolled by Dems meddled in race
articles.excerpt:
Rep. Andy Ogles believes his advocacy against energy subsidies have invited millions in opposition spending in his upcoming primary.

Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., was defeated in a primary challenge on T...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Andy Ogles believes his advocacy against energy subsidies have invited millions in opposition spending in his upcoming primary.

Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., was defeated in a primary challenge on Thursday evening by Republican challenger Charlie Hatcher, a farmer and the state's former commissioner of agriculture.

Although the primary was far from a top-watched contest coming into the 2026 primaries, it served as a microcosm of larger forces at play in the Republican Party. From a break in endorsements between President Donald Trump and Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to millions being pumped into the district over environmental policy, the race attracted attention well beyond its borders.

The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC had spent roughly $2 million opposing Ogles and supporting Hatcher. The group has raised $6.7 million this year, making Ogles a sizable portion of their spending this cycle.

TOP TRUMP ALLY WARNS SUPER PAC BANKROLLED BY DEM BILLIONAIRE IS MEDDLING IN GOP PRIMARY

Charlie Hatcher, Republican candidate for Congress, left, pictured next to incumbent Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., right. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect; Brett Carlsen/Getty Images)

The way that Ogles sees it, it’s an attempt to show Republicans what happens when lawmakers attempt to claw back government funding for renewable energy sources.

Like many other Republicans, Ogles has called to scale back renewable energy investments made under the Biden Administration.

"When you have a group spending roughly $2 million in a Republican primary, that tells you how much money they're making off of government subsidies, and they're upset that the government welfare has been taken away from them," Ogles told Fox News Digital in an interview.

A Fox News Digital review of FEC filings discovered that the super PAC is bankrolled by Chris Larsen, the California-based billionaire chairman of Ripple, a financial technology company that, according to its website, offers crypto solutions for businesses.

Larsen is also a frequent Democratic donor, having contributed $5,444,975 to support Kamala Harris's failed presidential campaign.

More than just his opposition to government-backed renewable energy initiatives, Ogles thinks it’s his proximity to Trump that has made him a target.

"It's because I'm close to the president. It is because I am outspoken. And quite frankly, it is because I speak plainly on these issues," Ogles said.

GOP GOVERNOR ENDORSES CANDIDATE CHALLENGING TRUMP-BACKED CONGRESSMAN IN REPUBLICAN US HOUSE PRIMARY

Rep. Andy Ogles (R-TN) addresses the New York Young Republican Club's 113th Annual Gala at Cipriani Wall Street on December 13, 2025 in New York City. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

For his own part, Hatcher, a fifth-generation Tennessee dairy farmer, has pitched himself as someone unencumbered by the political scene and ensnaring interests.

"I think there’s something missing in Washington. There’s a lack of farmer common sense. There’s a lack of work ethic. One of my strengths is problem-solving, looking for solutions, looking for collaborations and supporting the Trump Administration and Speaker Johnson on their agenda," Hatcher said in a campaign video.

Notably, Tennessee’s Republican governor put his weight behind Hatcher late on Tuesday evening, citing a personal relationship between them.

"He served as my commissioner of agriculture; I know Charlie. I know his conservative values and how much he loves our country. Charlie has stood with President Trump since day one," Lee said in a video.

Trump, who has endorsed Ogles, reaffirmed his support for the conservative firebrand ahead of the primary.

"Andy will be really enshrined as one of the best congressmen that you’ll ever see. He’s just fantastic," Trump said. "Andy has always been there when we needed him and when I needed him. He’s been a great help. He’s been a source of inspiration to a lot of people in Congress," Trump said in a post to Truth Social earlier this year.

TENNESSEE PASSES NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP LIKELY TO FLIP FINAL DEM SEAT AS PROTESTS ERUPT INSIDE CAPITOL

Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., walks through the U.S. Capitol on February 03, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Having captured the Republican nomination, Hatcher now advances to a general election he’s heavily favored to win on Nov. 3. He won re-election in 2024 in a 56.9% to 39.5% victory over Maryam Abolfazli.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

articles.title: Australian aviation crew carries out daring midwinter Antarctica rescue
articles.excerpt:
The Skytraders plane landed in Antarctica in total darkness and a temperature of -43°C

An Australian aviation crew has carried out a daring midwinter mission to rescue a US expedition member from a s...
articles.body_text:
The Skytraders plane landed in Antarctica in total darkness and a temperature of -43°C

An Australian aviation crew has carried out a daring midwinter mission to rescue a US expedition member from a station in Antarctica in freezing temperatures and total darkness.

Skytraders said the "extraordinary" mission took place last Friday after a request for urgent help with a medical evacuation from McMurdo Station.

After an initial delay due to the weather, the aviation company said it was able to land its Airbus A319 in "extremely challenging conditions" including temperatures of -43C (-45.4F).

The patient was then safely transferred onto the plane, known as Snowbird 1, which carried on to Christchurch in New Zealand, where the patient was treated. He is now recovering well.

Skytraders deputy chief executive Duncan Mackay told the Australian newspaper the plane had undergone a complete refit into a specialised medevac configuration within 24 hours of the call.

However takeoff was then delayed for 12 hours while the crew waited for a suitable window in the weather.

The plane eventually took off from the Tasmanian city of Hobart in the early hours of Friday morning, before landing at the US research station on Ross Island.

No details were given about the patient or his condition, other than that he was now recovering well.

Pilot Al Wallach said conditions were 'right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability'

Mackay said his company believed it was the closest a civilian airliner had operated so close to winter solstice, which was on 21 June.

"Skytraders has conducted winter medevacs previously, but never this close to the winter solstice," he told the paper. He said "an enormous amount of experience and familiarity with the conditions" was needed to safely land an airliner on an ice runway in total darkness at -43°C.

The pilot, Captain Al Wallach said the successful mission reflected the specialist expertise of the team's people, which included the flight crews, meteorologists, operational planers, runway teams and medical personnel.

"Every Antarctic mission demands absolute precision, but winter operations raise the complexity significantly," he said "The conditions we encountered were right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability."

Skytraders carried out a similar mission in March 2020, when the US requested help evacuating a member of the US Antarctic Program also based in McMurdo, although temperatures were slightly warmer at -30°C.

articles.title: Trump’s birthright citizenship attack the latest effort in obsessive campaign
articles.excerpt:
For more than a decade, president has been fixated on trying to undermine a key constitutional right

With a pair of executive orders on Thursday, Donald Trump has tried – once again – to undermine th...
articles.body_text:
For more than a decade, president has been fixated on trying to undermine a key constitutional right

With a pair of executive orders on Thursday, Donald Trump has tried – once again – to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship, a right enshrined in the US constitution and reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago.

The orders attempt to broaden the categories of children who would be ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”, which the president claimed is practiced by “hundreds of thousands” of people.

That estimate appears to be wildly inflated. According to the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024”.

It was the latest attack in a quixotic campaign that the US president has waged for more than a decade.

At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for the US-citizen children of undocumented immigrants.

“You can’t come into the country – you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment, it’ll take 15 years, it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.”

If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over.”

Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth.

“It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told the interviewer Jonathan Swan. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.”

As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, a former law clerk to supreme court justice Clarence Thomas who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born.

Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica.

In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous”, and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, 32 other nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed then that an executive order was in the process of being drafted.

Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, and was struck down in June by the supreme court, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had an overtly political element from the start.

After all, Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US.

Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural-born citizen.”

Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”.

Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on January 6 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public.”

While asserting the right to deny citizenship to some children of non-citizens is clearly still a priority for Trump, it remains to be seen if his latest attempts to curtail the right will succeed. The two new orders are likely to face legal challenges, and come just weeks after the US supreme court struck down Trump’s previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, issued on the first day of his second term.

In the court’s June decision, chief justice John Roberts said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution.

“Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.”

articles.title: Mamdani repeatedly sidesteps questions on reported plan to revive tax hikes on wealthy New Yorkers
articles.excerpt: The democratic socialist mayor declined to say whether he plans to launch a public push for higher taxes before November after Gov. Kathy Hochul previously rejected similar proposals. (Fox 5 New York)...
articles.body_text:
The democratic socialist mayor declined to say whether he plans to launch a public push for higher taxes before November after Gov. Kathy Hochul previously rejected similar proposals. (Fox 5 New York)

New York City democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani repeatedly sidestepped questions Thursday about reported plans to launch a public pressure campaign this fall pushing tax hikes on wealthy New Yorkers and corporations.

Mamdani reportedly plans to build public support after Labor Day for similar proposals that Gov. Kathy Hochul previously rejected in early 2026. The reported push is expected ahead of the New York Legislature's return to Albany in January 2027 and Hochul's re-election campaign this fall, according to The New York Post.

During an interview with Fox 5 New York, Mamdani repeatedly declined to answer questions about the potential campaign before later saying such discussions would only come after the November election.

Asked whether he had spoken with Hochul about the reported campaign, Mamdani did not answer directly, instead using the opportunity to tout the opening of 2,000 free child care seats for New Yorkers through their policy efforts.

NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED'

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters about the city's finances during a news conference in New York, Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026. (Seth Wenig/AP Photo)

"The governor and I are in constant communication and, frankly, I appreciate her partnership because if it wasn't for the governor, then we wouldn't have been able to stand together to announce that we had more than 5,000 New Yorkers come forward to apply for these 2,000 free child care seats," he said. "And I'm so excited about that, and the fact that we're going to expand to 12,000, and the work that's still to come."

The reporter then pressed Mamdani on whether the Democratic Socialists of America would join the potential campaign this fall, but he again declined to answer directly, saying his focus remains on the present.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, left, and Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, speak during an announcement in New York, US, on Tuesday, Jan. 6, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"My focus right now is where we are, which is August, and ensuring that everything that we're doing is keeping New Yorkers safe amidst a heat wave and preparing for the school year," Mamdani said. "A lot of the conversation about what comes after November, I think, is a conversation for what comes after November."

"So you don't plan to launch a campaign to tax the rich before the November election?" the reporter asked.

"The conversations I've been having with the governor and with my team are about the here and now and there will always be time for the conversations that come after that," Mamdani said.

MAMDANI EXTENDS DEADLINE FOR NYC HOMEOWNERS TO SEEK EXEMPTION FROM NEW PIED-À-TERRE TAX

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani previously backed a proposal to tax luxury second homes owned by non-residents, targeting ultra-wealthy property owners. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The reported campaign would revive a previous push by Mamdani to close the city's multibillion-dollar budget gap through tax increases, a proposal Hochul previously rejected. Mamdani's earlier plan called for raising the city's personal income tax rate on filers earning $1 million or more, a move he projected could generate roughly $3 billion annually, while also increasing corporate tax rates.

As an alternative, Hochul and Mamdani jointly advanced the state's first pied-à-terre tax, an annual surcharge on certain high-value second homes, which passed in May 2026. State and city officials have projected the measure could raise about $500 million annually.

Mamdani also said his May 2026 executive budget closed what his administration described as an inherited $12 billion budget gap, crediting aggressive savings, new investments, his partnership with Albany and new tax revenue, including the pied-à-terre tax.Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Israeli raid in West Bank’s Qalandiya injures 51 Palestinians
articles.excerpt:
A “large-scale” Israeli raid in the Qalandiya refugee camp in the occupied West Bank has injured at least 51 Palestinians, the Jerusalem Governorate told Al Jazeera.

Israeli forces demolished commerc...
articles.body_text:
A “large-scale” Israeli raid in the Qalandiya refugee camp in the occupied West Bank has injured at least 51 Palestinians, the Jerusalem Governorate told Al Jazeera.

Israeli forces demolished commercial shops near the Qalandiya checkpoint on Thursday, before imposing a curfew on the neighbouring town of Kafr Aqab and sealing off roads linking the area to Jerusalem.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) said 35 people were hospitalised after severe beatings and six more were treated at the scene. One person was hit by a rubber-coated steel bullet.

Six others suffered tear gas inhalation, according to PRCS.

The organisation said its ambulance crews had been blocked from reaching the wounded since late at night on Wednesday, though crews still managed to evacuate several patients, including people requiring kidney dialysis.

Israeli soldiers fired stun grenades at journalists stationed at the camp’s entrance and ordered them to leave.

Dozens of Palestinians, including children and women, were detained for field interrogations inside homes converted into makeshift holding sites, according to local Palestinian media.

Israeli forces also raided the city of Jenin on Thursday, shooting one Palestinian and assaulting another, according to PRCS.

Israeli army attacks and settler violence against Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have intensified in the past months, moving in tandem with increased demolitions of Palestinian property and illegal seizure of their land.

Rights groups have recorded more than 11,000 Israeli military and settler attacks across the West Bank in the first half of this year alone – with more than 2,300 Palestinians forced from their homes due to settler violence and related restrictions.

A United Nations-appointed commission of inquiry concluded in June that Israeli authorities have repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and investigate and punish those responsible.

In some cases, Israeli authorities directly enabled violence through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding to settlers, the investigators said.

Israel has banned UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, from operating in occupied East Jerusalem and demolished several of the agency’s facilities there, including near Qalandiya.

Since taking on authority over civilian affairs in the occupied West Bank, Israeli Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich has approved, legalised or re-established more than 104 illegal settlements and 160 agricultural outposts. Meanwhile, Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir has distributed thousands of firearms to settlers through state-backed “civil defence” programmes.

Several Western governments, including the United Kingdom, Canada and France, have sanctioned individual settlers as well as sitting ministers, such as Smotrich, over their role in the violence.

In one of his first decrees after returning to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump revoked limited US sanctions against Israeli settlers accused of attacking Palestinians.

articles.title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harm to youths
articles.excerpt: A judge in New Mexico in the United States has ordered Facebook and Instagram owner Meta to pay $567m and change how its platforms function for young users in the state after finding the company is to...
articles.body_text:
A judge in New Mexico in the United States has ordered Facebook and Instagram owner Meta to pay $567m and change how its platforms function for young users in the state after finding the company is to blame for harming children’s mental health.

Thursday’s ruling came in the second phase of a landmark trial against the social media giant, with jurors in March finding that Meta had violated the state’s consumer protection law by misrepresenting the safety of Facebook and Instagram for young users. The jury ordered the company to pay $375 million in damages earlier this year.

After this latest ruling, Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money, $420m, will be used for treatment services for young people. The rest will go towards awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.

Prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.

The decision means the look of Meta’s platforms could change. The judge ordered Facebook and Instagram to build banner and informational screens to clearly explain their protection features, best practices and tools to address inappropriate comments, for example, and display them regularly.

Those changes and an educational campaign in New Mexico would be subject to review by the state.

Meta said it will appeal the ruling and that it has been working to identify and remove harmful content from its platforms.

“We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” the company said in a statement.

The judge had heard three weeks of testimony during the second trial over the lawsuit, which did not involve a jury. It focused solely on whether Meta’s platforms created a “public nuisance” under New Mexico law.

The case is being closely watched across the US as states, municipalities and school districts  pursue similar claims seeking to force changes at the industry level.

articles.title: Retired police chief helps subdue passenger after alleged midair outburst over alcohol cutoff
articles.excerpt:
Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara recounts helping restrain an allegedly unruly passenger after a midair disturbance aboard a United Airlines flight.

Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Bria...
articles.body_text:
Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara recounts helping restrain an allegedly unruly passenger after a midair disturbance aboard a United Airlines flight.

Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara found himself back in crisis mode Thursday, not on the streets of Mill City, but 35,000 feet in the air, when what should have been a routine United Airlines flight suddenly turned chaotic.

O'Hara told Fox News Digital he watched flight attendants spend nearly 45 minutes trying to de-escalate an increasingly belligerent passenger, prompting him and two off-duty Bergen County, New Jersey, sheriff's deputies to intervene.

The retired police chief, who was traveling with his wife aboard United Flight 1364 from Newark to Fort Lauderdale, said the passenger repeatedly berated flight attendants, tried to get out of his seat and behaved erratically as crew members worked to keep the situation under control.

FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT

Law enforcement officers escort an unruly passenger off a United Airlines flight after retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara and two off-duty Bergen County sheriff's deputies helped restrain the man following a midair disturbance. (Wafiyyah O'Hara)

"About like for the last 45 minutes of the flight ... all the flight attendants came over, and they were incredible," O'Hara told Fox News Digital. "Incredibly professional, just trying to talk to this guy to de-escalate things."

According to O'Hara, the passenger became increasingly agitated after flight attendants refused to serve him more alcohol, a detail O'Hara said he later learned from the Broward Sheriff's Office after the arrest. The man reportedly continued shouting profanities and making threatening remarks before the encounter turned physical.

"It was infuriating to hear a man speak to these women who were just incredibly professional and trying to keep everybody safe that way for so long," O'Hara said. "And, finally, he just kind of got up and lunged towards them."

That's when two passengers seated near the back of the aircraft grabbed the man from behind as O'Hara rushed forward from his seat.

OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN

The three men worked together to restrain the passenger using plastic flex cuffs before securing him back in his seat, so the flight attendants could take their seats and the plane could land safely.

O'Hara later learned the two passengers were Bergen County Sheriff's deputies from New Jersey.

United Airlines also confirmed the incident in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Local law enforcement met United Flight 1364 upon its arrival in Fort Lauderdale to address an unruly passenger," the airline said. "We thank our crew and customers for assisting with the situation and helping ensure the safety of everyone onboard."

UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT

A United Airlines Boeing 737 Max aircraft prepares for takeoff at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., July 10, 2025. A United flight was diverted to Pittsburgh Saturday after a reported security issue. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

The airline said the Boeing 737-900 was carrying 174 passengers and six crew members, including two pilots and four flight attendants.

While cellphone video of the confrontation has circulated widely on social media, O'Hara said it doesn't capture the nearly hour-long effort by the flight crew to peacefully resolve the situation before passengers stepped in.

"No one should take the kind of verbal abuse that they did," he said. "They were absolute professionals trying to keep everybody safe."

O'Hara, who spent 25 years in law enforcement before retiring after leading public safety operations in Newark, New Jersey, and later serving as Minneapolis police chief, said the incident underscored just how dangerous violent outbursts can become aboard an aircraft.

Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara speaks during a news conference in Minneapolis Jan. 10, 2026. (Jen Golbeck/AP)

"I started to think, ‘Well, geez, what are we going to do if somebody really wants to fight the whole time?’" he said. "It's dangerous. We're in such a confined space like that, and someone's going to act out like that because you don't know potentially what the motivation might be."

His wife, who is a lieutenant with the Newark Police Department, was seated nearby throughout the ordeal.

"The only thing I was thinking about was if this goes bad, I know at least she has my back," O'Hara said with a laugh, adding he has seen her "handle herself on the street" and knew she would be ready if the situation worsened.

Afterward, O'Hara's wife praised her husband's actions in a social media post.

"Proud of my husband today," she wrote. "When a disruptive passenger created a dangerous situation on a flight, he stepped up to help federal agents safely arrest him. Leadership isn’t just about the job you hold, it’s about being willing to help when others need it. Grateful everyone on board arrived safely."

Minneapolis Chief of Police Brian O'Hara called out the city's "bourgeois liberal mentality" after the death of George Floyd. (Getty Images)

Looking back on the incident, O'Hara said he hopes Americans choose action over standing by when innocent people are in danger.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

"We're coming up on the 25th anniversary of September 11," he said. "I would hope everybody in this country now knows that if things are escalating to the point where there's going to be some kind of violence, I think every citizen that is able to has a duty to try and help to stop it."

He also said airlines should ensure restraints are readily available and that crew members are trained to use them if passengers become violent.

"I think it would be good to make sure that they have restraints that are available, that at least some people are trained in some way to use them safely to get somebody restrained if they needed to," O'Hara said.

As of Thursday afternoon, authorities had not publicly identified the passenger or announced any criminal charges.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Broward Sheriff's Office and the Federal Aviation Administration for additional information and comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Squad-backed ‘Tennessee Three’ lawmaker wins House primary in newly redrawn district
articles.excerpt:
Fox News correspondent Matt Finn has the latest on the competitive seats up for grabs on 'Special Report.'

Squad-backed Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, District 86, part of the trio of lawmakers...
articles.body_text:
Fox News correspondent Matt Finn has the latest on the competitive seats up for grabs on 'Special Report.'

Squad-backed Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, District 86, part of the trio of lawmakers in his state referred to as the "Tennessee Three," won the Democratic primary Thursday in Tennessee's newly redrawn 9th Congressional District.

Pearson defeated state Sen. London Lamar, District 33, community activist Marion LaTroy Alexandria-Williams and attorney Jim Torino. He will face Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, in November with his campaign warchest of millions of dollars he has raised throughout his campaign, significantly outpacing his Democratic opponents.

The Memphis-area state lawmaker entered the primary with the backing of prominent Democrats who are part of the progressive group of lawmakers called "the Squad," including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., and Summer Lee, D-Pa., who all joined Pearson at a campaign rally in Memphis last month.

'SQUAD' MEMBER'S COMEBACK BID THWARTED AS ESTABLISHMENT DEMS NOTCH VICTORY AGAINST SOCIALISTS

Known for his fiery, preacher-style speeches, Pearson has also received support from national left-wing groups including Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, MoveOn and Indivisible.

The so-called "Tennessee Three" lawmakers seen pictured above. From left, Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, Rep. Gloria Johnson, D-Knoxville, and Rep. Justin Jones, D-Nashville, raise their fists as they walk across Fisk University campus after hearing Vice President Kamala Harris speak, Friday, April 7, 2023, in Nashville, Tennessee.  (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Pearson rose to national prominence in 2023 as one of the "Tennessee Three" lawmakers who participated in a gun-control protest on the state House floor following the Covenant School shooting in Nashville that killed three young kids and three adults.

Republican lawmakers subsequently expelled Pearson and fellow state Rep. Justin Jones over the protest, though they later regained their seats.

A third Democrat, Gloria Johnson of Knoxville, avoided expulsion by a single vote, according to local media reporting.

Tennessee state Reps. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, Rep. Justin Jones, D-Nashville, and Rep. Gloria Johnson, D-Knoxville, holding their hands up as they exit the House Chamber doors at Tennessee State Capitol Building in Nashville, Tenn., Monday, April 3, 2023. (Nicole Hester /The Tennessean via AP)

'JUMPING SHIP': HOUSE DEM FINDS EXIT STRATEGY AFTER SCOTUS RULING SHIFTS ADVANTAGE TO GOP

The open-seat primary won by Pearson on Thursday followed a redrawing of Tennessee’s congressional map that divided Memphis among three Republican-leaning districts and prompted longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tenn., to retire.

Before the new map, heavily Democratic Memphis was largely kept together in the 9th District, giving Tennessee Democrats one reliable congressional seat in an otherwise deeply Republican state.

U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) questions Special Counsel Jack Smith as he testifies during a hearing before the House Judiciary Committee in the Rayburn House Office Building on Capitol Hill on January 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Cohen has been the lone Democrat in Tennessee’s nine-member House delegation alongside eight Republicans since 2023, but the new map favors the GOP in all nine districts.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: Wisconsin man flies helicopter to Cabela's because the drive was too long
articles.excerpt: Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation into an airspace incident involving President Donald Trump's Marine One helicopter....
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation into an airspace incident involving President Donald Trump's Marine One helicopter. Official reports confirm a commercial plane coming from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport caused a momentary loss of separation with the presidential helicopter.

Look, sometimes you just really need to go to Cabela's.

And when the store is 50 miles away, you have two options: get in the car and sit in traffic like a schmuck, or fire up the helicopter and be there in minutes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

Helicopter ready for departure at heliport. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The 69-year-old Wisconsin pilot flew from Rosendale to the Cabela’s in Richfield on Saturday evening, landing in a mostly empty section of the store’s parking lot so he could pick up some bowhunting supplies.

Naturally, some busybody saw a helicopter descend outside Cabela’s and called the police.

Washington County sheriff’s deputies arrived to investigate the unusual landing, only to discover there was no emergency, no dramatic getaway and no criminal activity.

Nothing to see here. Just a man who values his time and urgently needed a fresh pack of broadheads.

"So I asked my neighbor friend if he wanted to take a ride to Cabela’s to get some shopping done," Pipping said.

Pipping, who has decades of flying experience, said he called the store before making the approximately 20-minute flight. He also circled the parking lot beforehand to make sure he had enough room to land safely.

Signage is displayed outside a Cabela's Inc. retail store in Greenville, South Carolina, on Tuesday, Oct. 4, 2016. Cabela's agreed to be bought by Bass Pro Shops in a $5.5 billion deal, handing a victory to the activist investor that had been pushing the outdoor-sports equipment retailer to put itself up for sale. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

When asked why he decided to fly rather than make the roughly 45-minute drive, Pipping responded with a question of his own.

"Why would you drive if you can fly there in a helicopter?" he said.

OREGON BALLOT MEASURE THAT WOULD HAVE CRIMINALIZED HUNTING AND FISHING FAILS TO QUALIFY FOR VOTE

Pipping said there were no vehicles near the far end of the massive parking lot, allowing him to land, head inside and complete his shopping without incident.

By the time he returned, however, a deputy was waiting to check out the aircraft.

A small commercial helicopter parked at an airport. (Getty Images)

Pipping was properly licensed, had landed safely and complied with applicable Federal Aviation Administration regulations. He was not arrested or cited.

The sheriff’s office ultimately described the incident as a "unique way to make a shopping trip."

Love all things hunting, fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick Outdoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: Australia news live: Richard Marles insists Tony Burke’s speech on Labor’s new restrictive immigration policy ‘hasn’t been called off’
articles.excerpt:
Deputy prime minister says Burke’s speech before National Press Club was not cancelled. Follow today’s news live

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the Na...
articles.body_text:
Deputy prime minister says Burke’s speech before National Press Club was not cancelled. Follow today’s news live

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the National Press Club about migration policies.

The deputy prime minister said the decision was merely a move of date, not a cancellation. Marles said:

double quotation markIt’s not unusual for dates to be moved around in people’s diaries and in terms of presenting speeches of that kind. I think what’s important here in terms of migration policy is complex. It’s one that we’ve been working on since we’ve come to government.

Tony Burke will be talking about that and he’ll be talking about that at the National Press Club at the earliest opportunity.

double quotation markMoving around dates in a diary for senior members of government is very routine. It happens literally all the time. The speech hasn’t been called off. A date has been changed. That literally happens every week. And there’s nothing more to it than that.

Australia’s best sustainable architecture for 2026 – in pictures

This year’s finalists for the National Architecture awards’ sustainability category include a compact Canberra housing development and the largest commercial use of hempcrete in the country.

New Victoria premier pushes on with work-from-home laws

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, who took over as leader after an internal revolt against Jacinta Allan, will continue pursuing the laws she championed, AAP reports.

The legislation would give full-time, part-time and casual workers the right to work from home two days a week on a pro-rata basis where reasonable.

The bill has already passed the Labor-controlled lower house and will soon be debated in the upper house as the November state election approaches.

It has attracted staunch opposition from business lobby groups, which have met with Carroll since his elevation to premier. But a Victorian government spokesperson confirmed on Friday the government’s position had not changed.

Among the more contentious elements of the bill is a requirement for employers to pay any reasonable costs to allow an eligible employee to work remotely. This may include essential equipment and secure access to work systems.

Federal parliament is returning from winter break next week.

Do you have a question you’d like to ask Guardian Australia’s team of political reporters in Canberra? Our political editor, Tom McIlroy, and the team will be answering readers’ questions on the Australian Politics podcast.

Please send us your questions to australianpolitics@theguardian.com.

Can Australia make housing affordable while avoiding a major market crash?

The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates and the property market is in retreat. So far, so normal.

There is a sense that this year’s fall in home prices feels different from previous episodes. The data tells another story.

Over the past four decades there have been seven property market downturns of varying length and depth, according to analysis put together by Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist.

They are often triggered by interest rate hikes, which make home loans more expensive, but they also occur during crises and policy changes.

Police investigating after 23-year-old found dead at rural property with injuries consistent with animal attack

Police are investigating after the body of a man was found with significant injuries in Sydney yesterday, with initial inquiries indicating he may have been attacked by animals prior to his death.

NSW police said emergency services were called to a rural property in the suburb of Eschol Park in south-west Sydney on Wednesday around noon. On arrival, officers found the body of a 23-year-old man.

A crime scene was established and detectives have begun an investigation into the death.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

EV imports more than doubled in June quarter

Electric vehicle imports have also surged as the US-Iran conflict drove up petrol prices and sent motorists flocking to Chinese manufacturers such as BYD, AAP reports.

Battery electric vehicle sales more than doubled in the June quarter to 69,414, data from the Australian Automobile Association showed.

On the other hand, imports of automated data processing (ADP) equipment – including equipment used to fit out AI datacentres – fell by more than a quarter in the three months to June after a surge at the start of 2026.

Fuel diplomacy tanks Australia’s trade surplus

Australia has recorded its lowest quarterly trade surplus in almost a decade as the federal government raced to secure fuel cargoes during the Middle East oil crisis, AAP reports.

The jump in imports narrowed Australia’s goods trade surplus to $1.1bn in the June quarter, the lowest figure since 2017, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed on Thursday.

The Albanese government’s deal-making blitz to secure supplies from Australia’s fuel trading partners was evident in country-specific data.

Despite the decline in the quarterly trade surplus, the trade balance increased $4.3bn in the month of June, above forecasts. That was largely driven by a 60% jump in non-monetary gold exports, reversing a 35% decline in May.

Former ABC executive says Race Around the World clip about Rinehart not a breach, but worthy of apology

Alan Sunderland, a former editorial director at the ABC, has said he was not surprised the broadcaster’s ombudsman found an episode of its Race Around the World program did not breach its editorial standards related to harm and offence.

The program included a four-minute documentary that ended with crude and offensive comments about mining magnate Gina Rinehart, including a line about “mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll”. The ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, later apologised for the episode amid Rinehart’s threats of legal action, and the broadcaster edited the footage to remove the offending lines.

Sunderland said there was a “long history of latitude” at the ABC for content, “particularly with satirical entertainment programs where people ascertain that the depiction of violence, whatever it is, was clearly meant to be humorous”:

double quotation markIt is not per se a breach of standards to depict violence where nobody would reasonably in good faith think that it was an actual direct threat of violence.

Still, Sunderland said he believes it was probably right for Marks to apologise:

double quotation markI think the ABC needs to take account of public tastes on this. Public tastes move and shift over questions of what is and isn’t offensive, but I think there was a pretty common acceptance, even from the film-maker herself, that it was inappropriate. And I think they did the right thing to make that call, regardless of whether it breached editorial standards or not.

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the National Press Club about migration policies.

The deputy prime minister said the decision was merely a move of date, not a cancellation. Marles said:

double quotation markIt’s not unusual for dates to be moved around in people’s diaries and in terms of presenting speeches of that kind. I think what’s important here in terms of migration policy is complex. It’s one that we’ve been working on since we’ve come to government.

Tony Burke will be talking about that and he’ll be talking about that at the National Press Club at the earliest opportunity.

double quotation markMoving around dates in a diary for senior members of government is very routine. It happens literally all the time. The speech hasn’t been called off. A date has been changed. That literally happens every week. And there’s nothing more to it than that.

Marles maintains gambling reforms about striking a ‘balance’ over ‘complex’ issue

Richard Marles, the deputy prime minister, said the government still intends to get its gambling reforms past parliament despite opposition from the Greens and the Coalition, who both argue that they do not go far enough.

Marles spoke to RN Breakfast, echoing the government line that they are the “strongest reforms in respect of gambling advertising that have ever been put forward”. He went on:

double quotation markI mean, we are doing more in terms of breaking the link between gambling advertising and sport, more in terms of protecting our kids from being exposed to gambling advertising on TV and radio at the times when they would be watching and listening. We’re doing more in terms of supporting BetStop, which helps people who identify to restrict their own gambling habits.

So this is really important legislation and we’ll work with the parties across the parliament to get it passed.

When asked about criticism of the legislation, Marles said gambling was a “complex” issue with differing views.

double quotation markIt’s also an area where you need to strike a balance and we believe we’ve done that … We’re not saying that people should not be able to engage in betting but there needs to be a balance. And it’s important.

Penny Wong says Australia has ‘more work to do’ forging relationships in the Pacific

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is in Fiji today amid a meeting with her counterparts from across the Pacific.

Wong said Australia has been working to rebuild trust and Australia’s reputation in the region, as well as its “strategic position in the Pacific”.

double quotation markWe’ve got work more work to do. We’ve announced that we do want to engage with and negotiate with both Tonga and Solomon Islands. Obviously, there’ll be a lot of work there that we want to do with them in partnership.

Wong also said she hopes China “takes note” of the region-wide opposition to a ballistic missile test Beijing undertook in July.

double quotation markIt was a test which was destabilising and in a region where leaders have said we want an ocean of peace. It’s really important that partners respect that, and we would continue to encourage that respect.

Good morning, and welcome to Friday. It’s Nick Visser here to get us started. Here’s what’s on deck.

Australia has recorded its lowest quarterly trade surplus in nearly a decade amid a long push to secure fuel cargoes during the oil crisis in the Middle East.

Electric vehicle imports have surged, with battery EV sales more than doubling in the June quarter to nearly 70,000.

articles.title: After the floods, hunger: Mozambique’s second disaster
articles.excerpt:
Xai-Xai, Mozambique – Months after floodwaters tore through his neighbourhood, Joacim Pinto still walks past the empty plots where his crops once grew.

The ground that once gave his family food and i...
articles.body_text:
Xai-Xai, Mozambique – Months after floodwaters tore through his neighbourhood, Joacim Pinto still walks past the empty plots where his crops once grew.

The ground that once gave his family food and income now stands as a reminder of what was lost. His livestock disappeared, and the gardens that provided food and security were swallowed by the floods.

But for Pinto, 50, the disaster did not end when the water receded.

For the resident of Xa-Xai, in Mozambique’s southern Gaza province, surviving the floods was only the beginning of the struggle.

“We either die from the floods, or if we survive, hunger takes over,” Pinto tells Al Jazeera.

The floods swept across Mozambique from late December 2025 into early 2026, leaving communities like Pinto’s facing a second crisis: finding enough money to buy food after losing the ability to produce much of it themselves.

“The floods destroyed our wells, pipes, livestock and gardens,” Pinto says. “The price of basic food increased sharply.”

Mozambique is still recovering from one of its most damaging flood seasons in recent years. The disaster affected communities across several central and southern provinces, including Gaza, Maputo, Inhambane, Sofala and Zambezia.

For farming families, the destruction was immediate. Fields disappeared under water, harvests were lost, and roads used to move food between farms and markets were damaged.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), about 275,405 hectares (680,540 acres) of farmland were affected, threatening the livelihoods of approximately 314,783 farmers.

In rural Mozambique, farming is not simply a source of income. It is a household safety net.

Before the floods, Pinto’s garden reduced his dependence on shops and traders. It provided food for his family and helped protect them from sudden price increases.

Now the gardens around his neighbourhood lie empty, and families who once relied on their own harvests must turn to markets where prices have climbed.

The United Nations’ World Food Programme (WFP) warned that flooding has disrupted access to food across many affected areas.

Roads became impassable, markets stopped operating in some communities, and transport costs increased. In places where floodwater cut roads, food could not easily reach people who needed it.

At the same time, local production fell as farmland was damaged.

“So, while the exact inflation rate varies by district, what we see on the ground is significant pressure on food prices driven by a dramatic reduction in supply, alongside a surge in humanitarian needs,” Ana Mato Hombre, WFP Mozambique spokesperson, tells Al Jazeera.

“In many flood-affected areas, food stocks were lost, cropland destroyed and several markets are not functioning at all,” she adds.

Hombre says isolated cases of traders taking advantage of shortages cannot be ruled out, but the main force behind rising prices appears to be the loss of production and disruption of supply routes.

The effects of the floods have travelled far beyond damaged fields.

“Every time we have floods or droughts in the Southern African region, food prices rise because of supply shortages and the high cost of importing food,” says Tafadzwanashe Mabhaudhi, a professor of climate change and food systems at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

Mabhaudhi, who is originally from the region and has studied climate-related threats to food systems across Southern Africa, says repeated disasters are changing how vulnerable communities survive.

“It also means poorer diets because people cannot access a range of foods,” he tells Al Jazeera.

The latest floods came while communities were still recovering from the severe drought linked to the 2024–2025 El Nino weather pattern, which affected agricultural production across parts of southern Africa.

For families already weakened by drought, another disaster leaves little time to recover.

The crisis has also reached traders trying to keep food moving.

“We had no choice but to add 10 percent in markup to the price of rice, flour, live chicken and other products,” says Shuwa Anolis, a truck driver and food trader in Xai-Xai.

Flooding disrupted major transport routes linking southern and northern Mozambique, pushing up fuel and delivery costs.

“Look at the main highway linking south to north of the country; it was flooded and impassable. Our fuel costs remain high too,” Anolis tells Al Jazeera.

He says the price of prepared chicken increased after the floods because transporting and supplying food became more expensive.

But for families who lost their crops, higher prices add another burden.

Traders are trying to recover rising costs while households that once fed themselves from their own land are struggling to buy what they need.

Mozambique is repeatedly absorbing the costs of climate extremes despite contributing little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country’s exposure is shaped by geography, dependence on agriculture and limited resources to rebuild after disasters.

Mabhaudhi says Mozambique’s position downstream of major river systems also increases its vulnerability because flooding can be influenced by rainfall and land-use activities beyond its borders.

But the impact is not only measured in lost crops and damaged homes.

Repeated disasters are shrinking the time communities have to recover. Families lose crops, begin rebuilding and then face another shock before they have regained their footing.

For Pinto and thousands of other survivors, the disappearance of the floodwaters has not marked the end of the crisis.

The challenge now is rebuilding livelihoods before the next shock arrives.

“The same communities whose crops were devastated by drought are still recovering, and now they have been devastated by floods,” Mabhaudhi says. “There is a limit on people’s ability to cope with back-to-back disasters.”

articles.title: Disneyland, actors' union clash over parental leave, benefits as union negotiates first contract
articles.excerpt:
Flag retreat ceremony honors members of all U.S. military branches daily with an updated look for the 70th anniversary celebration.

Magic United, an affiliate of Actors' Equity representing 1,700 par...
articles.body_text:
Flag retreat ceremony honors members of all U.S. military branches daily with an updated look for the 70th anniversary celebration.

Magic United, an affiliate of Actors' Equity representing 1,700 parade, show and character cast members at Disneyland, and Disney are in the midst of negotiations on a first contract, and they're telling Fox News Digital it's not going smoothly.

While most Disneyland employees have been represented by unions for decades, the Characters and Parades department remained nonunion until workers voted to organize in 2024 amid California’s cost-of-living crisis after the pandemic. This has led to negotiations between the newly formed union and Disney in order to negotiate a first contract both parties can agree on.

Because this is the workers' first union contract, both sides disagree over how to characterize Disney's proposals. Disney argues it is negotiating the initial terms of employment rather than eliminating existing union benefits. The union counters that workers currently receive benefits such as paid parental leave, so excluding them from the first contract would effectively mean employees lose those benefits.

The Los Angeles Times noted that, "Although the union said it has been getting movement on a number of health and safety issues, there are other points in contention, including the amount the company matches for employee contributions to their 401(k) retirement savings plans and a proposal that limits the number of times a worker can give away a shift without managerial approval."

DISNEYLAND MAY SCRAP LONG-STANDING PARK RULE THAT FRUSTRATED VISITORS

The union to represent Disneyland's character and parade performers only formed recently after the COVID-19 pandemic. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital contacted both parties about the ongoing negotiations, recalling founder Walt Disney’s famous anecdote about having founded the Disneyland park as a place where parents and their children can have fun together, asking whether Disney is fulfilling that mission as negotiations continue.

"Disneyland is often presented as ‘the ultimate family-friendly destination,’ but that’s no longer the case for 1,700 Cast Members in the Characters and Parades departments who create Disney magic by bringing beloved characters to life in shows, meet and greets and character dining experiences," a representative for the union responded.

"Disney has proposed eliminating paid parental leave for these workers and in the first year of a contract the company presented a zero percent wage increase – despite a period of high inflation. Orange County, California where Disneyland is located also is rated as one of the costliest places to live in the United States," the spokesperson added.

The representative claimed further that Disneyland "wants to eliminate paid parental leave, cut the number of paid holidays and size of401(k) contributions and make it unnecessarily harder for Character and Parade workers to swap shifts."

Al Vincent Jr., Actors’ Equity’s Executive Director, told the Los Angeles Times in a report about these negotiations, "When you propose to take away paid parental leave from those who work day in and day out to give other families great experiences, that’s not family friendly."

CHEAPEST DAYS TO VISIT DISNEY: HERE'S WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW BEFORE BOOKING YOUR TRIP

Jessica Jakary, a Disneyland Resort spokesperson, told Fox News Digital, "Disneyland Resort values its cast members, offers competitive benefits and is proud of its long history of working collaboratively with the unions that represent them." (David McNew/Getty Images)

Jessica Jakary, a Disneyland Resort spokesperson, has contested these claims, declaring to Fox News Digital, "Disneyland Resort values its cast members, offers competitive benefits and is proud of its long history of working collaboratively with the unions that represent them."

Disney as a company has stated that it is committed to ongoing negotiations with Magic United, noting to Fox News that there appears to be some confusion in the comparison to Walt Disney World in Florida where there are no state disability payments for parental leave like those provided for in California.

Disney has also said to Fox News Digital that it has not proposed to limit the ability to trade shifts, but instead the proposal only limits the number of times a cast member can give away a shift without managerial approval.

Disney also said that Disneyland Resort has proposed wage increases over the term of the agreement, and that while it is not offering an immediate wage increase, it has continued to provide annual increases to this bargaining unit as negotiations progress.

In one example provided, Disney claims that as of December 2025, full-time and part-time cast members in this bargaining unit have received a 4% increase.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Disneyland is in California, one of the most expensive states in America to live in. (iStock)

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant
articles.excerpt:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has seen his company face an increasing number of lawsuits over child safety.

A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure t...
articles.body_text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has seen his company face an increasing number of lawsuits over child safety.

A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to children, marking the largest ruling against the company over child safety.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the social media giant is a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution and that it must put the money in a fund aimed at reducing future harms.

The ruling is in addition to $375m in fines Meta was already ordered to pay in the case, for a total of $942m.

Judge Biedscheid compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and content as its product and "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated".

Meta, which owns and operates Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, has been contacted by the BBC for comment.

Regarding the earlier $375m verdict against in the case, Meta had said it intended to appeal the ruling. It was the first time that a state had successfully sued Meta over child safety issues.

The case stems from a 2023 lawsuit brought by attorneys for the State of New Mexico, arguing Meta should be held liable for the way in which its platforms endangered children and exposed them to sexually explicit material and contact with sexual predators.

In the first phase of the trial, Meta was found to have repeatedly violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act as its recommendation algorithms essentially "steered" young users toward harmful content and contacts.

Recommendation algorithms are the tools that Meta uses to automatically curate the content a user sees on its platforms.

In ruling on this second phase of the trial, Judge Biedscheid found that Meta's harms reached the level of "public nuisance", or an issue of health and safety that has become so widespread it is negatively impacting a general public.

In addition to being the largest fine Meta has received over child safety issues, the ruling also appears to be the first time that a social media company has been deemed a public nuisance.

"Just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world and create a common, societal burden on and harm to the affected children and their families and schools, as well as hospitals and law enforcement," the judge wrote.

Meta told to pay $375m for misleading users over child safety
