articles.title: Primary showdown: Polls close in Tennessee as conservative firebrand eyes governor's office
articles.excerpt: Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., analyzes the Democratic strategy to limit President Donald Trump's war powers regarding Iran, calling it a 'delay tactic.' She emphasizes confronting Iran's nuclear amb...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., analyzes the Democratic strategy to limit President Donald Trump's war powers regarding Iran, calling it a 'delay tactic.' She emphasizes confronting Iran's nuclear ambitions and its role in funding terrorist groups like Hamas. Blackburn also criticizes a Michigan Senate candidate for his anti-Israel comments.

The polls have closed in Tennessee as conservative firebrand Sen. Marsha Blackburn aims to change her work address from Washington D.C., to Nashville.

The former longtime congresswoman and two-term senator with a robust national profile thanks to her regular cable news appearances is considered the front-runner in Thursday's Republican gubernatorial primary, in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee.

The Republican face-off for governor of Tennessee, where Democrats haven't won a gubernatorial election in two decades, takes top billing as the red-leaning southeastern state holds nominating contests for state and federal offices.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee is running for governor in the 2026 race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Blackburn is running in a race that also includes four-term Rep. John Rose, who like Blackburn is a staunch Capitol Hill supporter of President Donald Trump, and state Rep. Monty Fritts.

Even though the president handed out endorsements in other GOP gubernatorial primaries this cycle, Trump remained neutral in the Tennessee contest.

"Unfortunately, she’s running for governor. She’s running for governor of Tennessee. I’d love her not to, I begged her," Trump said in January. "‘I said, ‘Marsha, don’t. We don’t want to lose you in the Senate.’"

But the president has said Blackburn would be a good governor, and also noted that Rose has been a staunch loyalist.

Even though she didn't land Trump's endorsement, Blackburn has showcased her support for him.

"As President Trump sends power and authority back to the states, I'm ready to deliver for the people of the Volunteer State and make our state America's conservative leader," she wrote on the eve of the primary in a social media post that included a photo of her and Trump.

Five Democrats, including Memphis City Councilwoman Jerri Green, are bidding for their party's gubernatorial nomination.

Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., is seen inside the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 4, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)

Tennessee's other U.S. senator, Republican Bill Hagerty, is unopposed in the GOP primary as he seeks a second six-year term in the Senate.

Five Democrats are vying to challenge Hagerty in the general election. Then-Sen. Al Gore's re-election 36 years ago was the last time a Democrat won a Senate contest in Tennessee.

In U.S. House battles, Memphis voters will cast ballots for their Democratic and Republican nominees using a new GOP-drawn congressional district map that created an extra right-leaning seat and forced longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen to not seek re-election.

Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) walks through the U.S. Capitol on February 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, two-term Republican Rep. Andy Ogles, a major Trump ally in the House who is backed by the president, is facing a stiff primary challenge from Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, who was endorsed earlier this week by Lee. The race has seen a large infusion of money from outside groups.

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

articles.title: Sam Acho Q&A: Former NFL player and ESPN analyst speaks out on civility and accountability in sports and media
articles.excerpt:
Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho is working with the Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy to promote civility.

Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Ac...
articles.body_text:
Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho is working with the Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy to promote civility.

Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho attended the Ronald Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy’s inaugural Reagan Civility & Democracy Forum last week.

There, he advocated for improving civility among Americans, especially in sports.

"We talked about civility in sports and how many of the same attributes athletes use can be applied to civil discourse: sportsmanship, winning and losing the right way, and playing within a set of rules," Acho told Fox News Digital.

PATRIOTS LEGEND ROB GRONKOWSKI REVEALS THE IMPACT POLITICS HAS ON LOCKER ROOM DYNAMICS

As a former pro athlete and now a top sports media figure, Acho shared his vision for the role of athletes and sports media in promoting civility across the country, and how Sophie Cunningham fits into it, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Questions and answers have been shortened for brevity and focus.

Sam Acho No. 74 of the Buffalo Bills looks on during a preseason game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field in Detroit on Aug. 23, 2019. (Getty Images)

Q: What does civil discourse look like to you?

Sam Acho: It can include disagreement. You don’t always have to be on the same page. In football, some people believe in a 3-4 defense; others prefer a 4-3. Some say you have to blitz to get to the quarterback... others believe in playing coverage... but the goal is the same: to win the game.

In society — especially among political leaders — the goal should be to serve the country and make it better... People may disagree about which law or approach is best, but at the end of the day, it’s about wanting the country to be better.

Q: Did conversations about politics and other issues happen in NFL locker rooms?

Sam Acho: Nowhere in the locker room was it not allowed to have certain conversations...

We'd have debates about, um, is it harder to, to be a track athlete or a golfer.

We'd also have political debates. We'd talk about politics, talk about certain rules, certain laws. "Hey, what do we think about what the president said? What do we think about what this governor is trying to do?"

... I remember we were, when Colin Kaepernick was taking a knee and protesting during the national anthem, we weren't shying away from that.

Colin Kaepernick, center, kneeled during the national anthem before an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys. ( )

Q: Did those conversations ever become uncivil?

Sam Acho: In any family, in any team, in any conversation, you may cross the line, but usually when you cross the line, you either apologize or they apologize, or you try to find a way to make it right.

I'm not, I'm not gonna pretend that we lived in a utopia... But when you cross the line or when you go out of bounds or when you make a mistake, okay, you either apologize, or when you lose, right, you shake hands, you move on, right?

When the conversations did become uncivil, or maybe we had a big disagreement, I didn't drop my ball and walk away. No, I actually went and said, "Oh, we have practice in like 15 minutes." Then we had meetings in two hours. Then we were together at lunch the next day.

Q: How could the NFL and its players, coaches and executives help promote civility?

Sam Acho: I think one thing that athletes have that many other people don't is a platform. A lot of athletes have a platform... And I think one area that quarterbacks, that coaches, that players, that athletes can continue to use is their platform, not only to speak out on issues that matter to them, but also to educate themselves on issues that matter.

And so one area I think that athletes... and coaches and executives can do is to continue to speak up and, and stay educated on topics.

Q: Do you believe using that platform to speak up on topics comes with the risk of promoting uncivil discourse?

Sam Acho: Everything comes with risk. Life comes with risk... But oftentimes it's not really about risk, it's more about... how do you respond to defeat? How do you respond to adversity? How do you respond to, uh, something not going your way?

When I'm on TV... there's a risk that people may disagree with my opinion, but that doesn't mean that I just absolve myself from the conversation. It's understanding the risk... and still moving forward with an educated perspective.

Q: But in general, you would encourage more athletes, especially those with platforms, to make their feelings on certain topics known?

Sam Acho: I would encourage athletes to continue to understand that they are more than just what you do on a field. That's probably my biggest encouragement. Oftentimes... you, as an athlete, you think that, or people tell you that you are what you put on tape.

That you're only that, and you're more than just that. There's our human capital. There's your physical capital. Yes, you train, you eat right, you go to sleep on time to be the best athlete you can be. But there's also your intellectual capital.

KATIE UHLAENDER: ATHLETES RISK PAYING THE PRICE IF PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS PASSED

Athletes should know they are more than one dimension of a human being. The same is true for people in politics: You are more than a governor or a senator. You should ask who you are becoming as you make decisions. Are you simply trying to gather as much power as possible, or do you recognize that there is something beyond one election or one vote?

Q: What do you think about Sophie Cunningham’s recent use of her platform?

Sophie Cunningham #8 of the Indiana Fever looks on against the Minnesota Lynx in the fourth quarter at Target Center on August 02, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Lynx defeated the Fever 108-100. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) (David Berding/Getty Images)

Sam Acho: So I'd have to get, I'd have to dial myself back more in to see what kind of what Sophie Cunningham has been saying and not saying, but I will say, I go back to this. Like, as an athlete, you have an opportunity to use your platform and to steward it well. You absolutely do.

And I don't think that athletes should shy away from speaking up for what they believe. I think so many people in society, they speak up for what they believe. And know that, yeah, there's a risk involved for sure. I think that athletes should continue to use and to steward their platform, knowing that you may not be liked you may not be liked, but I think athletes should continue to use their platform and steward it well.

Q: How can sports media figures do a better job of promoting civil discourse?

Sam Acho: It goes back to the idea of platform. A lot of sports media figures, not all, but many were former athletes. So they put down that physical side, now they're using the intellectual side.

And I think it is remembering that even as a sports media, media figure, you do have a platform. Pat McAfee has a huge platform on ESPN. I think about, um, and what he's been able to do with his platform, and then using that to realize that people follow you. People listen to you. People may not agree with everything you say, but you do have a platform, and you want to steward it well.

Your voice, your opinion, those things are yours. So they're yours to steward. They're not yours to say, "Okay, how can I gather as much power, as many followers as I can?" And just waste it. No, you're a steward.

Q: What does it look like to steward a sports media platform poorly?

Sam Acho: There was a game last year, last season, or maybe the season before, and Texas played Georgia. And third quarter of the game or so, late third quarter, there was a call that didn't go Texas's way. Texas was the home team. They were hosting Georgia. And a lot of the fans were upset the referees missed the call. Well, while the referees missed the call, all of a sudden the fans at Texas started to throw cans and, and bottles and things on the field in order to delay the game so that the referees could go and maybe look at the call and try and reverse the call.

And the referees did end up going and changing the call. Texas still lost the game, number one. Number two, it wasn't a good look for, uh, it wasn't a good look for Texas, and I think it's even being willing to say that, right? Not just saying, "Well, look, I went there and I'm a broadcaster and we won or we lost or they got the call right." No, the call was wrong, but you don't go and say, "I'm gonna just throw bottles on the field," and say that that's okay. I think that no matter who you are in sports and sports media and, and no matter what avenue you have, I think it's wise to say, "Hey, that was wrong. He was out of bounds.

"We were out of bounds." And, and realizing that it may cost you the game. And even if you try to, even if you do that thing that was wrong and, and, and, uh, you get the call that goes in your favor, what did you actually win??

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: Some of Doge's $110bn saving reports are wrong or lack evidence, US watchdog finds
articles.excerpt:
Elon Musk (left) was formerly in charge of

Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evid...
articles.body_text:
Elon Musk (left) was formerly in charge of

Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evidence", a watchdog has found.

A report released on Thursday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has given an extensive review of Doge's claims about its so-called Wall of Receipts, which reported savings of $110bn (£82bn) across contracts, grants and leases.

"Several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the report stated.

Asked for comment, a White House official said the administration told the GAO that all employees had to complete ethics training and follow financial disclosure requirements.

Doge, the Department of Government Efficiency, was not an official government department. It launched at the start of President Trump's second term but closed last month. Its Wall of Receipts was a way of showing its purported savings in taxpayer money online.

Elon Musk, the billionaire boss of Tesla and SpaceX who formerly led Doge but left in May 2025, initially promised to save as much as $2tn a year by slashing federal jobs and shuttering government programmes, among other cost-cutting measures.

Even by Doge's own estimates, it fell short of that goal, as its website claims to have saved an estimated $214bn.

"While Doge provided some information about estimated savings, several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the GAO report stated.

It said Doge had not been transparent regarding the methods it used to calculate savings, highlighting it "did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of Doge-reported savings".

Among its specific findings was that 108 of the 264 leases identified by Doge for termination were already in the process of ending before the body was established. That accounts for about $15.3m of the total $53.5m in savings Doge claimed.

"The Wall of Receipts does not include an explanation of how the savings from terminated leases were calculated," the GAO said.

Claims were also made about savings that were not achieved, like $1.7bn for ending a defence department contract for IT services. However, the contract was never terminated and thus no savings were achieved, according to the congressional watchdog's report.

"While the Wall of Receipts includes some information about the data and sources underlying reported savings, it does not sufficiently disclose limitations affecting data quality," it assessed.

The GAO audit, which was carried out at the request of Democratic Senators Gary Peters and Richard Blumenthal, covered savings data reported from 20 January  2025 through 7 July 2026.

"Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but Doge was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement on Thursday.

Under Musk, Doge pushed for massive reductions in the federal workforce, as well as the shuttering of programmes and even agencies such as the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

Some of Doge's moves were met with legal fights, or were reversed. When the group's cost-cutting resulted in bird flu officials at the US Department of Agriculture being fired, the Trump administration looked to re-hire them days later.

In a social media post last month announcing its closure, Doge said: "While the formal mission of Doge has come to an end, the mission to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse will continue. Good stewardship of taxpayer dollars and accountable government are not temporary initiatives."

Elon Musk says Doge was 'somewhat successful' but he would not do it again

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Michigan House speaker calls for answers over $300M taxpayer-funded Rx Kids program
articles.excerpt: Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses concerns over Michigan's Rx Kids initiative, including taxpayer funding, unrestricted cash payments, eligibility requirements and what he calls a broader gua...
articles.body_text:
Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses concerns over Michigan's Rx Kids initiative, including taxpayer funding, unrestricted cash payments, eligibility requirements and what he calls a broader guaranteed income effort.

The Republican leader of Michigan’s House says a state-funded maternal health initiative has become something far different than lawmakers were promised, accusing Democrats of using more than $300 million in taxpayer funding to advance a broader guaranteed-income agenda.

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall made the remarks in an interview with Fox News Digital as House Republicans continue scrutinizing Rx Kids, a taxpayer-funded program that provides unrestricted cash payments to pregnant women and new mothers.

Hall argued lawmakers believed they were funding a maternal and prenatal health initiative, not what he described as a broader experiment in guaranteed income.

GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses his concerns about Michigan's Rx Kids program. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"I think the Democrats kind of slipped this in here under the idea that it was for prenatal care," Hall told Fox News Digital. "Lawmakers did not have the complete picture."

Rx Kids launched in Flint in 2024 and provides expectant mothers with a $1,500 lump-sum payment during pregnancy, followed by $500 monthly payments after the child is born.

According to materials provided to Fox News Digital by Hall’s office, the program has expanded to communities across Michigan with more than $300 million in taxpayer funding.

Rx Kids has promoted the initiative as a maternal and infant health program designed to reduce financial stress for new families. According to podcast interviews and program materials, its leaders have also discussed expanding the model to communities across Michigan and beyond.

EXCLUSIVE: VIDEO SHOWS MICHIGAN LAWMAKER TOURING DAYCARE IN $1.1M TAXPAYER FUNDING PROBE

Hall argued the program lacks the eligibility requirements found in traditional public assistance programs.

"We have a lot of social safety net programs in our country that are working very well," Hall said. "They have eligibility checks. They look at citizenship. They look at income verification.

"Rx Kids, by design, is given to anyone that has a child," he continued. "They don’t look for citizenship. They just pay out anyone that has a child."

Hall’s office also provided Fox News Digital with video of legislative committee testimony in which program officials acknowledged payments had been made to individuals who were not legally present in the United States.

CALIFORNIA ‘BASIC INCOME’ EXPERIMENT FAILS TO PROVIDE ‘FINANCIAL INDEPENDENCE,’ STUDY FINDS

Hall argued taxpayer-funded cash assistance should include income and legal status requirements similar to those used by existing public assistance programs.

"What we prefer are the traditional welfare programs like Medicaid, the food stamp program and the WIC program," Hall said. "They make sure you’re here legally, they make sure you’re not making a lot of money and then they give you the benefit. That’s not what Rx Kids is."

Hall also criticized the program’s unrestricted cash payments, noting recipients are not required to spend the money on diapers, formula, housing or other expenses related to pregnancy or caring for a newborn.

"They give you this free cash and there are no strings attached by definition," Hall said.

MAYORS WANT TO KEEP HANDING OUT FREE CASH AFTER FEDERAL FUNDS DRIED UP

The cover of the Rx Kids playbook describes how communities can replicate the Michigan-based maternal cash assistance program. (rxkids.org)

Hall said caseworkers had told him they had seen recipients use the money for alcohol, drugs and gambling. Fox News Digital has not independently verified those claims.

The speaker also pointed to public comments from Rx Kids leaders that he said reinforced Republican concerns that the initiative is intended to become something larger than a maternal health program.

Hall's office also shared podcast interviews in which Rx Kids co-founder Luke Shaefer discussed the expanded Child Tax Credit and the role he believes Rx Kids can play following the expiration of those federal payments.

In a separate interview, Dr. Mona Hanna, the leader of Rx Kids, discussed her vision of expanding the initiative into a government-scale public program.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED RECOUNTS SMASHING VODKA BOTTLE AFTER BEARD CRITICISM

Hall said those remarks aligned with his assessment of Rx Kids.

"This is a progressive left-wing experiment toward basically a universal income," Hall said. "They’re trying to move the welfare state down that lane."

Hall also questioned the program’s advisory network.

Hall's office also shared archived versions of the Rx Kids website that listed Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan Secretary of State and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson's husband Ryan Friedrichs and Community Change official Dorian Warren as members of the program's advisory circle.

MICHIGAN’S TOP ELECTION OFFICIAL WINS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR, ADVANCES TO BATTLEGROUND RACE

The advisory circle page was removed from the organization’s website days after lawmakers questioned program leaders during a June 2 Michigan House Oversight Committee hearing.

The timing of the removal does not establish why the page was taken down.

"Our secretary of state’s husband is on the advisory board. Abdul El-Sayed is on the board," Hall said. "It’s like a who’s who of radical left Democrats."

Hall’s office also pointed to an Rx Kids white paper examining voter turnout among recipients and the program’s promotion of Vot-ER, a physician-backed voter registration organization powered by TurboVote.

Materials provided by Hall’s office also identified Hanna as an adviser to Vot-ER.

Hall said those connections and the program’s research into voting behavior deserved additional scrutiny.

"We’re trying to understand why are you so interested in the voting pattern of the people that are receiving your no-strings-attached welfare," Hall said. "We aren’t getting good answers."

Hall said House Republicans did not include additional funding for Rx Kids in Michigan’s newly signed budget, though the program still has access to previously appropriated funds.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSING OVER $1B IN MEDICAID PAYMENTS TO MINNESOTA, CALIFORNIA OVER FRAUD, COMPLIANCE CONCERNS

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall, left, stands with Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Hall has criticized the state's Rx Kids program. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"The good news is that we cut off funding to this program in the new budget," Hall said. "In the future, we’re going to try to put guardrails around it so that it goes to the people that truly need it."

Rather than eliminating assistance for struggling families, Hall said he wants taxpayer dollars directed toward existing programs that assess financial need and place restrictions on how certain benefits can be spent.

"I think people support those programs," Hall said. "They have eligibility requirements to ensure that you’re not taking advantage of the system."

Fox News Digital reached out to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s office, Rx Kids and Michigan State University for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Travel restrictions – from Israel and Europe – trap students in Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Mariam al-Najar, a 24-year-old student from Khan Younis in Gaza, was waiting for a message that could change her life.

When an email arrived two weeks after she applied for a scholarship from the Uni...
articles.body_text:
Mariam al-Najar, a 24-year-old student from Khan Younis in Gaza, was waiting for a message that could change her life.

When an email arrived two weeks after she applied for a scholarship from the University of Cassino and Southern Lazio in Italy, she felt, for a brief moment at least, that years of studying had finally paid off.

The university confirmed that she had been offered a place for a master’s degree in economics and management, one of the few times during a long period of despair that Mariam had felt any hope about the future.

“Being accepted was like a ray of light that suddenly appeared and gave me a sense of life and hope again,” she told Al Jazeera. “I was applying for scholarships while feeling deeply hopeless and I never expected to receive an acceptance.”

The scholarship offer was not just an opportunity for Mariam to continue higher studies at a leading university but also offered hope of a new future amid Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.

But securing a place at the university opened the door to a whole new set of challenges for Mariam.

Italy was a main destination for the evacuation of Palestinian students from the Gaza Strip between 2025 and 2026.

Approximately 229 students were evacuated from Gaza prior to May 2026, with another group of around 40 students joining in June 2026.

Part of the reason for the high demand is attributed to the lower living and tuition costs in Italy compared to many other European countries. In Italy, the annual figure for students is around €10,200 ($11,773), compared with the United Kingdom and 30,000 pounds ($40,408) to 60,000 pounds ($80,820) per year.

For Mariam, these still substantial costs were not the immediate challenge, the difficulty was how to reach Italy amid Israel’s siege on Gaza.

“I did not believe that travel had become guaranteed, because the acceptance was only the beginning of the journey,” she said. “There are still many steps and challenges that need to be overcome.”

Mariam applied for a visa and was approved, before she then contacted several organisations who may have been able to facilitate her journey to Italy. But Israeli restrictions on travel, made even tougher as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, mean that she has not yet been given permission to leave Gaza. That has put her arrival at the university in time for the start of autumn term in doubt.

Every passing day in besieged Gaza brings a sense of lost opportunities for Mariam, particularly as Israel has almost completely destroyed the enclave’s educational sector and infrastructure.

“It feels as though this is not just a journey for education; it has become a major challenge. Many students have had their visa applications rejected more than once and there are obstacles preventing students from travelling and continuing their studies abroad,” she said.

“After years of trying and holding on to hope, losing this opportunity or having my studies postponed has become a nightmare that I fear could come true. This scholarship represents more than just education for me. It is a path towards a future I have tried to reach despite all circumstances.”

Many students in Gaza have faced similar offers to study abroad, but seen their hopes crushed due to difficulties in travel and funding.

“Behind every application and every scholarship, there is a student with a dream who is simply trying not to lose their future,” she said.

“The scholarship is not just an opportunity to study; it is a hope that the years of our resilience and struggle during the war will not turn into a lost dream.”

The Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it works with universities to help facilitate travel for students from Gaza to Italy.

But the main obstacle facing them is not obtaining university admission itself, but navigating a Kafkaesque bureaucracy, both to leave Gaza and to enter Italy, said Professor Giovanna Citti from the University of Bologna.

“The main obstacle facing Palestinian students from Gaza is not obtaining university admission itself, but their ability to leave Gaza and complete the procedures required to reach Italy,” Citti said. “Even after receiving admission, students need authorisation to leave Gaza and, in many cases, they have to transit through Israel and Jordan.”

“Humanitarian corridors required intensive diplomatic negotiations because obtaining exit permits from Gaza is extremely difficult,” Citti added. “The students are academically qualified and highly motivated. The problem is not their ability to study; the problem is creating a clear and reliable pathway for them to reach their universities.”

“The delay in travel procedures has become a major concern for students who have already received scholarships and university places.”

As increasing numbers of students find themselves in similar situations to Mariam, initiatives focused on scholarships and student travel have emerged to address the growing challenge.

One of those is Gaza40+, which has more than 1,200 registered Palestinian students seeking help in continuing their education outside Gaza. Students risk losing their scholarships or university places if they fail to reach the university in time for fixed enrolment deadlines.

More than 500 of these students have already received university offers from institutions across Europe, while others continue receiving support throughout the application and scholarship process. The initiative says registrations continue to increase, with about five to 10 new student and volunteer registrations received each day.

Gaza40+ has helped 120 students leave Gaza to continue their studies abroad since it was formed, in addition to 20 family members who travelled with them.

Despite hundreds of students securing university admissions and scholarships, leaving Gaza remains the biggest obstacle to continuing their education.

Gaza40+ says the absence of a clear and consistent humanitarian pathway to exit Gaza for universities abroad is one of the biggest challenges for Palestinian students.

The initiative says that while some countries had previously provided relatively easier routes for students from Gaza, that was now changing.

In Italy, for example, students were recently informed that they must demonstrate Italian language proficiency before being considered for evacuation from Gaza. While the government says the requirement is essential, it creates another barrier for students already in the heart of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

“Students are not losing opportunities because of their academic qualifications or their commitment. They are losing them because of circumstances beyond their control,” said Nasser Taha from Gaza40+.

“We need stronger coordination between governments, universities, and international organisations to ensure that Gaza students can reach their universities and do not lose their educational opportunities.”

Gaza40+ says ensuring a pathway for students from Gaza to their studies abroad requires coordination between governments, universities and international organisations.

Doaa Fawzi Hamdan, a student at the University of Bologna, said that scholarship had appeared to provide an opportunity for her to continue her education after three years of disruptions in Gaza.

Despite completing all the required paperwork – and frequent electricity shortages, weak internet connection and forced displacement – she is still waiting for an Italian visa.

“The most difficult part is receiving acceptance from a university but not knowing whether you will be able to reach it on time,” Doaa told Al Jazeera. “We are not asking for special treatment. We only want the opportunity to reach our universities and begin our studies like students everywhere in the world.”

articles.title: ‘No red line’: South Lebanon residents outraged as Israel resumes strikes
articles.excerpt:
As Israel resumes strikes and displacement orders in southern Lebanon, residents of the region are expressing anger and helplessness during ongoing talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials.

For d...
articles.body_text:
As Israel resumes strikes and displacement orders in southern Lebanon, residents of the region are expressing anger and helplessness during ongoing talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials.

For displaced families, Thursday’s latest round of strikes, which injured at least eight people, is further evidence that the June ceasefire has failed to protect them from Israeli military action. The Israeli military sparked this latest wave of panic by issuing a forced evacuation order for the town of Mansouri on Wednesday, marking its first displacement directive in weeks.

“Mansouri is not part of Israel’s occupation zone,” Yousef Shehemi, mayor of the neighboring town of Majdal Zoun, told Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr. “But Israel has no red lines—they target where they want. They have not respected any ceasefire.”

Families from Mansouri who fled were still gathered on the outskirts of the town on Thursday, waiting for word that it was safe to return.

Outrage was mounting on the ground as residents watched the Israeli military demolish homes and set fire to farmland, with many expressing little faith that ongoing negotiations between Beirut and Israel will secure their safe return.

Abu Rached, a resident of Majdal Zoun, said the destruction had gone unanswered by Lebanese officials. “Can’t you see what they did to south Lebanon? They’re destroying it, displacing people—even the [Lebanese] army can’t stay in Mansouri,” he told Al Jazeera. “Where are the officials?”

Representatives from Lebanon and Israel met in Rome for another round of negotiations earlier this week, after both governments signed a “framework” intended to secure an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon once Hezbollah is disarmed.

Hezbollah, which is not a part of the ongoing talks, has publicly opposed the deal.

The deal also envisioned “pilot zones” where Israel would pull back and the Lebanese army would move in to ensure there are no weapons outside the control of the state, allowing displaced people to return. But so far, the agreement has not secured any significant Israeli withdrawal in southern Lebanon.

The Israeli military has been systematically wiping out villages in south Lebanon, demolishing buildings and burning olive groves —a push that critics say amounts to an ethnic cleansing campaign.

Still, the region had seen relative calm over the past months. Hostilities renewed this week after an explosive device killed two invading Israeli soldiers, though it is not clear whether it was planted before or after the ceasefire.

Hezbollah did not claim responsibility for the attack.

The Israeli attacks were concentrated in Mansouri but not confined to it.

Further north, in Burj al-Shemali, an Israeli strike hit a residential home, marking the first attack on the town since the ceasefire took effect in June. Almaza Hazim, a resident, described to Al Jazeera the chaos of trying to help a neighboring family caught in the blast.

“Our neighbour was screaming from the explosion. We ran to help them—there were injuries—before another strike destroyed the house,” Hazim said.

articles.title: Cruise line's tougher booking rules ignite backlash over higher deposits and payments
articles.excerpt: Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from vi...
articles.body_text:
Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from viewers online.

Princess Cruises is introducing stricter booking policies, including higher deposits and earlier final payment deadlines, fueling mixed reactions among travelers.

Among the biggest changes is an update to the timeline for final payments, the cruise line confirmed in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Beginning with new bookings for sailings departing in 2027 and beyond, we are implementing a 120-day final payment and a modified cancellation fee schedule," the company said.ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST MAJOR LINE OVER SURPRISE DAILY GRATUITY HIKE"These changes bring greater consistency to the booking process and reflect broader industry practices, while also helping ensure that guests have fair access to the staterooms and sailings they want to experience," the statement continued.

The new rules will take effect on Sept. 2 for new bookings on sailings departing Jan. 1, 2027. Guests were notified of the policy changes in an email from the cruise line, according to industry website Cruise Critic.

Princess Cruises is tightening its booking policies by requiring larger deposits and moving final payment deadlines earlier. (iStock)

The cruise line is also increasing standard deposits. Guests booking seven-day cruises in inside, oceanview, balcony and mini-suite staterooms will now pay $300 per person, up from $250, while suite deposits will increase from $500 to $600 per person, according to the review website.

Princess Cruises also noted that reservations will automatically be canceled if final payment is not received by the deadline, though guests will continue receiving payment reminders before the due date, according to reports.

The policy changes have prompted debate among cruise fans on social media. Some travelers said the earlier deadlines will not affect their vacation plans because they typically pay off cruises as soon as possible.

"I pay it all as soon as I book," one person wrote on TikTok. "I get my reservations in that day, and I'm always sail ready."

The new rules will take effect Sept. 2 for new bookings on sailings departing Jan. 1, 2027. (iStock)

Another commenter said, "I don't mind these changes because I like to pay off my trips as fast as I can so that I'm able to begin saving for the next one."

Others, however, questioned why passengers would be required to put down more money earlier in the booking process.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Those deposits are crazy," one commenter wrote.

Another person argued that the earlier payment deadline could create problems for travelers using payment plans.

Princess Cruises' decision to tighten its booking policies has generated mixed reactions from cruise fans on social media. (iStock)

"120 days out for final payment is the worst of all of it!" the commenter wrote. "Especially people who are on payment plans."

The booking changes come as other cruise lines have also introduced policies that have frustrated some travelers.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Celebrity Cruises faced backlash after raising its automatic gratuity charges with little notice, prompting some passengers to say they would tip crew members directly in cash instead.

The cruise line increased its daily automatic gratuities by $1.50 per person across all stateroom categories, raising the charges to between $19.50 and $24.50 per guest, per day.

Many passengers criticized the timing of the announcement, saying they were notified the same day the higher rates took effect.

"At this point, they just need to include gratuities in their fare like the luxury lines do," one Reddit user wrote.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Iran’s Ghalibaf accuses Trump of conducting show diplomacy ‘on loop’
articles.excerpt: Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator has accused Donald Trump of conducting “theatre diplomacy on loop” after the United States president’s repeated claims that he was ordering attacks on Ir...
articles.body_text:
Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator has accused Donald Trump of conducting “theatre diplomacy on loop” after the United States president’s repeated claims that he was ordering attacks on Iran, and then calling them off.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made the remarks in a social media post on Thursday, just days after Trump called off his latest planned strikes, claiming that “the perimeters of a deal” had already been agreed to with Tehran. Dismissing the narrative, Ghalibaf said that Washington keeps switching from military threats to offers of negotiation as a failed pressure tactic.

“‘Massive attack coming…wait, never mind, they want to negotiate.’ That’s theater diplomacy on loop,” Ghalibaf wrote on X.

“Using bullying + broken promises + fake news as leverage is a failed strategy.”

He called on the US to “acknowledge the facts” and fulfil its commitments.

On Saturday, Trump cancelled a planned large-scale military attack on Iran, claiming that Tehran and other countries in the region had asked the US to call off the strikes as a diplomatic breakthrough was close.

Trump claimed the agreement would bring the “immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and end “Iran’s nuclear threat”.

Iran has been holding talks with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran claiming that a deal is “on the verge of being finalised“, after both countries agreed on the coordinates of routes through the critical waterway.

The strait, a major artery for global energy, was a free international passage before Israel and the US attacked Iran on February 28, launching what has turned into a months-long regional war.

After the attacks, Tehran effectively shut the strait, and now asserts sovereignty over the waterway, parts of which pass through Iranian and Omani territorial waters.

The closure of the strait and attacks on energy infrastructure in the region, by both the US and Iran, have sent oil prices soaring.

Trump told reporters on Thursday that he believed the war on Iran was close to an end, promising that petrol prices would drop when the conflict is over.

“I think it’s going to end pretty soon. I don’t think they can go much longer,” he said in the Oval Office.

He added that he is involved in the negotiations with Tehran. “I think we’re doing fine,” Trump said.

Trump has been asserting for months that Iran is already defeated and that the conflict is on the verge of ending. Iranian officials, however, have emphasised that they are prepared for a long war.

articles.title: US Senate committee votes to hold Fauci in contempt over Covid hearing
articles.excerpt: A US Senate committee has voted to hold former top health official Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions during a hearing examining his handling of the Covid-19 pa...
articles.body_text:
A US Senate committee has voted to hold former top health official Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions during a hearing examining his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The vote - which fell along party lines - clears the way for the committee to refer the case to the justice department for potential prosecution for failing to comply with a congressional subpoena.

It remains unclear whether the department will pursue the case.

During his testimony last week, Fauci invoked his constitutional right against self-incrimination more than 100 times, arguing that Kentucky Senator Rand Paul was trying to put him "behind bars".

In a statement following the vote, Fauci's lawyer called it a "crude political stunt" being conducted to "punish Dr Fauci for exercising his constitutional right".

The origins of the pandemic have been a matter of strong debate in the US, including between President Donald Trump, who was in office when it began in 2020, and public health officials, including Fauci.

Senator Rand Paul has for years accused Fauci of attempting to hide its origins and of funding a research lab in the Chinese city of Wuhan, where some believe the pandemic began with a lab-leak.

Most scientists believe that exposure to an infected animal is a more likely origin for the pandemic.

Former President Joe Biden gave Fauci a pre-emptive pardon on his last day in office in 2025, protecting him from federal prosecution for his actions between 2014 and 2025.

But Fauci could still face charges for anything after that date, including contempt of Congress. He could also face state or local charges that are not covered by the pardon.

"The chair directed Anthony Fauci to answer. He refused," Kentucky Republican Rand Paul said ahead of the vote. "That is what we are voting on today — not his opinions, not his policies, not anything he said from the podium six years ago. "

"We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence," he added.

The Top Democrat on the committee, Michigan Senator Gary Peters, defended Fauci, accusing Paul of a "rushed investigation" and a "yearslong campaign" to prosecute Fauci.

Fauci has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and last week accused Paul of having an "obvious obsession" with prosecuting him.

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something - anything - that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars'," Fauci said.

Paul, the committee's Republican chairman, bypassed a full senate vote on the contempt resolution saying he did not "want to waste time" going through the procedure.

Normally, contempt resolutions passed by the committee go to the full Senate, where they require a 60-vote majority. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member Senate.

In a statement quoted by US news outlets, Dr Fauci's lawyer, David Schertler, called on the Senate to "reject Senator Paul's meritless and politically-motivated contempt resolution".

"For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison," Schertler added. "Dr Fauci has committed no crime — and Senator Paul knows it."

Schertler had previously argued that he believes that the former top health official is on "solid legal ground" going forward, adding that Paul "may be a doctor, but he is not a lawyer". Paul worked as an eye surgeon until he got elected to the US Senate in 2010.

"We are completely confident that Dr Fauci has a valid Fifth Amendment privilege here and is on solid legal ground in asserting it," attorney David Schertler said in an e-mail to CBS, the BBC's US partner, last week.

Taking the Fifth is not an admission of guilt - it is designed to protect individuals against coercion, mistakes, and unfair shifting of the burden to provide proof of wrongdoing.

Contempt prosecutions - and convictions - are rare.

In 2024, former Trump allies Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro were both convicted of contempt and sentenced to jail sentences, marking the first convictions since the 1980s.

articles.title: Trump says US has 'massive' munitions stockpile, vows 'treasonous' leakers being hunted down
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump signals a potential diplomatic breakthrough with Iran, declaring his preference for a deal over conflict. Fox News' Trey Yingst reports the latest on the conflict from Tel Aviv ...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump signals a potential diplomatic breakthrough with Iran, declaring his preference for a deal over conflict. Fox News' Trey Yingst reports the latest on the conflict from Tel Aviv and Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs also joined 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the latest on the effort to secure a deal.

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the U.S. has a "massive" munitions stockpile and "treasonous" leakers are "being hunted down" after reports emerged claiming the U.S. Army has burned through nearly all of its stockpiles of two of its primary long-range precision weapons.

The Army has used "virtually all" of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) during the five-month conflict with Iran, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with internal U.S. military data.

"The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history," Trump wrote on Truth Social early Thursday.

"The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" the president added.

ALARMING MISSILE REPORT DRAWS FORCEFUL RESPONSE FROM TRUMP AS IRAN WAR TESTS AMERICA’S ARSENAL

President Donald Trump arrives at an event at the Red Rock Resort in Las Vegas on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)

Trump’s message was reposted on X by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

If accurate, the Reuters report underscores a longstanding Pentagon concern: America's most sophisticated precision weapons can be expended in months but often take years to replace.

Officials fear the drawdown could complicate the military's ability to respond to future crises involving adversaries such as China and Russia, according to the report.

WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

U.S. Soldiers and civilians observe a MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile (SAM) systems during a static-display demonstration Aug. 15, 2019, at Katterbach Army Airfield in Ansbach, Germany. (U.S. Army photo by Charles Rosemond)

Reuters also reported that the conflict significantly reduced inventories of Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors, along with Tomahawk cruise missiles, though the Pentagon has maintained the U.S. military retains the capabilities needed to carry out operations worldwide.

Exact U.S. weapons stockpile figures remain classified for national security reasons.

Some estimates show the U.S. has used more than half of its stockpiles of some weapons systems in the war with Iran. The Center for Strategic and International Studies found the U.S. has enough missiles to continue fighting in Iran under any plausible scenario, but the group says the true issue with the shrinking stockpiles is future wars.

"The depletion of munitions was a major topic and a major reason for the suspension of air attacks," Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marines colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, told Fox News' Bret Baier. "Our inventories were getting way below what the war planners wanted. That might encourage China to do something."

CSIS notes many munition stockpiles are substantial but focused its analysis on seven key weapons that have been effective in Iran and would also be valuable in a possible Pacific conflict.

Trump said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Wednesday that, "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need, despite the fact that an unprecedented amount was given away by Crooked Joe Biden and the Biden Administration to Ukraine and Europe at no cost, in one of many of their extremely dumb moves."

The Pentagon has also pushed back on the reporting.

Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, at an undisclosed location, February 28, 2026. (U.S. Navy/Handout via Reuters)

"America’s military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President’s choosing. We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the U.S. military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and our interests," chief spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

Fox News' Bret Baier and Amy Munneke and Fox News Digital's Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US firm
articles.excerpt:
EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a £5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo.

The deal was announced after rival suitor Castlelake said it was dropping out of the bid battle for the no-frills airline.

Eas...
articles.body_text:
EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a £5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo.

The deal was announced after rival suitor Castlelake said it was dropping out of the bid battle for the no-frills airline.

EasyJet is one of Europe's largest airlines. It employs more than 19,000 people, and flies around 1,200 routes across 35 European countries.

It was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer cheap air fares to Europe from the UK.

Its first flights took off in November 1995 flying from Luton to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with its first international flights the following year.

EasyJet accepted an offer from Apollo of £7.15 per share, which trumped Castlelake's final offer of £6.90 per share.

Apollo said it was "highly supportive" of EasyJet's existing strategy, adding there was "a significant opportunity to accelerate the operational and commercial ambitions" for the EasyJet Group.

"EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand," said Alex van Hoek, partner and European private equity lead at Apollo.

EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said "We welcome Apollo's commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for EasyJet."

EasyJet agrees to surprise takeover bid as rival US firm swoops in

articles.title: Israel charges West Bank settler over death of renowned Palestinian activist
articles.excerpt:
Yinon Levi faces trial for reckless manslaughter related to the 2025 killing of Awdah Hathaleen

Israeli prosecutors have charged a Jewish settler over the killing of a Palestinian community leader in...
articles.body_text:
Yinon Levi faces trial for reckless manslaughter related to the 2025 killing of Awdah Hathaleen

Israeli prosecutors have charged a Jewish settler over the killing of a Palestinian community leader in the occupied West Bank last year – the ⁠first such indictment in nearly three years.

In papers filed by the state attorney’s office, Yinon Levi is charged with reckless manslaughter in the death of Awdah Hathaleen, a prominent ⁠activist who was involved in the 2025 Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land.

The charges against Levi also include armed trespassing and malicious property damage during a July 2025 incident in which settlers operated ⁠a large excavator in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, setting off a confrontation with residents.

Hathaleen filmed the moment ​he was shot during the confrontation. Footage released by ‌the Israeli rights group B’Tselem shows ‌Levi draw a weapon and fire in Hathaleen’s direction. Hathaleen is then heard moaning as he falls to ‌the ground.

Levi, whom the UK and EU have placed under sanctions over violence against Palestinians, has previously denied firing the shot that killed Hathaleen. Reuters was not able to reach his lawyer for comment.

Thursday’s indictment is the first since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks that set off Israel’s war in Gaza and led to a sharp rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, B’Tselem said.

Israeli soldiers and settlers have since killed at least 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank, among them at least 240 children, according to UN data.

“The decision to indict Yinon Levi is the ​exception that proves the rule. The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system. It is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate,” B’Tselem said.

Israel’s military says it investigates instances of wrongdoing by its soldiers and that it and the Israeli police take steps ⁠to crack down on settler violence.

Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have settled among millions ​of Palestinians in land that Israel ​captured in a 1967 war, and which ​Palestinians seek as the core of an independent future state.

UN bodies, Palestinians and most countries ​view the settlements as illegal ‌under international conventions ​and a major obstacle to ​peace. Israel disputes that view, saying a Jewish presence has existed in the West Bank for thousands of years.

Eighteen Palestinians have been killed in incidents linked to settler attacks so far this year, compared with 17 in the whole of 2025, according to UN figures.

articles.title: Sanders' answer when asked if he will endorse socialist Hong in Wisconsin sparks instant mockery: 'Says a lot'
articles.excerpt: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday on the Pod Save America podcast that he doesn't think he'll endorse Wisconsin Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong. (Credit: YouTube/Pod Save Americ...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday on the Pod Save America podcast that he doesn't think he'll endorse Wisconsin Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong. (Credit: YouTube/Pod Save America - Aug. 5)

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., was asked if he will endorse Democratic Socialist of America (DSA) member Francesca Hong’s Wisconsin gubernatorial bid and his response sparked immediate mockery on social media.

"I don’t think so," the Vermont socialist told Pod Save America host Jon Favreau when asked if he is going to endorse Hong’s campaign for governor. "I met Francesca a couple of years ago, I was in Wisconsin, and she seems very, very nice, but again this is a race I’m just not that familiar with."

Sanders added that "we have not gotten involved in many governors races" other than recently in Maine where he endorsed Democrat Troy Jackson, who ultimately replaced disgraced Senate candidate Graham Platner, a candidate Sanders endorsed.

Political commentators quickly chimed in on social media suggesting that Sanders not endorsing Hong shows the senator doesn’t think she can win, with many pointing to Sanders’ strident support of Platner despite all of his political baggage.

AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday on the Pod Save America podcast that he doesn't think he'll endorse Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong. ( )

"Bernie says he’s not backing Francesca Hong because he’s focused on the Senate," Washington Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross posted on X. "Yet he’s endorsed in mayoral races, House races, and Troy Jackson’s failed governor race in Maine. That’s how whacky Hong is ."

"Says a lot," Politico reporter Will Steakin posted on X.

"Guy with the Nazi Tattoo ‘hey everyone makes mistakes’," conservative commentator Stephen L. Miller posted on X. "Crazy communist lady - ‘not my cup of tea sorry.’"

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong listens to Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speak before being introduced during a campaign rally on Aug. 2, 2026, in Milwaukee. Hong, a democratic socialist in the state legislature, has seen an uptick in recent poll numbers. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

"This guy endorsed a guy with a natzi [sic] tat but thinks @FrancescaHongWi is not worth an endorsement……," Jerry Ponio, legislative director for Americans for Prosperity - Wisconsin, posted on X. "Yikes."

"Well, I guess even Bernie enjoys celebrating Thanksgiving at one of his three houses," an account ran by Hong’s likely general election opponent, Republican Tom Tiffany, posted on X.

Tiffany’s post references a controversial quote from Hong that went viral on social media where she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.

"Francesca Hong, who is a Socialist candidate for Governor of Wisconsin is too radical...even for Bernie Sanders," Turning Point Action Northeast Manager Brandon Maly posted on X.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Hong campaign and Sanders’ office for comment.

Critics have argued that Francesca Hong's politics are too far to the left for a swing state like Wisconsin, contending that her identification as a socialist and support for ambitious progressive policies could make her less competitive in a general election.

Hong’s social media account is littered with far-left pledges like abolishing the U.S. Senate and defunding the police.

Sen. Bernie Sanders reacts to questions from a Fox News Digital reporter about Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner’s resurfaced Reddit posts while walking through the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Hong recently tried to walk back those positions in recent interviews ahead of Tuesday’s gubernatorial primary against Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, former Wisconsin Department of Administration secretary Joel Brennan, and Democratic state Sen. Kelda Roys.

Polls suggest Hong is likely to comfortably win that contest which will advance her to a race against Tiffany, the likely Republican nominee, in November.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

articles.title: South Yorkshire man who killed lodger and hid body in concrete gets 35-year sentence
articles.excerpt:
Christopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum term

A man who killed his lodger and concealed his dismembered body in a barrel filled with concrete ...
articles.body_text:
Christopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum term

A man who killed his lodger and concealed his dismembered body in a barrel filled with concrete for more than five years has been jailed for a minimum of 35 years.

Christopher Wright, a 73-year-old farmer from South Yorkshire, was convicted in July in Sheffield crown court of murdering Richard Dyson, 55, in 2019. Dyson had been living in his car on Wright’s farm in Hoyland and had been doing jobs for the then 67-year-old when the pair had a falling out.

Wright, an antique firearms collector who was described as a “weapons fanatic” during his trial, suspected Dyson of stealing some of his prized possessions and selling them. The court heard that when Wright confronted Dyson with his suspicions in November 2019 an argument broke out that ended with Dyson being shot in the chest and arm with a shotgun, killing him.

Wright, a former butcher, dismembered Dyson’s body over the course of several days, then placed the remains in a barrel which he filled with concrete. He then placed the barrel in a trailer and asked an unsuspecting neighbour to keep the vehicle on their property. Wright was aided in covering up his crime by Karl Schwalbe, a lifelong friend who received a three-year sentence for conspiracy to pervert the course of justice.

Dyson’s disappearance was initially treated as a missing person’s inquiry and his remains went undiscovered for more than five and a half years. While South Yorkshire police were aware that he had been on Wright’s land in the days leading up to his disappearance, they could not find evidence implicating the farmer, who denied any knowledge of Dyson’s whereabouts.

Dyson remained missing until July 2025 when South Yorkshire police, driven by new evidence that showed Wright had contacted a local farmer about storing a vehicle on his property in the days after Dyson disappeared, searched the farm and found a barrel containing concrete and human remains which were later identified as Dyson.

Speaking after sentencing him on Thursday, Mr Justice Cotter told Wright that he would probably die in prison and said Wright’s experience as a butcher made him “skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for”.

Dyson’s daughter, Bethany Dainty, who filed a missing persons report in the days after her father was murdered, read a victim impact statement in court detailing how hard it had been not knowing her father’s fate: “I couldn’t grieve because I did not know the truth.”

She continued: “While I cried myself to sleep, while I begged for answers, while I prayed my dad would walk through the door again, someone already knew where he was. Someone watched me suffer for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand.”

After the sentencing, DCI Andy Knowles praised Dyson’s family for the strength they showed during a “long, complex and emotionally draining” investigation.

Knowles said: “Wright and Schwalbe knew what happened to Richard and even with the evidence against them, they continued to deny accountability, making Richard’s family endure a trial, listen to harrowing evidence and distressing testimonies. The strength and dignity in confronting each moment of this process has been nothing short of extraordinary.”

articles.title: Trump denies US weapons shortage and says information 'leakers' being 'hunted down'
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump has denied reports that the US is suffering a munitions shortage and vowed in a social media post that his administration would seek "long term jail sentences" for those suspect...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump has denied reports that the US is suffering a munitions shortage and vowed in a social media post that his administration would seek "long term jail sentences" for those suspected of leaking information.

"The U.S. has massive amounts of 'munitions,' especially of certain types," Trump posted on Thursday morning. "Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed."

With the war with Iran in its sixth month, Trump and the Pentagon are facing mounting questions about the state of the military's arsenal.

The US and Iran have continued to trade strikes, despite multiple pauses in fighting, and a deal to fully end hostilities remains elusive.

As the US pauses the war with Iran, is Trump really running out of weapons?

The administration has sought to assure Americans that US missile stockpiles remain robust, even after the military used vast quantities of difficult-to-manufacture weapons during the combat operation known as Operation Epic Fury and the tit-for-tat strikes since.

CBS News, the BBC's US partner, reported the US has used much of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the war, citing two unnamed sources with direct knowledge of the subject.

Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday evening that Trump had confronted Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week over a possible weapons shortfall, also citing unnamed sources. The BBC has not confirmed the report.

"The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," Trump said in the post on Truth Social. "Long term jail sentences will be sought!"

Precise information on US missile stocks remains classified. Since becoming secretary, Hegseth has sought to put in place strict controls limiting information reporters can gather from the Pentagon, as well.

Using publicly available data, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a national security think tank, estimated that by the end of July, the US had between 759 and 827 Patriot missiles left, down from 2,330 before the conflict began.

It also estimates the US has now used around 60% of terminal high altitude area defense (THAAD) missiles, which are deployed to intercept strikes, Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, said on Wednesday.

The US is also facing demand for its weapons beyond the conflict with Iran.

It has given Ukraine significant supplies of Patriot missiles since Russia invaded in 2022, but as US stocks shrink Cancian expects the Pentagon to hold onto them. At a cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump told reporters that granting Ukraine's recent request for additional Patriot missiles would be a "big step", but the two countries were "still talking about" it.

Many modern weapons have long funding, order, production, and delivery timelines, making it hard to swiftly replace munitions once they are used.

The administration has consistently stated the US has enough in its stockpile.

Trump told the Wall Street Journal last month: "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need."

Hegseth, meanwhile, called reports of a stockpile shortage a "manufactured story" on a 14 June appearance on CBS' Face the Nation.

But the administration has also said it is ramping up production, with Hegseth saying the US was working quickly to manufacture more weapons.

Last month, he asked the US Senate for emergency funds totalling $87bn (£68bn) to pay service members and "rapidly replenish equipment and munitions."

Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is in final stages

UN rights chief alarmed by rise in Iran executions since March

articles.title: India-Bangladesh relations hit new low over exiled PM’s speech to press in Delhi
articles.excerpt:
Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists

Bangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime minister Sheikh Has...
articles.body_text:
Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists

Bangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to address journalists in New Delhi, plunging already strained bilateral relations to a fresh low.

Dhaka accused India of giving a platform to a fugitive it labelled a “convicted genocider” and of undermining efforts to repair ties, after Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh in December despite facing a death sentence on charges of “crimes against humanity”.

The angry response late on Wednesday came hours after Hasina, speaking on the second anniversary of the massive student-led uprising that led to her flight to India, declared: “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people.”

Bangladesh’s foreign ministry said it was “outraged” Hasina had been allowed to participate in the event, where it said she and her allies launched “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh and its people.

“This interaction by Hasina on Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh,” the ministry said. Dhaka also renewed its demands for India to extradite Hasina.

India earlier distanced itself from the news conference – Hasina’s first since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, saying it had no role in organising it and would not endorse any political views voiced.

Hasina said she was ready to face whatever fate awaited her in Bangladesh where her Awami League party is now banned. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but I still have to go,” the 78-year-old said via audio link.

“My life moved beyond calculations of personal safety long ago.”

After 15 years in power, Hasina fled to India in 2024 following weeks of student-led protests. Her government was accused of misusing state institutions to entrench its hold on power and stamp out dissent, including through the killing of opposition activists.

In her speech, she dismissed criminal cases against her as politically motivated and accused Bangladesh’s new government, led by Tarique Rahman, of economic mismanagement, political repression and persecution of her supporters.

Hasina was sentenced in absentia to death by hanging over her government’s deadly crackdown on the uprising. She said she wanted to return in December because it marked Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, commemorating Pakistan’s defeat in the 1971 independence war.

She claimed thousands of Awami League activists had been killed or jailed since her downfall.

Her son Sajeeb Wazed Joy stoked the diplomatic row by extolling India’s hospitality. “She’s being treated very well and has been provided with the full services and security accorded to a head of state,” he said. “Prime Minister Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect.”

Hasina was joined at the event by Shakib Al Hasan, a former national cricket captain. Hours later unidentified attackers hurled petrol bombs and smashed windows at his home in Bangladesh, but nobody was hurt, police said. Shakib, elected to parliament as an Awami League candidate, has remained outside Bangladesh since Hasina’s overthrow.

articles.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
articles.excerpt:
David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone

The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatal...
articles.body_text:
David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone

The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan Police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital where he was later pronounced dead.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”

articles.title: Miss North Carolina USA loses crown after organizer condemns 'racism, homophobia, transphobia'
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Miss North Carolina USA was stripped of her crown weeks before the Miss USA pageant after organizers cited an extended...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Miss North Carolina USA was stripped of her crown weeks before the Miss USA pageant after organizers cited an extended pattern of conduct violating the organization's standards.

Miss USA Chairman Thom Brodeur did not specify what conduct prompted the decision to take the crown away from Brittany Boltinhouse but said in a statement that the organization "does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia nor language that strips any person of their dignity," adding the conduct occurred "over an extended period of time."

The decision ends Boltinhouse's reign just weeks after she won the state title and less than three weeks before she was scheduled to represent North Carolina at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant on Aug. 27.

SEN BERNIE MORENO CALLS FOR EX-SON-IN-LAW TO RESIGN FROM HOUSE, GET 'SERIOUS PSYCHOLOGICAL HELP'

Brittany Boltinhouse pictured as Miss Wilmington, USA at the North Carolina Azalea Festival in Wilmington, North Carolina, in April. (Instagram/espino.sosa)

Myla Hadley, the first runner-up in the state competition, will now represent North Carolina on the national stage "with our full confidence and our support," Brodeur said in a statement.

Brodeur said the decision was made in consultation with Boltinhouse, her state directors and the Miss USA organization. He added that while the organization has a "zero tolerance" standard for conduct, accountability "is not permission to strip someone of their humanity."

Brittany Boltinhouse pictured as Miss Wilmington, USA. (Instagram/espino.sosa)

"There is a young woman at the center of this," Brodeur said. "She has been named, examined, and judged in public in a way that most of us would not survive, and she is still a human being with a family, a future, and a life ahead of her that is longer than this part of her journey."

"I have never believed that accountability requires cruelty, or that holding a line means enjoying the fall of the person who crossed it," he continued.
