Brodeur said Boltinhouse plans to issue her own statement to speak to the matter "in her own voice." The chairman said he has reviewed her statement and described it as showing "ownership, accountability and apology."

Brittany Boltinhouse was crowned Miss North Carolina just weeks ago, and was set to represent the state at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant on Aug. 27. (Instagram/espino.sosa)

"I believe people can change," Brodeur said. "Change is not a statement. It is a record. It is built over time, in the open, through conduct rather than apology alone."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Boltinhouse for comment.

WASHINGTON POST OPINION EDITOR TO EXIT PAPER AFTER JUST ONE YEAR, STAFF COMPLETELY 'BLINDSIDED'

State pageant organizer A Blaize Productions similarly announced the decision after what they described as a "thorough review of recently surfaced information" but did not elaborate on the nature of the allegations.

"We ask our pageant family, supporters, and the public to extend kindness and respect to both Brittany and Myla during this transition," the organization said in a statement. "Moments like these are never easy for anyone involved, and we remain committed to treating everyone with dignity while continuing our mission of empowering the next generation of women leaders."

Hadley acknowledged the abrupt transition in a social media post, saying she understands "the seriousness and level of prestige that this title carries."

"While this may seem like a two-week turnaround given the circumstances, I've been preparing to represent at Miss USA since I first competed with this organization," Hadley wrote. "I am ready to represent North Carolina."

articles.title: NCAA ignored the warnings. Now It's fighting for survival in courtrooms across America over eligibility
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

The NCAA has spent the past few years pleading with Congress to help rein in the chaos engulfing colle...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

The NCAA has spent the past few years pleading with Congress to help rein in the chaos engulfing college athletics, with a large chunk of the focus centered on the wave of lawsuits challenging student-athlete eligibility.

At this point, it feels like a daily occurrence. The organization tasked with enforcing its own rules is constantly reacting to another lawsuit filed in state or federal court by an athlete seeking an additional year of eligibility.

While NCAA officials continue lobbying lawmakers to pass the 'Protect College Sports Act'—which would provide the organization with greater antitrust legal protections against these challenges—they had the opportunity to avoid the chaos centered around the most recent flurry of lawsuits themselves.

When the NCAA adopted its new age-based eligibility model, giving athletes five years to play five seasons, it made one critical decision that is being argued in courtrooms across the country on a daily basis: it excluded the 2022 recruiting class from the new rule.

From that moment on, pure chaos has reigned down upon state courtrooms, while senators try to push the 'Protect College Sports Act' through congress.

Tennessee Coach Unloads On NCAA's 'Bulls–t', After Star Linebacker Suspended For Outdated Rule

Athletes who believed they were unfairly denied an extra season of competition began filing civil lawsuits across the country, arguing they should receive the same benefits as those covered under the new eligibility structure.

Had the NCAA implemented the five-and-five rule a year earlier—or simply grandfathered in the 2022 class—college athletics might not be facing its current legal mess that has lawyers fielding more phone calls than a 9-1-1 operator on a Saturday during the football season in a college town.

NCAA President Charlie Baker attends the game between the Seton Hall Pirates and Providence Friars on February 11, 2026 at Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey. (Rich Graessle / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

One of the bigger problems in the aftermath of some injunctions granted is that there are too many athletes and not enough roster spots. As college football teams open fall camp to prepare for the 2026 season, there are not just a plethora of open spots on the roster left for those who now have eligibility, or will gain eligibility.

INDIANA TAKES FULL ADVANTAGE OF NCAA COURTROOM CHAOS WITH STUNNING ROSTER MOVE AMID ELIGIBILITY FIGHT

In college basketball, teams were anticipating the potential for madness this summer, so leaving one or two spots open for an occasion like this was a tad easier to navigate for the sport compared to football.

But even then, being in this spot of pure legal chaos was on the mind of plenty, including the NCAA.

The mind-boggling part of this entire saga is that attorneys, like Ryan Downton, essentially told the NCAA this was coming.

When former Vanderbilt linebacker Langston Patterson sued the organization in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee over the amount of years athletes are allowed to participate in college athletics, the warning shot to the NCAA was clearly given.

"We asked the NCAA to give everyone five years last year when we filed the Patterson lawsuit. They said no," Ryan Downton told OutKick-FOX News. "Now they’ve done it, but excluded the athletes asking for the change.  It feels like the NCAA is saying, ‘you had a good idea, but we can’t let you enjoy the benefits of it.’ Just like they changed the name. We called it ‘five-for-five.’ They call it ‘age-based eligibility.’  It’s the same thing, but the NCAA tries to pretend it isn’t."

Langston Patterson #10 of the Vanderbilt Commodores sacks Bryson Barnes #16 of the Utah State Aggies during the first half at FirstBank Stadium in Nashville, Tenn., on Sept. 27, 2025. (Getty Images)

I've seen a few public relations' nightmares over the years that involve the NCAA, but this summer has been one for the ages. But, they cannot stop fighting these lawsuits, no matter how many are filed against them.

Why? Well that comes down to the organization actually granting a blanket-waiver themselves, and then having thousands of athletes gain an additional year of eligibility with nowhere to go. The NCAA might not want to admit it, but they are most likely in this for the long haul, though not for the reasons you might think at first.

Lost in the noise surrounding each statement from the NCAA desperately pleading for Congress to pass legislation that would provide some type of antitrust cover that keeps them out of courtrooms, is the fact that if they would have at least 'grandfathered' in the 2022 class with this new eligibility rule, they most certainly would not have their own lawyers racking up frequent-flyer miles on a consistent basis.

TRUMP ADVISOR, EX-NFL PLAYER CODY CAMPBELL WARNS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS FINAL CHANCE TO RESTORE ORDER

"The NCAA is fighting tooth and nail to stop my clients from playing this year. Meanwhile, the NCAA is intensely lobbying Congress to pass the PCSA," plaintiff attorney Ryan Downton told OutKick-FOX News. "The irony is that if the PCSA (Protect College Sports Act) became law today, all of my clients become immediately eligible and get to play this year.

"The NCAA is like a referee who thinks he’s bigger than the game he’s officiating - just do the right thing and get out of the way."

From courtrooms to Zoom hearings that allow attorneys to appear before multiple judges in a single day if needed, much of the current chaos feels entirely self-inflicted. And, that would most likely be the easiest way to comprehend one side of this fight.

Plaintiffs (athletes) are going at the NCAA in multiple courtrooms, in multiple states, arguing that if the new five-and-five rule was being implemented, then athletes who exhausted their clock this past season under the old rule should be granted the same rights that players under the new guidelines are utilizing.

NCAA Rocked By Colorado Judge's 2022 Class Eligibility Ruling That Could Reshape College Sports This Year

And then came U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney of Colorado, who granted a bombshell injunction in the [Wisne v. NCAA] class action lawsuit that has now sent the college athletics world into further chaos. That was filed by former Northern Colorado men's basketball player Brock Wisne.

This meant that athletes across all sports were given a blanket waiver to compete this season, if they had a year of eligibility left to use as part of the 2022 class. These rulings are not just being used in basketball, even if the sport is garnering most of the headlines.

In some states, like Tennessee and Ohio, injunctions granted in those cases will allow players who were plaintiffs in the lawsuits to utilize the transfer portal. But, in the Colorado case, the plaintiffs are not being granted an additional portal window.

"This is one of those situations where the facts really drive a lot of the story," Associate professor at Boise State's College of Business and Economics, Sam Ehrlich told OutKick-FOX News. "The law has already been winning on a lot of these eligibility rule cases, but judges are really resonating with the idea that these players in particular are being put in a bad spot -- having to compete against guys who played five or six years and the players after them getting five.

"It feels fundamentally unfair to judges who look for even treatment, and I think that drives a lot of the legal conclusions too, especially since the legal theories are all about whether the treatment is arbitrary or unfair."

Indiana Hoosiers defensive lineman Stephen Daley (8) during a college football game between the Illinois Fighting Illini and Indiana Hoosiers on Sept. 20, 2025, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

In reality, if the NCAA were to now just give in, and grant blanket waivers on their own, then they'd be admitting fault while also opening the floodgates to thousands of athletes who would be eligible, but have nowhere to play this season.

So, whether they like spending the money and resources or not, the NCAA has to continue fighting these cases in courtrooms across the country.

On Tuesday, Indiana announced that star defensive lineman Stephen Daley, who was injured in a postgame celebration following the 2025 Big Ten championship, was returning for the 2026 season by way of the court ruling in Colorado.

"If it all works out and he can participate and help this football team, then his life could change," Curt Cignetti said about Daley returning. "I know one thing about him, he’ll give it his best shot, he really will, and we’ll just see what happens."

College Football Is Finally Back After Months Of NCAA Lawsuits, NIL Drama And Congressional Fights

That line from Cignetti on how Indiana will 'see what happens' mainly centers around the NCAA appealing the Colorado court's decision.

If the organization is awarded an 'administrative stay', then the injunction would be lifted while proceedings continue and the rules would go back in place, meaning Stephen Daley would be ineligible once again.

But, who's to say the Indiana lineman wouldn’t then file a lawsuit in state court?

The other problem for NCAA officials, and lawyers, is that there is no end in sight. Whether it's athletes suing for an additional year or monetary damages they feel are owed for the organizations misdoings, this is not slowing down any time soon.

And one of the most interesting parts of this entire ordeal centers around the fact that if Congress were to pass the 'Protect College Sports Act', I don't know if there's enough antitrust protection wrapped in this legislation to keep them out of court in the future.

Don't worry though, it will all get sorted out and cooler heads will prevail.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

articles.title: Foster + Partners cleared over man’s death when window fell from London penthouse
articles.excerpt:
Crown court rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breaches

The architecture firm founded by Norman Foster has been clear...
articles.body_text:
Crown court rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breaches

The architecture firm founded by Norman Foster has been cleared over the death of a man killed by a window that fell 90 metres from a newly constructed London penthouse.

Foster + Partners, the practice behind some of the world’s most recognisable buildings such as the Gherkin and revamps of the British Museum and Germany’s Reichstag, were not held to be responsible for the death of Mick Ferris, a 53-year-old coach driver, in 2018.

However, St James, the project managers of the building where the incident took place, and the project’s engineers, Lindner Prater, were found guilty of safety breaches over the death by a jury at Inner London crown court.

Ferris was killed instantly when the 130kg (287lbs) window fell from the penthouse of The Corniche, a luxury tower block development on Albert Embankment, on to the street below.

The court heard that just over a year earlier a window panel had also fallen from the same development. “Miraculously” no one was hurt but no changes were made to the designs as a result of that incident, the court heard.

The prosecution, which was brought by the Health and Safety Executive, said Ferris’s death was foreseeable and the designers had ignored concerns about the proven danger of outward-opening windows.

After more than 11 hours of deliberation the jury cleared Foster + Partners (F+P) and the building’s design engineers, Wintech Ltd. But it found St James and Lindner Prater had failed in their duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

The prosecutor Gordon Menzies told the jury it “wasn’t an accident waiting to happen … it was an accident that had already happened in August 2017. The prosecution say it was an accident waiting to happen again.”

Ferris was killed by the falling window which had been blown off its hinges when the building was almost complete, the court heard. A woman coming towards him, who was pushing a wheelchair, narrowly missed being hit, jurors were told. A restrictor put in place to prevent the window being blown off had been removed, they heard.

The designers had failed to consider the “catastrophic” consequences if something went wrong with this restrictor, the prosecution said. They also failed to take into account the fulcrum effect of an 85cm (33in) window being prised off its hinges, the prosecution said.

Jurors were told that after the first window panel fell from the building the designers failed to use the incident as a reason to “go back to the drawing board”. The jury was told of 12 “missed opportunities” where the designers should have considered the risk of the outward-opening, side-hung windows.

All four defendants denied the charges and claimed they did all that was reasonably practicable to ensure safety.

Menzies told the court: “The wind was sufficiently strong to blow the window open further than 8 and a half inches and the oversailing glass clashed with the frame and, as a result, the hinges were prised off.”

Originally the windows had been designed to open inwards, but the design was changed to avoid them clashing with an internal ceiling coffer containing wires and pipes that they would have cleared, the court was told.

It was only after Ferris’s death that the window design was changed back to inward-opening, the court heard. The prosecution said F+P should have known such risks due to their specialist knowledge of glass-covered buildings including the Gherkin.

Lawyers for F+P said the firm’s role was limited and it was not involved in technical issues. They said it was there to focus on the visual aspects of the design.

A spokesperson for F+P said: “Our thoughts remain with Mr Ferris’s family, as they have since October 2018. We note the court’s decision and are grateful to the jury for the time and care they have taken in considering this matter.”

A spokesperson for Wintech said: “While the court has reached its conclusion, the tragedy of what happened remains. It is vital that we continue to reflect and learn, and as an industry, remain committed to strengthening standards and practices to help prevent such incidents in the future.”

St James and Lindner Prater have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Why $370bn tech group Palantir pays 1.4 percent tax rate: Report
articles.excerpt: Palantir Technologies, the United States data analytics and artificial intelligence company which has contracts with the country’s military and intelligence apparatus, has “engineered its corporate st...
articles.body_text:
Palantir Technologies, the United States data analytics and artificial intelligence company which has contracts with the country’s military and intelligence apparatus, has “engineered its corporate structure” to pay no US federal corporate income tax, according to a new report.

The study by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (CICTAR) comes as Palantir reports soaring revenues, driven partly by government contracts, while it faces continued criticism for providing technology to the Israeli military amid the genocide in Gaza.

Earlier this week, Palantir reported second-quarter revenue of $1.94bn, up 93 percent from a year earlier. But despite its rapid growth, CICTAR said its global effective tax rate was just 1.4 percent in 2025.

CICTAR’s report also identifies what it describes as a pattern of profits arising from contracts in the United Kingdom and Europe being shifted to the company’s US parent company, leaving relatively little taxable profit in the locations where the work is carried out.

In the UK, Palantir recorded a corporate tax charge of about two million pounds ($2.7m) in 2024, despite securing more than 670 million pounds ($900m) in government contracts in recent years.

CICTAR claims its investigation shows that Palantir shifts profits to the US, where earlier losses and tax breaks help it pay little or no federal corporate income tax.

Palantir has also benefitted from tax changes introduced under US President Donald Trump, including the reduction of the federal corporate rate from 35 percent to 21 percent in 2017.

The report does not allege that any of the arrangements identified are illegal. But they have raised ethical questions about whether a company receiving billions of dollars in public contracts worldwide should be able to contribute so little in tax.

A spokesperson for Palantir told the UK’s Guardian newspaper that it fully complies with all tax regimes. “Transfer pricing, which allocates a company’s profits among entities within the Palantir group of companies, is an entirely standard practice that is virtually universal for large multinational companies,” the spokesperson said.

Al Jazeera has contacted Palantir for comment about this story, but has not received a response.

The company was founded in 2003 by a group that included chief executive Alex Karp and billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel. Palantir initially received backing from In-Q-Tel, a nonprofit venture capital fund created in 1999 by the CIA to support high-tech startups developing technology for US intelligence and national security.

Palantir’s market value was around $370bn during early trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, making it one of the world’s biggest 50 publicly listed companies.

Palantir has faced growing controversy over its work with the Trump administration’s immigration authorities, including providing technology used by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency. More than 60 people have died in ICE custody or been shot and killed during federal immigration enforcement operations since Donald Trump returned to office

According to the CICTAR report, Palantir technology enables agencies like ICE and the Department of Homeland Security “to merge vast datasets, including financial, immigration, and health records, without adequate transparency or consent, raising alarms over privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and the rise of the surveillance state”.

Palantir has said it has a “strategic partnership” with Israel. The company opened offices in Israel in 2015.

The CICTAR report states: “There was a ‘surge’ of investment into Israel in response to increased demand for Palantir software following the October 7 attacks, and a major strategic partnership was signed between Palantir and the Israeli Ministry of Defence in [January] 2024 for data analytics and AI.”

Open Intel, a research platform tracking corporate involvement in Israel’s war on Gaza, has found that Palantir has recruited former members of Unit 8200, the Israeli military’s elite cyberintelligence division.

Open Intel has also reported that Palantir’s software can combine intercepted communications, satellite imagery and other intelligence to help Israeli forces produce military targeting lists.

CEO Karp has defended the company’s support for Israel. “I am the most publicly supportive CEO of Israel,” he told CNBC earlier this year, adding: “I think Israel is on the side of good.”

Palantir has also faced scrutiny over its vision for the future of artificial intelligence.

In The Technological Republic, a book co-written by Karp and Palantir executive Nicholas W Zamiska, the pair argue that Silicon Valley has abandoned its responsibility to develop technology that strengthens Western military power alongside advanced AI capabilities.

Some critics have described the philosophy as a form of “techno-fascism”.

Palantir paid no US federal corporate income tax in 2025 and just $2.5m in state income taxes, according to the CICTAR report. It was the third consecutive year in which the company paid no federal corporate income tax in the US.

CICTAR says Palantir has built up more than $3.5bn in deferred tax assets through previous losses, research and development credits and deductions linked to shares awarded to employees. In simple terms, these tax benefits can be used to cancel out tax due on future profits.

The report estimates these could shelter Palantir’s next $16.5bn in profits, allowing it to avoid federal corporate income tax for many years.

Palantir has also benefitted from the 2017 corporate rate changes introduced under Trump.

“The current 21% US federal corporate income tax rate (reduced from 35% in 2017 during the first Trump administration) should have seen Palantir incurring a $348 million US federal income tax expense in 2025. However, it paid zero in US federal income tax and only $2.5 million in US state income taxes,” the report states.

Palantir paid less than $21.7m in income taxes globally in 2025, net of refunds, despite recording pretax profits of $1.66bn.

Its global tax expense was only $22.7m, meaning that both the tax it recorded in its accounts and the cash tax it actually paid amounted to little more than 1 percent of its pretax profit.

Outside the US, its largest disclosed cash tax payments were $5.8m in South Korea and $4.8m in Japan. It paid $2.8m in France, $1.7m in Germany and a combined $4.1m across all its other foreign markets.

The UK, Palantir’s largest market outside the US, was not listed among the countries where it made its largest tax payments, despite generating $427m in revenue there in 2025.

In its UK accounts for 2024, Palantir recorded a corporation tax charge of about 2 million pounds ($2.7m).

CICTAR says its investigations show that Palantir reduces its European taxes by leaving relatively little taxable profit in the countries where its staff operate and its contracts are delivered.

In 2025, 26 percent of Palantir’s revenue was generated outside the US, but only 4 percent of its pretax profit was recorded overseas. By contrast, 96 percent of its profits were booked in the US, where its accumulated tax benefits meant it paid no federal corporate income tax.

In several European countries, local Palantir subsidiaries operate largely as service providers to the US parent. This leaves them with narrow reported profit margins and correspondingly small tax bills.

The CICTAR report states that Palantir’s tax arrangements are particularly significant because much of its rapid growth has been driven by public contracts.

In the US, the company holds multibillion-dollar contracts with government agencies, including the military, intelligence services and immigration authorities. More than half of Palantir’s revenue now comes from government customers, according to the report.

In the UK, Palantir holds at least 670 million pounds ($901m) in government contracts, including a 330 million-pound ($444m) agreement to build the National Health Service (NHS) Federated Data Platform and a 240 million-pound ($323m) Ministry of Defence contract awarded without a competitive tender.

The NHS contract has attracted criticism from health workers and digital rights groups, who have questioned the decision to entrust sensitive patient data to a company that has faced scrutiny over allegations that its technology has been used to aid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Although tax avoidance strategies can be legal and the report does not allege that Palantir has broken the law, CICTAR says Palantir “appears to do everything it can to avoid corporate income tax payments – the backbone of national economic security – which pay for the services it seeks to deliver, and many other essential public services”.

Duncan McCann, tech and data lead at the Good Law Project in the UK, told Al Jazeera the findings were “a slap in the face to ordinary taxpayers and local businesses who play by the rules”.

“It is completely unacceptable that multinational tech giants like Palantir are happy to extract huge profits from the UK market while allegedly exploiting accounting loopholes to dodge their corporate responsibilities,” he said.

Meanwhile, the UK Treasury’s own procurement guidance states that public bodies should not “engage in, or connive at, tax evasion, tax avoidance or tax planning” and should be vigilant not to facilitate tax arrangements that are “detrimental or disadvantageous to the Exchequer”.

Amnesty International has called on the UK government to reconsider Palantir’s government contracts. Both the UK government and NHS England should “cease the purchase of equipment and services from the company” until it can demonstrate it is “not contributing to Israel’s genocide, apartheid, unlawful occupation or other crimes under international law”, Amnesty said.

articles.title: FIFA pays up on overdue prize money after Jordan ‘blackmail’ remark
articles.excerpt: Jordan’s players and staff have received outstanding reward ⁠money for their participation in the 2025 Arab Cup, the Jordan Football Association’s president, Prince Ali bin Hussein, says, two days aft...
articles.body_text:
Jordan’s players and staff have received outstanding reward ⁠money for their participation in the 2025 Arab Cup, the Jordan Football Association’s president, Prince Ali bin Hussein, says, two days after he accused FIFA of ⁠blackmail.

Ali criticised FIFA President Gianni Infantino after he backed out of his proposal to sell a stake in the World Cup and found himself under pressure from confederations and national associations, saying FIFA had offered to help solve the kingdom’s problems in exchange ‌for his endorsement.

One of the problems he listed was that the association had been waiting since December for prize money for reaching the Arab Cup final in Qatar.

“Thank you to the FIFA administration for suddenly this morning delivering what was owed to our players and coaching staff, for the Jordan National team’s accession to the final of the FIFA Arab Cup in Qatar last December,”  Ali said on X on Thursday.

“This was funding that should have ⁠been received eight months ago.”

Ali had alleged FIFA verbally communicated during the World Cup that backing the president “would go a long way to helping our FA out”.

FIFA did not respond to requests for ⁠comment on the allegations.

Ali added that receiving the money was a welcome development but it would not change ⁠the concerns his organisation has about FIFA’s leadership.

“It ⁠is symptomatic of those exact difficulties that we all face and that are usually linked to the FIFA presidential elections,” he added.

“And it does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of FIFA: my ‌FA and I will not endorse President Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”

FIFA apologised to its members for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to ‌sell ‌commercial rights to the World Cup, but the body’s leadership reaffirmed its support for Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday.

Infantino is seeking to extend his decade-long presidency into a fourth and final term in an election scheduled for March.

articles.title: Senate committee set to vote on holding Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Hearing called after the former chief medical advisor invoked the fifth and refused to answer questions at a hearing on Covid-19

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of US politics.

The Senate is ...
articles.body_text:
Hearing called after the former chief medical advisor invoked the fifth and refused to answer questions at a hearing on Covid-19

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of US politics.

The Senate is expected to vote today on whether to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress.

Fauci, a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic, had invoked the fifth amendment and refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19.

The hearing had been called by Republican senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years – and who Fauci accused of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Ahead of the hearing, Paul released what he described as Fauci’s “diary”, in which he described Trump as “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Robert F Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services has also provided a copy of Fauci’s phone to the Republican-led Senate panel. Kennedy had written a conspiratorial book attacking Fauci in 2021 that sold more than a million copies – thanks in part to blurbs from fellow non-scientists Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Alan Dershowitz and Tony Robbins.

Scientists and Democrats have rallied behind Fauci, with a group of 155 scientists signing an open letter calling for the government to stop the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists”.

“This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service,” Gary Peters, a Democratic senator of Michigan, said.

In the Senate today, a vote to hold Anthony Fauci is scheduled for 8.30am ET in the homeland security and governmental affairs committee.

The Republican chair, senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, is hoping the panel’s GOP majority will vote in favor of the resolution, after Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (Niaid), consistently invoked the fifth during a rancorous hearing last week.

However, to guarantee holding Fauci in contempt of Congress, Paul will need 60 votes in the upper chamber before sending a criminal referral to the Department of Justice.

Donald Trump is in Washington today, and will spend most of the day in meetings that are closed to the press. Later, at 7pm ET he’ll hold a reception the Rose Garden for Team USA. We’ll bring you the latest lines as that gets under way.

Wealthy Republicans on the west coast received an emailed invitation in July to an upcoming fundraiser titled “Keep the Senate”. The email, obtained by the Guardian, described the event as a “private roundtable and dinner with the National Republican Senatorial Committee” where donors can pledge $50,000 for seats at the head table, and mingle with legislative heavy hitters from Capitol Hill including the Senator majority leader, John Thune, and Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan with Donald Trump’s endorsement.

One of the organizers listed on the invite was defense industry tycoon Palmer Luckey, the 33-year-old co-founder of sprawling weapons manufacturer Anduril Industries.

The invitation is one of dozens of emails obtained by the Guardian that unravel Luckey’s vast Maga political fundraising over the last seven years.

A longtime GOP donor and activist who spoke on condition he not be identified in order to preserve his political relationships said Luckey is now the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”.

“If you’re raising campaign money in California, you have to go to Palmer Luckey,” he said. “Luckey is the top tier. There are others who are important below him but no one at his level.”

Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, warning that its policies created “a climate of impunity and unbridled violence” that endangers both Palestinians and US citizens.

In a letter seen by the Guardian, a group of 19 Democratic senators and representatives call for the restoration of sanctions against extremist settlers and demand independent US investigations into the deaths of nine US citizens killed in the West Bank since 2022.

The letter, signed by Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren among others, is addressed to Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary.

It argues that Trump’s promise last year that “I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank” has been undermined by events on the ground. “In practice,” the Democrats write, “violent settlers and the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government have proceeded to rapidly extend Israeli control over civilian populations in the region.”

Katie Miller, an erstwhile Trump administration official and wife of Stephen Miller, once relied on Dr Anthony Fauci to get through Covid. Now, she’s calling for his imprisonment – a reversal that illuminates the politicization of Fauci and of public health writ large, a trend that could have major repercussions for America’s preparedness for future crises.

A US Senate committee will vote on Thursday morning over whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the physician and former public health official invoked his fifth amendment rights during a Senate hearing last week focused on Fauci’s actions during the Covid pandemic.

The invocation of the worst days of the Covid pandemic come as midterms loom and the administration struggles to address several infectious outbreaks, including cyclosporiasis and Ebola.

Rand Paul, a senator, released contemporaneous notes that Fauci took during his time in public office, which Paul called Fauci’s diary, that reveal the confusion and fear of the time and illuminate the private episodes of a man who became known as America’s doctor.

“By focusing entirely on one human being and by calling him all sorts of names, including ‘evil’, and by calling for him to be jailed, it abdicates Republicans’ own responsibility in the US response to the pandemic, which was under President Trump,” said Gavin Yamey, director of the Center for Policy Impact in Global Health at Duke University. “I think that this is all aimed at riling up the base ahead of the midterms and at washing their hands of any culpability themselves in the mass death event of Covid.”

And it comes after substantial cuts to the public health infrastructure; misinformation has spread at the highest levels of the government, and growing outbreaks of measles, whooping cough, cyclosporiasis, Ebola, and more.

“This is an extraordinarily good way to distract people from the very deliberate destruction of the US public health system,” Yamey said.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of US politics.

The Senate is expected to vote today on whether to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress.

Fauci, a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic, had invoked the fifth amendment and refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19.

The hearing had been called by Republican senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years – and who Fauci accused of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Ahead of the hearing, Paul released what he described as Fauci’s “diary”, in which he described Trump as “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Robert F Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services has also provided a copy of Fauci’s phone to the Republican-led Senate panel. Kennedy had written a conspiratorial book attacking Fauci in 2021 that sold more than a million copies – thanks in part to blurbs from fellow non-scientists Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Alan Dershowitz and Tony Robbins.

Scientists and Democrats have rallied behind Fauci, with a group of 155 scientists signing an open letter calling for the government to stop the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists”.

“This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service,” Gary Peters, a Democratic senator of Michigan, said.

articles.title: Myanmar leader visits Thailand in bid to bolster international legitimacy
articles.excerpt:
The head of Myanmar’s military-backed government has met Thailand’s prime minister in Bangkok as he seeks to boost his government’s legitimacy more than five years after seizing power.

President Min ...
articles.body_text:
The head of Myanmar’s military-backed government has met Thailand’s prime minister in Bangkok as he seeks to boost his government’s legitimacy more than five years after seizing power.

President Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Thailand’s capital on Thursday, on his first official visit to the country since taking power in a coup in 2021.

Myanmar remains in the midst of a bloody civil war triggered by the coup, which has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED).

During a meeting with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Min Aung Hlaing stressed that Myanmar’s military-backed government was focused on ending the civil war and restoring peace to the resource-rich country.

“Myanmar has now reestablished itself on the path to democracy and is moving toward a better future,” Min Aung Hlaing said. “As the new government, we have now begun working on national stability, peace, and national reconciliation.”

Min Aung Hlaing is pushing for Myanmar to be readmitted to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), from which his government was barred after failing to implement a peace plan agreed with member states in 2021.

Thailand is one of Myanmar’s top foreign investors and has called for a “calibrated re-engagement approach” with its neighbour, with which it shares a 2,400km (1500-mile) border.

Following the meeting, the two leaders delivered speeches at the Thailand-Myanmar Business Forum.

Anutin said Thailand and Myanmar are ready to “step into the new chapter of economic cooperation that is built upon mutual trust and benefit for the people of the two countries”.

Min Aung Hlaing told attendees they could “invest with confidence” in Myanmar’s energy, agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare, technology and other sectors.

The visit has drawn criticism from activist groups such as Justice For Myanmar, which stated that the trip lends “false legitimacy” to Min Aung Hlaing and the ruling generals.

About a dozen demonstrators gathered outside the United Nations regional headquarters in Bangkok to oppose the visit. Some protesters could be seen holding placards denouncing him as a “criminal” who was not welcome in Thailand.

Min Aung Hlaing was sworn in as president of Myanmar in April following an election that UN experts dismissed as a “sham”.

Western governments have shunned and sanctioned Min Aung Hlaing and his associates for overthrowing Aung San Suu Kyi’s government. Subsequent serious rights violations followed a deadly military crackdown on protests, which subsequently triggered a nationwide armed resistance movement and a bloody civil war.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who was overthrown in 2021 and remains under house arrest, was allowed to meet a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) on Monday.

Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris welcomed the development but cautioned that he has not yet received independent confirmation of his mother’s condition or wellbeing.

Critics say the visit was a government stunt as it tries to rehabilitate its image.

articles.title: Firefighters start to contain Washington state wildfires as tens of thousands remain displaced
articles.excerpt:
Fires have destroyed about 850 buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate since they erupted last weekend

Firefighters have taken advantage of cooler weather to begin getting a handle on wi...
articles.body_text:
Fires have destroyed about 850 buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate since they erupted last weekend

Firefighters have taken advantage of cooler weather to begin getting a handle on wildfires that have displaced tens of thousands of people around Washington state’s second-largest city, but hotter, drier and breezier days lie ahead.

Officials reported Wednesday that firefighters had established containment lines around the perimeters of all three fires affecting Spokane and that they were focused on reinforcing those lines. Temperatures were expected to climb from the 80sF the past two days into the upper 90sF (36C), with less humidity, late this week.

The fires – one of which authorities say was deliberately set by a man who was arrested and charged with arson – have destroyed about 850 buildings and forced the evacuation of about 67,000 people since they erupted last weekend. Damage assessment crews have yet to tally exactly how many houses have been lost or damaged. No deaths have been reported.

The other two fires were also started by people, though not necessarily deliberately, investigators have said. They remain under investigation. Those fires, the Autumn Lane and Fairview fires, started independently of the arson-caused Old Trails Fire, they said.

Spokane county’s sheriff, John Nowels, said during a Wednesday news conference that the evacuation zones will remain in place due to incoming weather and fire danger.

“We are not going to be downgrading these zones in any large way for many, many more days to come,” he said. “If we let people back in and we don’t have a high degree of certainty the fire lines will hold, we will put people in danger.”

Many evacuees remained in a shelter set up in a Spokane convention center, at hotels or rentals, or at the homes of friends or relatives, with no idea of how soon they might go back – if they have a house to return to.

The fires were among dozens across the western US that have stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them.

In Washington, there are 16 uncontained wildfires burning more than 672 sq miles (1,740 sq km) and being fought by more than 7,000 fire personnel, said Thomas Kyle-Milward, a spokesperson for the Washington department of natural resources.

“We’re looking down the barrel at one of the worst fire seasons in state history,” he said.

The man charged with starting the Old Trails Fire, Aaron F Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was expected to be arraigned Thursday. According to court documents, he was arrested after a resident reported him being in the area where the fire began. He denied having started it when questioned by deputies.

Authorities said they previously contacted him during two fire investigations last year, including one in a state park that prompted evacuation notices, though he wasn’t charged in either.

In California, authorities said Wednesday that they arrested a 65-year-old man on suspicion of sparking a major wildfire by recklessly operating equipment without complying with state fire prevention requirements. Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges. The blaze that erupted Monday had scorched nearly 15 sq miles (39 sq km) of forest in Calaveras county, south-east of Sacramento.

articles.title: The 8 healthiest beans you should be eating more often, according to nutrition expert
articles.excerpt:
TikTok user Koya Simpson says eating two cans of beans a day has curbed her appetite, eased anxiety and boosted her workouts and mood.

Beans and legumes are affordable, protein-packed and health-prom...
articles.body_text:
TikTok user Koya Simpson says eating two cans of beans a day has curbed her appetite, eased anxiety and boosted her workouts and mood.

Beans and legumes are affordable, protein-packed and health-promoting foods that deserve a more prominent place on your plate, health experts say.

"Fewer than 14% of American adults eat beans on a given day, and that's a problem, because they're some of the most nutrient-dense foods you can buy," New York City-based nutrition and wellness expert Samantha Cassetty, founder of Sam's Plate and co-author of "Sugar Shock," told Fox News Digital. "They deliver protein, fiber and slow-burning carbs for steady energy, plus folate, magnesium, iron and other essential nutrients."

Beans are also naturally cholesterol-free and contain no saturated fats, registered dietitian nutritionist Deborah Murphy told Food & Wine.

CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT

Studies have linked regular bean consumption with a lower risk of chronic diseases, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity, which may contribute to a longer life expectancy.

"In a moment when everyone's chasing protein and grocery bills are climbing, canned beans are one of the cheapest proteins on the shelf," Cassetty said. "The best part is that you can open a can, rinse, drain and call it dinner prep."

Beans are affordable, protein-packed and have been linked to a lower risk of chronic diseases, health experts say. (iStock)

Some beans and legumes stand out for their health benefits.

Black beans are prized for their protein, fiber and antioxidants, Cassetty told Fox News Digital. They contain about 8 grams of protein and 8 grams of fiber per 1/2-cup serving.

One of Cassetty's go-to salads incorporates black beans, corn (frozen and canned work as well as fresh, she said), diced bell pepper, avocado, cherry tomatoes and a spoonful of salsa. She said it can be enjoyed as "a light meal, hearty side or wrap filling."

Black beans are a good source of protein, fiber and antioxidants, according to health experts. (iStock)

Technically a legume – the broader plant family beans belong to – chickpeas are versatile because they work in sweet and savory dishes alike, Cassetty said.

"Air-fry them for a crunchy snack or salad topper," she advised.

"They're also great scattered over roasted veggies and grain bowls. Research shows people who eat chickpeas and hummus regularly have higher intakes of fiber, folate, potassium and iron than people who don't, and better overall diet quality scores."

Lentils are also legumes and offer a "ground-meat texture and a solid dose of plant-based iron," Cassetty said.

She recommended mixing them with chopped walnuts (Cassetty is a partner with the California Walnut Board) for extra fiber, protein and plant-based omega-3s.

Chickpeas, edamame and other legumes are easily incorporated into other dishes to add nutrients, a nutrition expert said. (iStock)

"That combo of beans and walnuts is powerful, supporting heart, brain and gut health in each bite. Use the crumble in spaghetti sauce, tacos or wraps."

Edamame are immature soybeans that people typically boil or steam and eat as a snack or appetizer with coarse salt. They're also used in many dishes.

"Frozen edamame is a freezer staple in my house," Cassetty said. "A 1/2 cup delivers about 9 grams of protein and 4 grams of fiber. Toss it with cucumber, brown rice, rice vinegar, tamari and sesame oil for a five-minute meal."

White beans also pack a powerful protein punch, with about 9 grams of the essential nutrient per 1/2 cup.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"I stir them into tuna and egg salad, but my favorite trick is blending leftovers into a smoothie," Cassetty said. "You won't notice next to the sweetness of the fruit, but they add the creamiest texture, plus protein and fiber."

Pinto beans may have "a special edge on cholesterol," Cassetty said.

While the soluble fiber in all beans helps clear cholesterol from the bloodstream, animal research suggests they may lower cholesterol synthesis in the liver and cholesterol absorption in the small intestine, Cassetty said.

Pinto beans may be especially powerful at stamping out inflammation from a high-fat diet, research suggests. (iStock)

"In one trial, a half cup of pinto beans a day dropped total and LDL cholesterol by more than 8%, outperforming oatmeal," she said.

If you're planning to eat a high-fat meal – think a bacon cheeseburger with onion rings – you may want to find a way to incorporate kidney beans in the mix.

Animal research suggests kidney beans can favorably shift gut bacteria and reduce inflammatory markers associated with a high-fat diet, Cassetty noted. She advised using them in chili or over nachos, or trying them in a three-bean salad with some roughly chopped toasted walnuts for crunch and added nutritional value.

Black-eyed peas deserve "a permanent spot in your bean rotation," a wellness expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)

The protein, fiber and iron in black-eyed peas mean they deserve "a permanent spot in your bean rotation," Cassetty said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

They're also "the unsung hero of cowboy caviar," a cold bean salad that also uses fresh vegetables, herbs and vinaigrette dressing and is typically served with tortilla chips, she said.

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Thomas Rhett reveals why he and wife Lauren reject celebrity perks for country life
articles.excerpt:
The country music singer told Fox News Digital that is the one piece of marriage advice she's received that has actually worked.

Thomas Rhett admitted this week that his wife didn’t think he was goin...
articles.body_text:
The country music singer told Fox News Digital that is the one piece of marriage advice she's received that has actually worked.

Thomas Rhett admitted this week that his wife didn’t think he was going to become a famous country singer.

"We've definitely had our fair share of ups and downs, ‘cause I think that Lauren really… she craves simplicity, at all costs, simplicity," the country singer said on the "Girls In Low Places" podcast on Sunday, clarifying that she believed he was talented, but knew that stardom was rare.

"She grew up, you know, real country, and her and her daddy would lay in the street at night and look at the stars," noting that "he would just call out different constellations and stuff like ‘That's a satellite and that's this.’"

He explained that was how she saw her life, calling it "a real suburban neighborhood thing."

Rhett said he and Lauren Akins have known each other since they were in first grade, and they briefly dated in high school before reconnecting after she graduated from college.

MARCUS MUMFORD SAYS BIBLE CAMP SPARKED DECADES-LONG LOVE STORY WITH WIFE CAREY MULLIGAN

Thomas Rhett said his wife, Lauren Akins, has always wanted a simple life. (Getty Images for CMA)

Admitting "there’s nothing normal" about fame, noting that it affects everyone.

"There's just so many crazy things that come with being famous," he said, giving the example of getting to cut lines, which he said he refuses to do.

"I think that's why so many people try to just live their life in search of such normalcy and I think my wife obviously has wanted that her whole life, and we do live very simply," the "Die a Happy Man" singer said. "But it took me a minute."

HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE

He said his career "really started to pop" around 2017 to 2019.

"I don't think I let it get to my head, but I do think I got really used to it," the 36-year-old admitted. "In probably not the best way."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Rhett admitted he has to actively focus on not letting fame get him, because "when you walk on stage in front of, you know, 10,000 people, that's like a rush that you can't like go replicate. You know what I'm saying? Like you can't just go like play flag football with your friends and think that's going to entice the same feeling."

For that reason, he has a difficult time "being content in simple situations because I think there's no super high going on."

COUNTRY STAR RILEY GREEN REVEALS WHY FAN EMOTION AT HIS SHOWS BEATS INDUSTRY AWARDS EVERY TIME

That’s forced him to "get really good" at being quiet, which he says doesn't come naturally to him.

Rhett and Akins married in 2012. (Jeff Kravitz/Getty Images for CMT)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Hearing people singing his songs while he’s performing on stage has always seemed surreal, but the one that "gets" him is witnessing people cry when they meet him "because I don't see myself that way. Period."

TYLER HUBBARD STAYS CALM AS WIFE PULLS FISH HOOK FROM HIS SCALP ON FAMILY CAMPING VACATION

"And I have, you know, definitely five kids that definitely don't see me that way," he joked.

The couple share, Willa, 10; Ada, who turns 9 on Aug. 12; Lennon, 6; Lillie, 4; and Brave, who was born in February.

He admitted trying to be "super dad" and taking his kids to school while he’s in the middle of doing late-night concerts can also be exhausting.

Later, in the podcast, when asked what marriage advice he would give, Rhett said, "Don’t forget to continue to date your wife."

Rhett and Akins share five children together. (Getty Images)

JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS

"It gets so much harder when you have children to make time for each other because there's so many other bodies that need your full-time assistance," he explained.

The singer said he and his wife recently spent two days just the two of them in London before joining friends in the Cotswolds, noting that "you feel sad, and your kids are like ‘Why are you leaving?' And you're like, ‘Because we want to stay married!’" he joked.

Earlier this year, he admitted during his years of early fame he felt like he was "living a double life," adding that it almost ruined his marriage.

"I look through my life and I think about all the things that have kind of twisted me or made me like not the best person to be around, and it has always been either around affirmation or lack of affirmation," the country star told Sadie Robertson Huff on her "WHOA That’s Good" podcast.

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Appearing on the podcast with his wife, Rhett said that at the height of his fame, he experienced "the most affirmation I think I'd ever received in my life. And I really liked it."

But he admitted that he didn’t feel he handled his marriage very well at the time.

Thomas Rhett performs during a show in Nashville last month. (Getty Images)

"I look back at our life during that time, and I'm not — I don't think I stewarded it very well, to be honest with you," he said.

Rhett, who is Christian, said publicly he kept up a façade of spirituality, "but internally I was dying. Like I genuinely, I just liked what was happening so much that I think so much of me was being sucked into the world so hard that it just kept pushing me and her like this," he said, moving his hands away from each other.

CLINT BLACK AND LISA HARTMAN BLACK'S ONE RULE THAT HAS KEPT THEIR MARRIAGE STRONG FOR NEARLY 35 YEARS

Rhett noted that he and his wife said from "day one, divorce is not an option," but "the more you actually think about it, anything is actually an option if you let it become that."

It wasn’t until 2020 that he "actually discovered bits and pieces of who I actually was at my core, without a microphone, without a stage with and without affirmation, because it was the first time it had ever been taken away from me, if that makes any sense," Rhett explained, referring to the pandemic.

"I’m not perfect," he continued. "I'll never be perfect, but I would say, like today, us looking at each other and being a married couple, I would say this is… I'm living my most true self now."

He pointed to his wife and added, "She always sort of has been."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military base
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops

Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which was set up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, has fi...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops

Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which was set up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, has finally issued its first construction contract in the devastated territory: a project to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian.

The contract, which has not yet been finalised, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based firm that has previously carried out work with the US government in countries such as Iraq.

The Board of Peace is chaired by the US president and led by a team that includes his son-in-law Jared Kushner and friend Steve Witkoff.

In an email, a Board of Peace official said the board and a group of Palestinian technocrats installed to oversee Gaza “are in the final stages of preparing several contract awards. None have been finalised.” The Palestinian group is known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.

The official said “one prospective contract concerns facilities to support the international stabilisation force (ISF), which will assist in implementing the roadmap’s security and governance arrangements”.

They added: “This contract will be one of many that are essential for the future of Gaza.”

The award comes just days after Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm, though there are considerable questions about how the group would give up its guns. Israel has opposed the plan, and increased airstrikes in Gaza after Trump’s announcement.

The Guardian reported in July that the board’s original Gaza reconstruction had shrunk dramatically from an ambitious blueprint to rebuild the whole territory to a small pilot project in the south of the strip.

The base now being planned is just 100 metres by 120 metres and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the source said. It would lie in the 60% of Gaza’s territory that the Israeli army directly controls. Israeli forces have also created a buffer zone beyond that area.

The source said the base was about a mile from the Israeli border and would have a “quick extraction route” in case the small force came under attack.

The UN resolution authorising the Board of Peace had approved establishing an “international stabilisation force” for Gaza, and there have been varying reports on which country would provide these troops. Morocco has promised a small contingent, but the legal framework for the ISF has yet to be finalised, and it is not clear when the deployment would begin.

In earlier contract plans seen by the Guardian, the 150-person base was the first phase of a plan to build a 5,000-person military base in Gaza for the ISF.

This base would have included “vehicle fighting positions” and a perimeter berm – or raised defensive bank – and would have rudimentary facilities suitable for short-term deployments. The earlier contract said the first phase would consist of “tents and cots for forces to sleep, as well as chemical toilets and handwashing stations. At this phase, this is what we would consider habitable.”

Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would “take over” and “own” Gaza, although the agreement that set up the Board of Peace fell short of that.

At the board’s first meeting in January, Kushner unveiled a “master plan” to build “New Gaza” with an expansive waterfront city with gleaming mixed-use towers. “It could be a hope, it could be a destination. A lot of industry,” he said.

At least 80% of Gaza’s buildings were damaged or destroyed in the war. Ten months after the ceasefire, most of the territory’s 2 million people are still living in makeshift and unsanitary camps.

articles.title: Eyewitness describes suspicious encounter that helped launch Washington wildfire arson probe
articles.excerpt: A Spokane arson suspect making his first court appearance in connection with the fires. Local CEO Brandon Schmidt joins to recount his evacuation efforts and describe the devastating impact of the fir...
articles.body_text:
A Spokane arson suspect making his first court appearance in connection with the fires. Local CEO Brandon Schmidt joins to recount his evacuation efforts and describe the devastating impact of the fires on the community.

A Washington grandfather said a stranger lingering near a dead-end road where almost nobody goes immediately caught his attention – moments before smoke began rising from the same stretch of railroad tracks and a devastating wildfire erupted.

Paul Child was driving his grandson to pick up a friend Saturday when he noticed a bald man standing near the railroad tracks along West Euclid Road and staring into the tree line.

"I really didn’t think anything of it at that point," Child told Fox News Digital.

SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH

About 10 minutes later, Child drove back along the same road and noticed the man was still there.

Aaron F. Farinacci was arrested on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire in eastern Washington. (Arizona Department of Corrections)

"This time he was kind of bent over and looked like he was doing something in the brush or the bushes and the grass and the trees," Child said. "When he saw us, then he kind of stood up and was acting kind of nervous."

Even Child’s grandson sensed something was off.

"My grandson said, ‘What’s he doing?’" Child said.

The family returned to their home and minutes later, Child’s daughter, Ana Dillon, glanced toward the same stretch of railroad tracks.

"I just happened to look up and saw a huge cloud of white smoke, then black smoke," Dillon told Fox News Digital.

Child immediately connected the smoke to the stranger he had seen lingering near the tree line.

Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged with first-degree arson. (Spokane County Sheriff’s Office)

"The first thing I thought was, ‘That SOB started the fire,’" Child alleged.

MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE

Child called 911 and tried to reach the only other homeowner on the dead-end stretch of road. The neighbor was not home, but Child reached him by phone and warned that a wildfire was moving toward the property, where workers were inside a shop behind the house.

"We drove down there and notified that person and told him maybe he should leave," Child said.

By then, firefighters had begun to arrive as flames spread across the dry grasslands and the family hurried to evacuate.

Heavy smoke blankets the Spokane area as firefighters battle several fast-moving wildfires that have forced thousands of evacuations and prompted a massive emergency response. (Spokane Valley Fire Department)

"The fire was coming toward us, so we packed up everything, everyone and animals," Dillon said.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Child said the family fled their nearly 17-acre property with five dogs and two cats, later flagging down an Airway Heights police officer and describing the man he had seen as a bald white male wearing a green T-shirt and backpack, court records show.

He also told officers where the man had been standing before smoke began rising from the area. Spokane County sheriff’s deputies soon detained a man matching the description.

Child, his grandson and the grandson’s friend then traveled with an Airway Heights police officer to where deputies were holding the suspect. Sitting inside Child’s pickup about 50 yards away, the three watched as deputies removed the man from a patrol vehicle and had him face them.

Chimneys are the only structures remaining in a residential neighborhood after a wildfire hit the northern part of Spokane, Washington, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (AP Photo / Lindsey Wasson)

"The only thing I could really identify on him was his build and what he was wearing," Child said. "There was no question in any of our minds that was the individual we saw."

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT DISPLAYED 'INCEL ENERGY,' MADE WOMAN UNCOMFORTABLE DURING UBER RIDE: PASSENGER

Authorities later arrested Aaron F. Farinacci on suspicion of first-degree arson, accusing him of intentionally setting the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three wildfires that destroyed hundreds of buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate.

Child said the family did not learn until the following day that deputies had initially released Farinacci before arresting him after investigators developed additional evidence.

Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Farinacci was previously charged with first-degree murder after fatally shooting his father during an argument in Arizona in 2010. He later pleaded guilty to reduced charges of manslaughter and aggravated assault, served about eight years in prison and was released in 2020.

Learning about Farinacci’s criminal history turned the family’s initial relief into concern, Child said.

"He knew where I lived," Child said. "Then to come to find out what his history was, it’s kind of like ... this dude could have come back down here."

Firefighters respond to a wildfire near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)

Child said the man initially caught his attention because strangers rarely venture onto the family’s road. The county permanently closed the dead-end stretch several years ago, leaving only two homes beyond the barricade.

"There hasn’t been a lot of trespassing now," Child said. "If we see somebody down there, a lot of times we take it upon ourselves to pull up and say, ‘Are you OK?’ ... Nine times out of 10, they’re gone after that."

Dillon said anyone lingering near the tracks would immediately stand out to the family.

"There’s only two houses on this street," she said. "If anyone is on this street, we most always call Crime Check. No one should be on this road. It’s a closed road. Anyone standing and kneeling down by the train tracks that’s not a city worker is a red flag."

While Child’s observations helped point investigators toward a suspect, retired Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives executive Scott Sweetow said eyewitness accounts are only the beginning of a wildfire arson investigation.

Allen Sather stands in front of his 1968 Chevrolet C20 at the duplex he rented on West Indian Trail Road that burned in a wildfire in Spokane, Washington, Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026. (AP Photo / Young Kwak)

Fire investigators must first determine where a blaze started before they can establish how it ignited, Sweetow told Fox News Digital. That requires them to work backward from the aftermath, examine how the terrain and vegetation burned and eliminate plausible accidental causes.

"Arson fire in general is very hard to investigate," Sweetow said. "It requires a very meticulous focused effort that is not present in a lot of other investigations. And what complicates it is the fact that the evidence that you have to examine is often badly damaged by fire."

WHAT HAPPENED TO LEAVING THE GROOM AT THE ALTAR LIKE AN ADULT? BRIDE-TO-BE ACCUSED OF SETTING FIRE TO CHURCH

Investigators can reconstruct a fire’s earliest moments using witness accounts, video, cellphone data, first-responder observations and physical evidence. They also examine potential causes such as lightning, power infrastructure, trains, discarded smoking materials or other ignition sources.

That process can allow investigators to determine that a person started a fire even when no single item definitively establishes how it began, Sweetow said.

An otherworldly scene in Spokane, Washington, as wildfires rage on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue)

"It’s not magic. The grass doesn’t just burst into flame for no reason," Sweetow said. "So by eliminating all the causes that weren’t you figure out the cause that was, if that makes sense."

Sweetow cautioned against placing too much weight on any single piece of evidence, including investigators’ claim that Farinacci was carrying waterproof matches and a butane lighter when deputies first contacted him.

He said windproof and waterproof matches are more specialized than ordinary paper or wooden matches and are designed to remain lit in conditions that could extinguish a conventional match. Investigators would likely look for remnants of the same type of match near the fire’s point of origin, he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

A Moses Lake Fire Department firefighter works to extinguish hotspots at a home destroyed in the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 5, 2026, in Spokane, Washington. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

"They’re very expensive. And they’re designed really almost like a little portable flare," Sweetow said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

The matches and lighter would still need to be considered alongside witness statements, physical evidence, electronic records and forensic findings. Sweetow said wildfire arson cases often depend on the combined weight of numerous facts rather than one decisive piece of evidence.

He also said the decision to release Farinacci before arresting him after further investigation was not inherently unusual, particularly in a fast-moving emergency in which deputies were focused on evacuations and investigators had not yet completed their work.

A burned home smolders during the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington on Aug. 4, 2026. (Josh Edelson / AFP via Getty Images)

"I wouldn’t say it’s particularly unusual, it just seems like good police and investigator work to put the case together," Sweetow said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Court records show fire investigators later concluded the blaze originated where Child reported seeing the man. They ruled out trains and nearby electrical infrastructure before determining the fire was consistent with dry grass being ignited by an open flame from a match or lighter.

For Child, the investigation has been about the people whose homes and property were destroyed.

"My heart goes out to everybody," he said. "Hopefully the individual that caused all their pain and suffering is going to be held accountable for those actions."

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Students using AI to cheat will face stricter rules, says Danish government
articles.excerpt:
Teenagers must make oral defence of essays and schools will monitor computers during exams under crackdown

Danish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI chea...
articles.body_text:
Teenagers must make oral defence of essays and schools will monitor computers during exams under crackdown

Danish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced.

Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known in Denmark as gymnasiet) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home.

The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action.

“Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.”

AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it.

The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector.

Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”.

The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known as større skriftlige opgave or SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this.

Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching.

The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”.

The ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene.

In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April.

Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. It risks affecting grades that should reflect students’ knowledge and in the long term, students are not actually learning what they should.”

articles.title: Eric Adams battles tense crowd as Wisconsin audience erupts over AI data center proposal
articles.excerpt:
Former New York City Mayor Eric Adams condemns Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s threat to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on ‘The Story.’

Former New York City Mayor Eric Adams struggled to get...
articles.body_text:
Former New York City Mayor Eric Adams condemns Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s threat to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on ‘The Story.’

Former New York City Mayor Eric Adams struggled to get a word in as a Wisconsin audience bombarded him with boos and insults while he pitched the crowd on a proposed AI data center.

Adams was told he belongs "in prison" amid a barrage of fierce heckles during a wild eight-minute exchange that showed residents repeatedly interrupting the former mayor over his support for the proposed data center.

"You belong in prison!" one crowd member shouted, seemingly referencing Adams’ dismissed federal corruption case.

TEXAS GOV GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

Eric Adams, mayor of New York, listens during a House Oversight and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, March 5, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Since leaving office, Adams has worked as a "pitchman" for several real estate-related technology companies, according to The Real Deal. He said he closes about 80% of the deals he pursues.

Adams appeared at the Wisconsin meeting on behalf of PNK Group, which is looking to develop a 209-acre data center at a former paper mill along the Wisconsin River.

"Whether we like it or not, folks, data centers are going to be here," Adams told the audience.

Many Wisconsin residents in the crowd opposed the proposal and let Adams know it throughout his presentation.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

"You’re here to steal our water!" one resident shouted.

As data centers expand across the country, communities are weighing new job opportunities against concerns over power, water and local impact. (Meta)

"Get out of here!" another resident shrieked.

"Put it in your backyard!," yet another said.

"Anyone can heckle, but not everybody can communicate," Adams said in response.

Adams offered to answer questions about the data center and engage in what he called a "dialogue."

The former NYC mayor urged the crowd to stop the "hate on technology," defending his stance with a personal anecdote, in which he said AI helped his doctor in his Type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

The audience, again, erupted in a loud chant of boos.

New York City Mayor Eric Adams speaks during a press conference at City Hall in Manhattan in New York City, March 24, 2025.  (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)

Adams attempted to regain the stage and tame the angry crowd. And although one audience member came to his defense, saying, "Let him talk!," he struggled to speak over the crowd of critics.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Adams’ chief communications officer Todd Shapiro said Hell Gate, which first reported the story, got the facts "wrong."

"A short video clip cannot accurately portray an event that lasted much longer," Shapiro wrote in part. "It omits the many attendees who approached Mayor Adams afterward to thank him, ask questions, and express appreciation for his willingness to engage directly with the community."

Shapiro also said Adams' support in proposing the Wisconsin data center is "helping communities better understand the economic opportunities that responsible AI and data center development can bring."

"Eric Adams has consistently supported policies that encourage responsible investment, create good-paying jobs, strengthen local tax bases, and position American communities to compete in the industries of the future," Shapiro told Fox Digital.

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.
